concept.question: How does the federal government identify, measure, time, classify, and collect a person’s income tax?

pillars.title: What belongs in the base?
pillars.description: §61 gross income, exclusions, deductions, AGI and taxable income

pillars.title: How much tax is charged?
pillars.description: Brackets, marginal vs average rates, deductions vs credits

pillars.title: What character/rate applies?
pillars.description: Ordinary income, capital gain, losses, and conversion

pillars.title: Who pays the tax?
pillars.description: Individuals, sole proprietors, partnerships, LLCs, S and C corporations

pillars.title: How is law enforced?
pillars.description: Sources, self-assessment, audits, litigation and penalties

concept.courseCoverage: Chapter 1 complete from user-provided pp. 1–33; chapters beyond it still pending.

syllabus.title: Capital Gains, Filing Status & Earned Income Credit

formulas.title: Taxable-income pipeline
formulas.formula: Gross income − above-line deductions = AGI; AGI − applicable below-line deductions = taxable income
formulas.meaning: Gross income inclusions/exclusions are determined first. Above-line amounts depend on §62; below-line amounts depend on §63 and other rules.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Classify receipts under §61 and statutory exclusions to obtain gross income. Step 2: Subtract deductions allowed under §62 (above AGI) to compute AGI. Step 3: Identify allowed standard or itemized deductions under §63 and other relevant deductions/adjustments to compute taxable income. Step 4: Apply marginal rates to taxable income. Step 5: Reduce preliminary tax by eligible credits and subtract withholding/estimated payments. This is the structural sequence from pp. 11–16; no universal dollar deduction applies to every taxpayer.
formulas.source: Class 1, Bankman et al. (19th ed.), syllabus-assigned Ch. 1 printed pp. 11–15

formulas.title: Gross profit from inventory
formulas.formula: Gross profit = sales receipts − cost of goods sold
formulas.meaning: COGS is recovered in measuring gross income from inventory sales.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Sell two hammers at $20 each → gross receipts = 2 × $20 = $40. Step 2: Their purchase cost is $12 each → cost of goods sold = 2 × $12 = $24. Step 3: Gross profit from inventory sales = $40 − $24 = $16. The $40 of cash receipts is not itself the $16 gross income from these inventory sales.
formulas.source: Class 1, Bankman et al. (19th ed.), syllabus-assigned Ch. 1 printed pp. 12–13

formulas.title: Deduction tax saving
formulas.formula: Approximate tax saving = usable deduction × marginal tax rate
formulas.meaning: This shortcut assumes deduction is fully allowed and does not cross brackets or affect phaseouts.
formulas.worked: Historical casebook assumptions only: Step 1: Single taxpayer has $13,000 of potentially qualifying mortgage interest and a $12,950 standard deduction. Step 2: Incremental itemized amount over the standard deduction is $13,000 − $12,950 = $50, assuming no other itemized deductions. Step 3: At an illustrative 33% marginal rate, additional savings = $50 × .33 = $16.50. For an actual 2026 return, use 2026 statutory amounts, eligibility and itemizing rules instead.
formulas.source: Class 1, Bankman et al. (19th ed.), syllabus-assigned Ch. 1 printed pp. 14–16

formulas.title: Tax credit offset
formulas.formula: Tax after nonrefundable credit = max(0, preliminary tax − usable credit)
formulas.meaning: Refundable credits can exceed liability and generate a refund; nonrefundable credits generally cannot.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Consider a taxpayer with at least $100 tax liability. Step 2: A fully usable $100 nonrefundable credit reduces that liability directly by $100. Step 3: A $100 deduction at a hypothetical 37% marginal bracket generally saves only $100 × .37 = $37. Step 4: A refundable credit may yield a refund beyond tax liability, subject to its own law.
formulas.source: Class 1, Bankman et al. (19th ed.), syllabus-assigned Ch. 1 printed pp. 15–16

formulas.title: Average tax rate
formulas.formula: Average tax rate = tax liability ÷ specified measure of income
formulas.meaning: Specify taxable income versus economic income; negative liabilities possible with refundable credits.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Under the casebook's hypothetical brackets, tax on $60,000 is $50,000 × .20 + $10,000 × .40 = $14,000. Step 2: Divide tax by taxable income: $14,000 ÷ $60,000 = 0.2333 = 23.33% average statutory rate. Step 3: The marginal rate on the next dollar is 40%. Be clear whether an effective-rate question uses taxable income or a broader economic-income denominator.
formulas.source: Class 1, Bankman et al. (19th ed.), syllabus-assigned Ch. 1 printed pp. 16–18

formulas.title: Layered marginal bracket
formulas.formula: Total tax = Σ (income in each bracket × its rate)
formulas.meaning: A higher bracket applies only to the slice of taxable income falling in it.
formulas.worked: These are invented sample rates in the casebook, not 2026 federal brackets. Step 1: First $50,000 × 20% = $10,000. Step 2: Remaining $10,000 (if taxable income is $60,000) × 40% = $4,000. Step 3: Total tax = $14,000. If income rises from $50,000 to $50,010, tax = $10,000 + ($10 × .40) = $10,004, not $50,010 × 40%.
formulas.source: Class 1, Bankman et al. (19th ed.), syllabus-assigned Ch. 1 printed pp. 16–17

formulas.title: After-tax marginal earnings
formulas.formula: After-tax extra earnings ≈ extra pay × (1 − marginal rate)
formulas.meaning: Assumes extra amount remains within relevant bracket and excludes other taxes/phaseouts.
formulas.worked: Under the book's simplified 25% marginal-rate assumption: Step 1: Additional weekend earnings = $10,000. Step 2: Income tax on those extra earnings = $10,000 × 25% = $2,500. Step 3: After-tax additional pay = $10,000 − $2,500 = $7,500. Ignore other taxes, benefit phaseouts and bracket changes for this textbook hypothetical.
formulas.source: Class 1, Bankman et al. (19th ed.), syllabus-assigned Ch. 1 printed pp. 18–19

formulas.title: Tax gross-up of charitable cost
formulas.formula: Net cash cost of usable deduction ≈ gift − gift × marginal rate
formulas.meaning: Only applies when deductible and incrementally useful.
formulas.worked: The book's charitable-gift illustration assumes full incremental deductibility. Step 1: At 15% marginal tax, savings on a $1,000 gift = $150; net after-tax cost = $1,000 − $150 = $850. Step 2: At 30%, savings = $300; net cost = $700. Step 3: If the deduction does not exceed the taxpayer's standard deduction or other constraints apply, the marginal savings can be smaller or zero.
formulas.source: Class 1, Bankman et al. (19th ed.), syllabus-assigned Ch. 1 printed pp. 18

formulas.title: Adjusted basis
formulas.formula: Adjusted basis = initial basis + capital improvements − prior basis reductions
formulas.meaning: General conceptual expression; include depreciation and other adjustments under the Code.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Begin with historical cost basis, usually acquisition cost. Step 2: Add capital investments or improvements: initial $100 + qualifying $20 improvement = $120. Step 3: Deduct relevant depreciation/basis reductions: if $5 applies, adjusted basis = $115. Step 4: If sale proceeds are $150, potential realized gain = $150 − $115 = $35. This is a newly worked illustration of the book's §§1012/1016 concepts, not a quotation of a numerical fact pattern.
formulas.source: Class 1, Bankman et al. (19th ed.), syllabus-assigned Ch. 1 printed pp. 21–22

formulas.title: Realized gain or loss
formulas.formula: Realized gain/loss = amount realized − adjusted basis
formulas.meaning: Recognition of realized gain may be delayed or excluded under a separate statute.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Taxpayer buys unimproved investment land for $1,000,000 (basis). Step 2: Its value increases to $5,000,000 while held: $4,000,000 economic gain, ordinarily unrealized. Step 3: Exchange land for an apartment building worth $5,000,000: realized gain = $5,000,000 − $1,000,000 = $4,000,000. Step 4: Separately test §1031 real-property, use, exchange and other requirements; if qualified, recognition may be deferred. Do not assume every swap qualifies.
formulas.source: Class 1, Bankman et al. (19th ed.), syllabus-assigned Ch. 1 printed pp. 22

formulas.title: Simple nominal versus real gain
formulas.formula: Nominal gain = proceeds − historical basis; real purchasing-power gain adjusts for inflation
formulas.meaning: Tax law does not generally inflation-adjust investment basis.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Original nominal cost basis = $100. Step 2: Property sells for $105 after a year with 5% inflation. Step 3: Nominal gain = $105 − $100 = $5. Step 4: Inflation-adjusted original purchasing-power cost ≈ $100 × 1.05 = $105, leaving approximately $0 real gain. Under the reading's general historical-cost principle, tax basis is not automatically increased for inflation.
formulas.source: Class 1, Bankman et al. (19th ed.), syllabus-assigned Ch. 1 printed pp. 23–24

formulas.title: Compound future value
formulas.formula: FV = PV × (1 + r)^n
formulas.meaning: PV initial investment; r return per period; n number of periods.
formulas.worked: Step 1: PV = $10,000, r = 10% = .10, n = 10. Step 2: FV = $10,000 × (1.10)^10. Step 3: (1.10)^10 ≈ 2.59374246. Step 4: FV ≈ $25,937.42. Under the book's simplified retirement deferral example, 40% tax at withdrawal leaves about $25,937.42 × .60 = $15,562.45.
formulas.source: Class 1, Bankman et al. (19th ed.), syllabus-assigned Ch. 1 printed pp. 25–27

formulas.title: Present value
formulas.formula: PV = FV ÷ (1 + r)^n
formulas.meaning: Discount rate r and number of periods n must match.
formulas.worked: Step 1: FV = $10,000 in 10 years, rate = .10, periods = 10. Step 2: PV = $10,000 ÷ (1.10)^10 ≈ $3,855.43. Step 3: The chapter's Table 1-5 gives a rounded 0.386 present-value multiplier; $10,000 × .386 = $3,860. Differences come from rounding, not different rules.
formulas.source: Class 1, Bankman et al. (19th ed.), syllabus-assigned Ch. 1 printed pp. 26–27

formulas.title: Deferral versus current taxation
formulas.formula: Deferral: P(1+r)^n(1−t_end); current tax: P(1−t_now)[1+r(1−t_annual)]^n
formulas.meaning: The source assumes constant tax rates, ordinary annual taxation of earnings, and equal pre-tax returns.
formulas.worked: Model assumptions: $10,000 gross investment, 10% annual return, 40% tax (both today and at withdrawal), no intervening taxes on qualified deferral. WITH DEFERRAL, n=10: $10,000 × 1.10^10 = $25,937.42 before withdrawal; × .60 ≈ $15,562.45 after tax. NO DEFERRAL: $10,000 × .60 = $6,000 initially; annual net growth = 10% × .60 = 6%; $6,000 × 1.06^10 ≈ $10,745.09. At 20 years: deferred ≈ $40,365 and current-taxed ≈ $19,243, rounded as in the book. A change in future tax rates can change the ranking.
formulas.source: Class 1, Bankman et al. (19th ed.), syllabus-assigned Ch. 1 printed pp. 25–27
formulas.laymanExplanation: With deferral you invest the entire $10,000 first and pay tax later; without deferral you invest only $6,000 and keep paying tax on growth, so compounding is smaller.

formulas.title: Penalty percentages (introductory)
formulas.formula: Illustrative accuracy-related penalty = 20% × relevant underpayment; civil fraud = 75% × fraudulent portion
formulas.meaning: Penalties require legal predicates, bases, exceptions, and interaction rules; do not use formula alone.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Determine if §6662 negligence or substantial-understatement standards apply to a particular portion of underpayment. Step 2: If applicable and no defense defeats it, multiply that portion by 20%. Step 3: If §6663 fraud is proven for a portion, separately consider 75% × the fraud-attributable underpayment under the statutory interaction rules. This is only a percentage illustration; defenses, penalty interactions and proof requirements are essential.
formulas.source: Class 1, Bankman et al. (19th ed.), syllabus-assigned Ch. 1 printed pp. 29–30

formulas.title: Refund / balance due
formulas.formula: Tax due after credits − withholding/estimated payments = remaining balance (if positive) or refund (if negative)
formulas.meaning: Eligibility, refundable credits, additional taxes, and payment credit details must be included in a full return.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Determine final tax after lawful credits. Step 2: Add withholding and estimated payments already paid. Step 3: Subtract prepayments from final tax. Example invented to illustrate the book's sequence: liability $8,000 − prepayments $9,000 = −$1,000, normally a $1,000 overpayment/refund; liability $8,000 − $6,000 prepayments = $2,000 balance due. Other refundable credits or offsets can change the result.
formulas.source: Class 1, Bankman et al. (19th ed.), syllabus-assigned Ch. 1 printed pp. 28

formulas.title: Haig–Simons income
formulas.formula: Y = C + ΔW (consumption + change in wealth)
formulas.meaning: Economic definition of personal income, distinct from statutory taxable income.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Annual consumption C = $11,000. Step 2: Net worth decreases by $1,000 because of use of old savings or new borrowing: ΔW = −$1,000. Step 3: Y = C + ΔW = $11,000 − $1,000 = $10,000. Step 4: This is the same economic income as spending $9,000 while increasing net savings by $1,000.
formulas.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 37–38
formulas.laymanExplanation: An economy-wide concept, not statutory taxable income.
formulas.sourceRole: Assigned textbook example or separately labeled illustrative calculation

formulas.title: Income as consumption plus saving
formulas.formula: Y = C + S
formulas.meaning: An alternate shorthand when saving measures the period's change in net worth.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Consumption = $9,000. Step 2: Net saving during the year = $1,000. Step 3: Y = C + S = $9,000 + $1,000 = $10,000. Step 4: Do not count borrowed money as additional economic income without considering the liability.
formulas.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 37
formulas.laymanExplanation: Income is split between spending and saving.
formulas.sourceRole: Assigned textbook example or separately labeled illustrative calculation

formulas.title: Valuation of noncash remuneration
formulas.formula: Generally include FMV of property or services received for services rendered
formulas.meaning: Treas. Reg. §1.61-2(d)(1) generally measures in-kind compensation by FMV.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Identify the property or services received in exchange for services rendered. Step 2: Determine a supportable fair market value under Reg. §1.61-2(d)(1). Step 3: Include the relevant compensation amount unless an applicable exclusion or specific valuation rule applies. Step 4: Analyze any additional expense or basis consequences independently. The reading provides this barter scenario without a numerical dollar amount.
formulas.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 46
formulas.laymanExplanation: A legal service traded for home repairs can be taxable even though neither party hands over cash.
formulas.sourceRole: Assigned textbook example or separately labeled illustrative calculation

formulas.title: Gain and per-share basis allocation
formulas.formula: Allocated basis = acquisition cost × (shares sold ÷ shares acquired); gain = proceeds − allocated basis
formulas.meaning: Useful for identical shares originally acquired as one block.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Original investment = $1,000 for 100 shares. Step 2: Allocated basis for 40 = $1,000 × (40 ÷ 100) = $400. Step 3: Sale proceeds = $700. Step 4: Realized gain = $700 − $400 = $300. Recognition and character remain separate questions.
formulas.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 68
formulas.laymanExplanation: When selling 40 of 100 identical shares, subtract only the purchase cost belonging to those 40.
formulas.sourceRole: Assigned textbook example or separately labeled illustrative calculation

formulas.title: Relative-value allocation of land basis
formulas.formula: Allocated basis = total basis × (relative FMV of portion at acquisition ÷ total FMV at acquisition)
formulas.meaning: Where land portions differ in value, allocate tax basis reasonably rather than by area alone.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Purchase entire property for $1,000. Step 2: Experts place 45% of purchase-date value on the wooded tract ($450 of the original total basis). Step 3: Allocate $450 basis to the wooded tract. Step 4: Sale price $700 − allocated basis $450 = $250 realized gain.
formulas.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 68–69
formulas.laymanExplanation: Two kinds of land can have different values; don't divide their cost just by acreage.
formulas.sourceRole: Assigned textbook example or separately labeled illustrative calculation

formulas.title: Inaja basis-reduction illustration
formulas.formula: Remaining basis = initial basis − payment treated as return of capital
formulas.meaning: Used only when legally appropriate and apportionment to disposed rights is impracticable.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Entire property original basis = $61,000. Step 2: Settlement = $50,000; settlement costs = $1,000; net receipt = $49,000. Step 3: Court found basis allocation to the affected rights wholly impracticable and net receipt lower than entire property basis. Step 4: Treat the $49,000 as return of capital, reducing property basis conceptually to $61,000 − $49,000 = $12,000, absent other adjustments. Step 5: Ordinary partial-sale allocation remains the general rule; Inaja is a narrow exception.
formulas.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 69–70
formulas.laymanExplanation: The court treated the city settlement as repayment of investment, not a taxable profit, because no sensible partial-basis calculation was possible.
formulas.sourceRole: Assigned textbook example or separately labeled illustrative calculation

formulas.title: 2026 wagering loss limitation
formulas.formula: Allowable loss deduction = min(90% × wagering losses, wagering gains)
formulas.meaning: The §165(d) tax-year-2026 statutory change supersedes the textbook's earlier full-offset example.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Suppose 2026 wagering gains = $1,000 and wagering losses = $1,000. Step 2: Compute 90% × losses = .90 × $1,000 = $900. Step 3: Compare with gains $1,000 and take the smaller: max allowable §165(d) deduction = $900. Step 4: Net of $1,000 winnings and $900 loss deduction is $100 before other relevant tax rules. Assess itemizing and year-specific restrictions. Source of the changed limitation: IRC §165(d), as amended for taxable years after 2025.
formulas.source: Tax casebook pp.71–73 (historical background) + CURRENT 26 U.S.C. §165(d), Public Law 119-21 §70114 (2025); IRS IRB 2026-19.
formulas.laymanExplanation: This is a 2026 CURRENT-LAW annotation, not the older calculation in the casebook.

formulas.title: Compensation for damaged business property
formulas.formula: Potential realized gain = recovery proceeds − adjusted basis (before §1033 relief)
formulas.meaning: Consider property basis and qualifying nonrecognition for reinvestment.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Recovery = $700,000 for destroyed building. Step 2: Adjusted basis of building = $600,000. Step 3: Potential realized gain = $700,000 − $600,000 = $100,000. Step 4: Determine whether §1033 allows qualifying nonrecognition when property is replaced within statutory conditions.
formulas.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 78
formulas.laymanExplanation: You don't treat an entire property-insurance check as profit; first recover the property's tax cost.
formulas.sourceRole: Assigned textbook example or separately labeled illustrative calculation

formulas.title: §107 minister housing allowance limits
formulas.formula: Excludable housing allowance = min(designated allowance, actual qualifying housing expenses, fair rental value including furnishings/utilities)
formulas.meaning: IRS conditions and current statutory limits apply; distinguish from self-employment tax treatment.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Hypothetical minister's officially designated housing allowance = $30,000. Step 2: Actual eligible housing expenses = $28,000. Step 3: Fair rental value cap, including furnishings and utilities = $25,000. Step 4: Potential income-tax exclusion is limited to the lowest amount: $25,000 (subject to qualifications). Step 5: Separately address possible self-employment tax treatment.
formulas.source: Separately assigned Gaylor v. Mnuchin opinion and IRC §107; numerical worked example constructed for study, not from casebook pp.35–102.
formulas.laymanExplanation: This example illustrates the separately assigned Gaylor handout and §107; the source does not supply the numbers.
formulas.sourceRole: Assigned textbook example or separately labeled illustrative calculation

formulas.title: Principal residence sale gain
formulas.formula: Potential taxable gain = max(0, realized gain − permissible §121 exclusion)
formulas.meaning: After computing gain, determine use/ownership tests, $250,000/$500,000 cap, and frequency limitations.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Amount realized from home sale = $400,000. Step 2: Adjusted basis = $100,000. Step 3: Realized gain = $400,000 − $100,000 = $300,000. Step 4: Assuming a qualifying single filer, §121 exclusion cap = $250,000. Step 5: Taxable gain = max(0, $300,000 − $250,000) = $50,000.
formulas.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 100–101
formulas.laymanExplanation: Compute the profit first, then the portion the home-sale exclusion lets you subtract.
formulas.sourceRole: Assigned textbook example or separately labeled illustrative calculation

formulas.title: Implicit tax from reduced bond yield
formulas.formula: (taxable yield − tax-exempt yield) / taxable yield
formulas.meaning: The 'hidden tax' is an investor's acceptance of a lower yield to obtain a tax preference.
formulas.laymanExplanation: The 'hidden tax' is an investor's acceptance of a lower yield to obtain a tax preference.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Comparable taxable U.S. Treasury bond yield = 10%. Step 2: Tax-exempt municipal bond yield = 6%. Step 3: Difference = 10% − 6% = 4 percentage points. Step 4: Implicit tax as fraction of taxable return = 4% ÷ 10% = 40%. This is economic incidence, not a tax paid to Treasury.
formulas.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., syllabus Week 3 printed pp. 118–119; new worked illustrations explicitly identified where applicable.

formulas.title: Value included when two people barter
formulas.formula: Each person's gross income = fair market value of what that person receives
formulas.meaning: Receiving work instead of money can be taxable to each side.
formulas.laymanExplanation: Receiving work instead of money can be taxable to each side.
formulas.worked: Step 1: A babysits B's child in exchange for B painting A's room. Step 2: The market value of each service is $100 under the book's hypothetical. Step 3: A receives $100 of painting and has $100 gross income; B receives $100 childcare and has $100 gross income. Step 4: Combined inclusion = $200, without a personal consumption deduction under these facts.
formulas.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., syllabus Week 3 printed pp. 115–116; new worked illustrations explicitly identified where applicable.

formulas.title: Social Security combined income framework
formulas.formula: Combined income (basic) = AGI + tax-exempt interest + 1/2 Social Security benefits + statutory adjustments
formulas.meaning: Social Security's included percentage depends partly on other income, rather than simply taking 85% of everyone's check.
formulas.laymanExplanation: Social Security's included percentage depends partly on other income, rather than simply taking 85% of everyone's check.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Identify AGI, qualifying tax-exempt interest and other required modifications. Step 2: Add one-half of Social Security benefits. Step 3: For married joint filers, source discusses $32,000 and $44,000 combined-income thresholds. Step 4: Apply §86's appropriate percentage and formula. The source does not reproduce all computational steps, so do not assume a universal 85% inclusion.
formulas.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., syllabus Week 3 printed pp. 133–134; new worked illustrations explicitly identified where applicable.

formulas.title: Personal gift: donor and donee inclusion
formulas.formula: Recipient's §102(a) inclusion = $0; donor's personal-gift deduction = $0
formulas.meaning: Giving money to a family member usually doesn't reduce your own income, and the family member ordinarily doesn't report it as income.
formulas.laymanExplanation: Giving money to a family member usually doesn't reduce your own income, and the family member ordinarily doesn't report it as income.
formulas.worked: Textbook example: Donna earns $100,000 and gives son Edward $30,000 purely as gift. Donna retains $100,000 taxable earnings before her other taxes/deductions; Edward's gift receipt is excluded under §102. The gift alone doesn't create a $30,000 donor deduction. Ignore donor gift tax as directed in the textbook.
formulas.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., syllabus Week 3 printed pp. 121–123; new worked illustrations explicitly identified where applicable.

formulas.title: Gifted appreciated asset: gain basis
formulas.formula: Donee gain = amount realized − donor's adjusted basis
formulas.meaning: The donor's old profit stays inside the gifted stock until the recipient sells it.
formulas.laymanExplanation: The donor's old profit stays inside the gifted stock until the recipient sells it.
formulas.worked: Illustration from Taft v. Bowers: Donor bought shares for $1,000. At gift, FMV = $2,000. Later donee sells for $5,000. Step 1: Donee's transferred gain basis = $1,000. Step 2: Amount realized = $5,000. Step 3: Gain = $5,000 − $1,000 = $4,000 (not just $3,000 appreciation after the gift).
formulas.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., syllabus Week 4 printed pp. 135–137; new worked illustrations explicitly identified where applicable.

formulas.title: Gifted depreciated asset: dual-basis rule
formulas.formula: Gain basis = donor's adjusted basis; loss basis = min(donor basis, FMV at gift)
formulas.meaning: When you receive a losing investment as a gift, tax law doesn't automatically let you use all the donor's historical loss.
formulas.laymanExplanation: When you receive a losing investment as a gift, tax law doesn't automatically let you use all the donor's historical loss.
formulas.worked: Constructed example distinct from assigned p141 problem: donor basis $3,000, FMV at gift $2,500. Step 1: If donee sells for $3,600, gain = $3,600 − $3,000 = $600. Step 2: If sells for $2,300, loss = $2,300 − $2,500 = −$200. Step 3: If sells for $2,700, proceeds fall between the two bases, so no gain or loss. Apply other recognition and character limits separately.
formulas.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., syllabus Week 4 printed pp. 135, 141; new worked illustrations explicitly identified where applicable.

formulas.title: Inherited property: §1014 basis
formulas.formula: General basis for qualifying inherited property = date-of-death FMV (or permitted alternate valuation)
formulas.meaning: Inheriting an appreciated asset can reset its tax cost to its market value at death, unlike a lifetime gift.
formulas.laymanExplanation: Inheriting an appreciated asset can reset its tax cost to its market value at death, unlike a lifetime gift.
formulas.worked: New illustrative figures, not an assigned problem: an investor bought stock for $25,000; qualifying value at death = $90,000. Step 1: Basis to qualifying heir under §1014 generally becomes $90,000, not $25,000. Step 2: If heir later sells for $95,000, realized gain from post-death increase = $5,000. Step 3: Check §1014 exclusions/valuation exceptions and other laws.
formulas.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., syllabus Week 4 printed pp. 139–140; new worked illustrations explicitly identified where applicable.

formulas.title: Qualifying §1041 transfer: recognition and transferee basis
formulas.formula: Transferor recognized gain/loss = 0; recipient's basis = transferor's adjusted basis
formulas.meaning: During qualifying divorce division, tax on a stock's appreciation generally isn't charged immediately, but its old tax cost carries over.
formulas.laymanExplanation: During qualifying divorce division, tax on a stock's appreciation generally isn't charged immediately, but its old tax cost carries over.
formulas.worked: Constructed illustration different from assigned p147 problem: transferor spouse has stock worth $85,000 with adjusted basis $25,000. Step 1: Evaluate §1041 eligibility. Step 2: Qualifying transfer produces no current gain recognized to transferor. Step 3: Recipient's basis = $25,000, leaving $60,000 of embedded appreciation. Step 4: A later sale by the recipient requires separate gain computation.
formulas.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., syllabus Week 4 printed pp. 142–147; new worked illustrations explicitly identified where applicable.

formulas.title: Section 166(d) bad-debt deduction basis limit
formulas.formula: Potential deductible bad debt <= adjusted basis in debt, subject to §166 conditions
formulas.meaning: Someone might legally owe you money, but a tax deduction generally requires that you invested or had tax basis in the debt.
formulas.laymanExplanation: Someone might legally owe you money, but a tax deduction generally requires that you invested or had tax basis in the debt.
formulas.worked: Illustrative scenario: $6,000 unpaid child support is due under decree, but no amount was advanced as a loan or included as taxable income, so recipient basis in receivable is $0. Step 1: Identify basis = $0. Step 2: Even if collection is impossible, a $6,000 claimed bad-debt deduction is not supported by basis. Step 3: Compare with a genuine $6,000 loan where adjusted basis may exist.
formulas.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., syllabus Week 4 printed pp. 151–152; new worked illustrations explicitly identified where applicable.

formulas.title: Lower future rates on deferred receipts
formulas.formula: Tax savings = deferred income × (current marginal rate − future marginal rate)
formulas.meaning: If you pay tax next year in a lower bracket, you may save actual dollars as well as delay payment.
formulas.laymanExplanation: If you pay tax next year in a lower bracket, you may save actual dollars as well as delay payment.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Hypothetical deferred income = $1,000,000. Step 2: 2030 tax at 40% = $400,000. Step 3: 2031 tax at 30% = $300,000. Step 4: Hypothetical nominal saving = $100,000, before timing and other effects. Note: one parenthetical sentence in the assigned book reverses the implication about accelerating when rates fall; the numerical example supports deferral.
formulas.source: Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 4 assigned pp. 155–156; textbook numerics unless expressly marked constructed.

formulas.title: Present value of tax postponed one year
formulas.formula: PV = FV / (1 + r)^n
formulas.meaning: A fixed tax bill is cheaper in today's dollars when you pay it later.
formulas.laymanExplanation: A fixed tax bill is cheaper in today's dollars when you pay it later.
formulas.worked: Step 1: $1 of tax due in one year; r=10%, n=1. Step 2: Present value = $1/1.10 = $0.90909. Step 3: A $0.30 tax due in one year has PV = $0.30/1.10 = $0.272727. Step 4: Do not confuse delaying the tax with delaying receipt of underlying cash, which may make taxpayer economically worse off.
formulas.source: Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 4 assigned pp. 155–156; textbook numerics unless expressly marked constructed.

formulas.title: Traditional and Roth IRA economic equivalence
formulas.formula: Traditional X×A×(1−t) = Roth X×(1−t)×A
formulas.meaning: Under the same tax rate before and after retirement, investing more pretax in a traditional IRA can produce the same after-tax result as a smaller Roth contribution.
formulas.laymanExplanation: Under the same tax rate before and after retirement, investing more pretax in a traditional IRA can produce the same after-tax result as a smaller Roth contribution.
formulas.worked: Step 1: t=33⅓%; equivalent contributions are $15,000 traditional (after current deduction costs $10,000) and $10,000 Roth. Step 2: Using the TEXTBOOK'S PRINTED FINAL FIGURES, traditional grows to $1,500,000 and Roth to $1,000,000; traditional after-tax payout = $1,500,000×2/3=$1,000,000, same as Roth. Step 3: SOURCE ARITHMETIC CAUTION: casebook says investments increase 'tenfold' but those printed balances represent 100-fold growth; true 10-fold produces $150,000 traditional×2/3=$100,000, equal to $100,000 Roth. Equivalence holds either way under equal rates.
formulas.source: Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 4 assigned pp. 156–158; textbook numerics unless expressly marked constructed.

formulas.title: NOL §172 80% limitation illustration
formulas.formula: Maximum eligible NOL deduction ≈ 80% × eligible taxable income before NOL
formulas.meaning: The earlier year's business loss may offset most, but not all, of next year's profit.
formulas.laymanExplanation: The earlier year's business loss may offset most, but not all, of next year's profit.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Consider a NEW illustrative eligible NOL of $500,000 from Year 1 (not Aerospace's assigned problem). Step 2: Year 2 otherwise taxable income=$400,000. Step 3: Hypothetical 80% NOL limit=$320,000. Step 4: Applied deduction=$320,000; current taxable income=$80,000; unused $180,000 eligible NOL may be carried forward. The Aerospace $1m/$1m problem on p.162 remains deliberately UNSOLVED in the Problem Bank.
formulas.source: Bankman et al., Ch.4 pp161–162, §172 method; constructed figures (NOT solution to p162 assigned Aerospace problem).

formulas.title: Straight-line cost recovery vs immediate expensing
formulas.formula: Annual straight-line depreciation = (cost − salvage value) ÷ useful life
formulas.meaning: A business machine that makes money for five years may spread its $10,000 cost as $2,000/year.
formulas.laymanExplanation: A business machine that makes money for five years may spread its $10,000 cost as $2,000/year.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Acme machine cost $10,000, life 5 years, salvage $0. Step 2: Straight-line annual cost = $10,000/5=$2,000. Step 3: Yearly revenue $2,100−$2,000 depreciation = $100 pretax profit in each of five years. Step 4: Immediate expensing would show Year 1 $2,100−$10,000=−$7,900 followed by $2,100 for other years under simplified assumptions. Actual tax depreciation schedules and 2025 law may vary.
formulas.source: Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 4 assigned pp. 163–164; textbook numerics unless expressly marked constructed.

formulas.title: AAA membership prepayment and expected service cost
formulas.formula: Prepaid dues $60; costs in Year 1 $18; future costs $42
formulas.meaning: A club may collect an annual membership fee now, even though most of its service costs occur next year.
formulas.laymanExplanation: A club may collect an annual membership fee now, even though most of its service costs occur next year.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Member joins October 1 and prepays $60 for twelve months. Step 2: Fixed service costs are $3/month ($36/year); variable costs expected $3/month Oct–Mar and $1/month Apr–Sep ($24/year). Step 3: Current Oct–Dec expected cost = three months×($3+$3)=$18. Step 4: Expected next-year cost = $60−$18=$42. Step 5: AAA opinion allowed IRS to require current reporting of full $60 under historical law; modern statutory deferral exceptions require separate testing.
formulas.source: Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 5 assigned pp. 171–176; textbook numerics unless expressly marked constructed.

formulas.title: §451(c) prepaid dance lessons example
formulas.formula: Current-year inclusion = receipts × share of lessons recognized for financial reporting (if eligible); remainder generally next year
formulas.meaning: Prepayment for 100 classes may allow some income to move to next year—but generally not beyond that.
formulas.laymanExplanation: Prepayment for 100 classes may allow some income to move to next year—but generally not beyond that.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Taxpayer receives $6,000 for 100 dance lessons in 2024. Step 2: 20 lessons in 2024 ⇒ 20/100×$6,000=$1,200 reported 2024 (if all §451(c) conditions met). Step 3: Remaining $4,800 included in 2025 even though 40 additional lessons won't occur until 2026. Step 4: §451(c) generally permits only limited one-year deferral, not spreading income over the full 2024–2026 contract.
formulas.source: Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 5 assigned pp. 177–178; textbook numerics unless expressly marked constructed.

formulas.title: Nonrecourse loan larger than original property basis
formulas.formula: Borrowed proceeds − basis is NOT §1001 gain unless there is a disposition
formulas.meaning: Borrowing more than you originally paid for property is not the same as selling it for that amount.
formulas.laymanExplanation: Borrowing more than you originally paid for property is not the same as selling it for that amount.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Wood originally bought property for $296,400. Step 2: Hypothetical nonrecourse refinancing increases debt to $400,000. Step 3: $400,000−$296,400=$103,600, but this arithmetic difference is NOT automatically a realized gain. Step 4: Woodsam says refinancing was not a disposition; future sale/foreclosure must be analyzed separately.
formulas.source: Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 5 assigned pp. 197–199; textbook numerics unless expressly marked constructed.

formulas.title: Cottage Savings — realized mortgage loss
formulas.formula: Realized loss = adjusted basis of relinquished mortgages − amount realized from replacement mortgages
formulas.meaning: A lender can recognize a loss when exchanging legally different mortgage claims.
formulas.laymanExplanation: A lender can recognize a loss when exchanging legally different mortgage claims.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Cottage transferred participation in original loans with approximate face value $6.9m. Step 2: Received mortgage interests worth about $4.5m. Step 3: Claimed $2,447,091 adjusted loss (not exactly the face-value difference due to adjustments). Step 4: The case focuses on realization through distinct legal entitlements; calculate using adjusted tax basis rather than simply face amounts.
formulas.source: Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 5 assigned pp. 200–206; textbook numerics unless expressly marked constructed.

formulas.title: §1031 boot — realized versus recognized gain
formulas.formula: Recognized gain = min(realized gain, boot received), subject to qualifying rules
formulas.meaning: Even when swapping investment land tax-deferred, extra cash or a tractor may make some of the profit taxable now.
formulas.laymanExplanation: Even when swapping investment land tax-deferred, extra cash or a tractor may make some of the profit taxable now.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Old Farm basis $10,000. Step 2: New Farm FMV $100,000, plus cash $15,000 and tractor FMV $8,000 ⇒ amount realized=$123,000. Step 3: Realized gain=$123,000−$10,000=$113,000. Step 4: Boot=$15,000+$8,000=$23,000. Step 5: Recognized gain=min($113,000,$23,000)=$23,000; deferred gain=$90,000. Book asks alternative old bases $110k and $130k separately; preserve those as unsolved problems.
formulas.source: Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 5 assigned pp. 215–216; textbook numerics unless expressly marked constructed.

formulas.title: §1031(d) basis of replacement property
formulas.formula: New like-kind basis = old basis + recognized gain − boot received + boot paid (simplified)
formulas.meaning: A like-kind exchange defers tax by keeping your new property basis low, rather than erasing the old profit.
formulas.laymanExplanation: A like-kind exchange defers tax by keeping your new property basis low, rather than erasing the old profit.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Simplified basis of old farm = $10,000, receipt of new $100,000 farm and $15,000 cash boot. Step 2: Recognized gain=$15,000; gross basis pool = old basis $10,000 + recognized gain $15,000=$25,000. Step 3: Allocate $15,000 basis to cash received; new farm basis=$10,000. Step 4: If instead taxpayer gives $15,000 cash plus old farm for replacement farm, replacement basis generally increases by cash paid to $25,000. Actual debt/other boot can change calculations.
formulas.source: Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 5 assigned pp. 216–217; textbook numerics unless expressly marked constructed.

formulas.title: Burnet v. Logan — closed vs open transaction
formulas.formula: Closed: cash + ascertainable FMV of promise − basis; Open: recover basis from receipts before gain in rare cases
formulas.meaning: Uncertain promised mining payments might not have a reliable value at sale, so taxpayer may recover original investment first.
formulas.laymanExplanation: Uncertain promised mining payments might not have a reliable value at sale, so taxpayer may recover original investment first.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Logan stock basis $180,000; cash received now $120,000; government's tentative FMV of contingent future rights $100,000. Step 2: CLOSED theory: amount realized=$220,000; immediate gain=$40,000. Step 3: OPEN holding: rights could not be reliably valued; treat $120,000 as cost recovery, leaving $60,000 unrecovered basis, and count later payments as gain only after full basis recovered under case's facts. Modern use is rare.
formulas.source: Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 6 assigned pp. 219–221; textbook numerics unless expressly marked constructed.

formulas.title: §453 installment principal payments
formulas.formula: Gross profit ratio = (sale price − adjusted basis)/contract price; gain per principal payment = ratio × payment
formulas.meaning: If two-thirds of a property's price is profit, two-thirds of each buyer payment is counted as gain.
formulas.laymanExplanation: If two-thirds of a property's price is profit, two-thirds of each buyer payment is counted as gain.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Seller basis $100,000, sale price $300,000 paid over years in installments: $30k,$60k,$30k,$60k,$120k. Step 2: Gross profit=$300,000−$100,000=$200,000; ratio=2/3. Step 3: Recognized gain by payments = $20k,$40k,$20k,$40k,$80k. Step 4: Total recognized gain=$200k; remaining one-third of each payment recovers basis. Step 5: Interest received is separate ordinary income; actual eligibility and contract price may differ.
formulas.source: Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 6 assigned pp. 227–229; textbook numerics unless expressly marked constructed.

formulas.title: NQSO exercise spread
formulas.formula: Compensation = (FMV on exercise − strike price) × shares exercised
formulas.meaning: Exercising an option at $200 when shares trade at $450 creates $250 compensation income per share.
formulas.laymanExplanation: Exercising an option at $200 when shares trade at $450 creates $250 compensation income per share.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Option strike $200/share. Step 2: At exercise WWS share FMV=$450. Step 3: Spread=$450−$200=$250/share. Step 4: Exercise 10 options ⇒ $2,500 ordinary compensation to Driftwood; employer matching expense deduction $2,500 under simplified source. Step 5: Grant in 2024 and vesting in 2027 generally did not trigger tax for this nontraded nonqualified option.
formulas.source: Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 6 assigned pp. 247–249; textbook numerics unless expressly marked constructed.

formulas.title: Qualified plan vs unsheltered savings, 25-year comparison
formulas.formula: FV of level annual contributions C at return r for n years = C × ((1+r)^n −1)/r
formulas.meaning: Investing retirement savings before tax and letting it grow tax-sheltered can roughly double retirement after-tax income in the book's example.
formulas.laymanExplanation: Investing retirement savings before tax and letting it grow tax-sheltered can roughly double retirement after-tax income in the book's example.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Qualified $10,000 annual employer contribution for 25 years at 10% = $983,471 accumulated. Step 2: 15-year retirement annuity at assumed 10% yields $129,301/year; 35% tax leaves $84,045/year. Step 3: Unsheltered cash bonus after 35% tax yields $6,500 annual investment; after-tax growth 6.5% gives $382,770 accumulated in 25 years. Step 4: 15-year annuity pays $50,324/year with $24,810 taxable, tax $8,684, net $41,640. Step 5: Ratio=$41,640/$84,045≈49.5%. These are 2023 textbook assumptions; real annuity/qualified-plan conditions may differ.
formulas.source: Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 6 assigned pp. 253–254; textbook numerics unless expressly marked constructed.

formulas.title: Annuity recovery-of-capital exclusion ratio
formulas.formula: Exclusion ratio ≈ investment in contract / expected return; each payment × exclusion ratio is nontaxable basis recovery
formulas.meaning: Part of each annuity check may simply return money already invested rather than being new profit.
formulas.laymanExplanation: Part of each annuity check may simply return money already invested rather than being new profit.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Book investment $382,770. Step 2: Expected return $50,324×15=$754,860. Step 3: Ratio=$382,770/$754,860≈0.507. Step 4: Excluded portion ≈$25,514 per $50,324 distribution; taxable ≈$24,810. SOURCE TYPO CAUTION: the book's footnote inconsistently mentions $25,524 instead of $25,514; the intended taxable figure uses $25,514. Check applicable §72 rules before real-world computation.
formulas.source: Federal Income Taxation 19th ed., Week 6 assigned pp. 253–254; textbook numerics unless expressly marked constructed.

formulas.title: Forgiven debt — basic CODI
formulas.formula: Potential CODI = old legally owed principal − consideration accepted in full settlement
formulas.meaning: A loan discharged for less than you owe may create taxable debt-forgiveness income.
formulas.laymanExplanation: A loan discharged for less than you owe may create taxable debt-forgiveness income.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Borrow $100,000 and repay nothing yet. Step 2: Lender accepts $90,000 in full satisfaction of the undisputed debt. Step 3: Potential CODI = $100,000 − $90,000 = $10,000. Step 4: Test §108 exclusions and any genuinely contested-liability or price-adjustment provisions before deciding taxable amount.
formulas.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 7 syllabus assigned pp. 262–263. Formula figures from the textbook unless an illustrative variation is identified.

formulas.title: §108 insolvency exclusion limit
formulas.formula: Insolvency = liabilities − FMV of assets immediately before discharge; excluded CODI ≤ insolvency
formulas.meaning: Being in debt more than your possessions are worth can shield some debt forgiveness from current tax.
formulas.laymanExplanation: Being in debt more than your possessions are worth can shield some debt forgiveness from current tax.
formulas.worked: Step 1: For a NEW illustration, immediately before discharge assets are worth $70,000 and liabilities total $120,000. Step 2: Insolvency = $50,000. Step 3: Creditor cancels $65,000. Step 4: Maximum insolvency exclusion (assuming eligibility) is min($65,000,$50,000)=$50,000. Step 5: Remaining $15,000 potentially included unless another rule applies; attribute reduction can follow.
formulas.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 7 syllabus assigned pp. 264. Formula figures from the textbook unless an illustrative variation is identified.

formulas.title: §108(b) attribute reduction
formulas.formula: NOL remaining after excluded CODI = prior NOL − required reduction (simplified)
formulas.meaning: Not paying income tax immediately can cost you future loss carryforwards.
formulas.laymanExplanation: Not paying income tax immediately can cost you future loss carryforwards.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Book example business NOL carryforward $3,000,000. Step 2: Qualified excluded CODI $1,000,000. Step 3: Assume statutory tax attributes are reduced dollar for dollar against the NOL in the example. Step 4: NOL after reduction $2,000,000. Step 5: The book contrasts later profits $7m and potential increased taxable income; actual §172 80% limitations and §108(b) reduction order may modify final tax-year computations.
formulas.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 7 syllabus assigned pp. 264. Formula figures from the textbook unless an illustrative variation is identified.

formulas.title: §108(e)(5) seller debt cut
formulas.formula: Adjusted purchase basis = original basis − qualifying purchase-price reduction
formulas.meaning: If seller financing is renegotiated, the reduction can lower tax basis rather than create CODI.
formulas.laymanExplanation: If seller financing is renegotiated, the reduction can lower tax basis rather than create CODI.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Pay $6,000 cash and give seller a $24,000 note for a car; basis=$30,000. Step 2: Dealer reduces note to $15,000 (a $9,000 reduction). Step 3: If §108(e)(5) applies, no CODI on $9,000; basis falls to $30,000−$9,000=$21,000. Step 4: A reduction by an unrelated bank may be governed by different rules.
formulas.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 7 syllabus assigned pp. 264–265. Formula figures from the textbook unless an illustrative variation is identified.

formulas.title: Zarin's settlement — disputed versus discharged amount
formulas.formula: Disputed liability theory: tax-recognized debt = bona fide agreed settlement amount
formulas.meaning: A true disputed debt may be treated as initially owed only in the amount settled.
formulas.laymanExplanation: A true disputed debt may be treated as initially owed only in the amount settled.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Casino asserted $3,435,000 debt; settlement $500,000. Step 2: IRS ordinary discharge theory: $3,435,000−$500,000=$2,935,000 potential CODI. Step 3: Under the Third Circuit's assigned holding, initial valid debt was not established and bona fide settlement fixed obligation at $500,000. Step 4: $500,000 paid discharges that fixed amount, resulting in zero CODI on these unusual facts. Step 5: State the Preslar circuit conflict.
formulas.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 7 syllabus assigned pp. 266–274. Formula figures from the textbook unless an illustrative variation is identified.

formulas.title: Debt counts in both purchase basis and sale proceeds
formulas.formula: Basis = cash paid + debt incurred/assumed (genuine); realized gain = cash + debt relief − adjusted basis
formulas.meaning: A $2m building bought with mortgage has $2m basis, and debt assumed on sale can count as proceeds.
formulas.laymanExplanation: A $2m building bought with mortgage has $2m basis, and debt assumed on sale can count as proceeds.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Alice buys Blackacre for $2m financed with $1m cash + $1m genuine debt. Step 2: Original basis $2m. Step 3: She sells for $1m cash + buyer assumes $2m debt, amount realized $3m. Step 4: Assuming $2m unadjusted basis and no other adjustments, realized gain $1m.
formulas.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 7 syllabus assigned pp. 275–277. Formula figures from the textbook unless an illustrative variation is identified.

formulas.title: Depreciation reduces basis before sale
formulas.formula: Adjusted basis = cost basis − depreciation allowed or allowable + other adjustments
formulas.meaning: You save tax while owning a building but have a lower basis—and possibly more gain—when selling.
formulas.laymanExplanation: You save tax while owning a building but have a lower basis—and possibly more gain—when selling.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Start $100 asset basis. Step 2: Eligible depreciation deductions $60, adjusted basis $40. Step 3: Sell for $35. Step 4: Realized loss $35−$40=−$5; prior $60 deductions and $5 loss total $65 tax-recognized cost recovery/loss under simple assumptions.
formulas.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 7 syllabus assigned pp. 276–277. Formula figures from the textbook unless an illustrative variation is identified.

formulas.title: Crane — mortgage plus cash sale
formulas.formula: Amount realized = net cash proceeds + nonrecourse mortgage assumed/relieved (subject to facts)
formulas.meaning: Taking over a property's mortgage can count the same as paying cash to the seller.
formulas.laymanExplanation: Taking over a property's mortgage can count the same as paying cash to the seller.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Inherited property had approximately $262,042.50 basis and matching debt. Step 2: Property later transferred subject to mortgage plus $2,500 net cash. Step 3: After depreciation adjustment, government calculated $233,997.40 basis and $257,500 amount realized. Step 4: Gain = $23,502.60. Source presents Crane in textbook prose; NOT a separately reproduced opinion.
formulas.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 7 syllabus assigned pp. 278–280. Formula figures from the textbook unless an illustrative variation is identified.

formulas.title: Tufts full nonrecourse liability amount realized
formulas.formula: Amount realized includes entire genuine nonrecourse debt relief even if debt > collateral FMV
formulas.meaning: You can have taxable gain selling underwater property because you escaped a large mortgage counted in your cost basis.
formulas.laymanExplanation: You can have taxable gain selling underwater property because you escaped a large mortgage counted in your cost basis.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Nonrecourse mortgage balance $1,851,500. Step 2: Adjusted tax basis $1,455,740. Step 3: FMV only about $1,400,000, but do not cap mortgage amount at this value. Step 4: Simplified §1001 realized gain=$1,851,500−$1,455,740=$395,760. Step 5: Assess other transfer consideration and character; example reproduces Supreme Court's key numbers.
formulas.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 7 syllabus assigned pp. 282–289. Formula figures from the textbook unless an illustrative variation is identified.

formulas.title: Net gift — taxes paid by donee
formulas.formula: Donor recognized gain = max(0, gift taxes paid by donee − donor adjusted basis)
formulas.meaning: If your child pays your gift-tax bill to receive stock, your gain may be based on that bill.
formulas.laymanExplanation: If your child pays your gift-tax bill to receive stock, your gain may be based on that bill.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Original donor stock adjusted basis $51,073. Step 2: Donees pay $62,992 of donors' legally owed gift tax. Step 3: Recognized donor gain=$62,992−$51,073=$11,919. Step 4: No deductible loss if tax payment less than basis under part-sale/part-gift rules. Distinguish donees' §102 gift exclusion.
formulas.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 7 syllabus assigned pp. 294–297. Formula figures from the textbook unless an illustrative variation is identified.

formulas.title: Charitable bargain sale — allocated basis
formulas.formula: Sale share of basis = total basis × (cash consideration / FMV)
formulas.meaning: Selling part of appreciated property value to a charity and donating the rest splits your old cost.
formulas.laymanExplanation: Selling part of appreciated property value to a charity and donating the rest splits your old cost.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Gift/sale property FMV=$100, basis=$20. Step 2: Charity pays $20, fraction sold=20%. Step 3: Basis allocated to sale=$20×20%=$4. Step 4: Realized gain on sale component=$20−$4=$16. Step 5: Potential charitable contribution $80 subject to §170 rules.
formulas.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 7 syllabus assigned pp. 297. Formula figures from the textbook unless an illustrative variation is identified.

formulas.title: Two-year OID compounded interest
formulas.formula: OID = redemption price − issue price; accrued interest in Year t = outstanding adjusted issue price × yield
formulas.meaning: A bond growing from $100 to $121 in 2 years at 10% earns $10 then $11 of interest.
formulas.laymanExplanation: A bond growing from $100 to $121 in 2 years at 10% earns $10 then $11 of interest.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Issue price $100, maturity proceeds $121; OID=$21. Step 2: Constant yield 10% ⇒ Year 1 interest $100×10%=$10, ending issue price $110. Step 3: Year 2 interest $110×10%=$11, closing value $121. Step 4: Straight-line $10.50/$10.50 misstates timing; modern OID rules require accrual.
formulas.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 7 syllabus assigned pp. 298–301. Formula figures from the textbook unless an illustrative variation is identified.

formulas.title: Compounding over 30 years
formulas.formula: FV = principal × (1 + interest rate)^years
formulas.meaning: Compound interest means even unpaid interest earns more interest.
formulas.laymanExplanation: Compound interest means even unpaid interest earns more interest.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Bond/loan $100, rate 10%, 30 years. Step 2: FV=$100×1.1^30≈$1,744.94. Step 3: Year 1 interest $10; Year 2 $11; Year 30 interest approximately $158.63. Step 4: Old straight-line model ($1,744.94−$100)/30≈$54.83 per year is economically inaccurate.
formulas.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 7 syllabus assigned pp. 298–299. Formula figures from the textbook unless an illustrative variation is identified.

formulas.title: Five-year zero-coupon bond OID schedule
formulas.formula: Total OID = redemption amount − issue price; annually accrue at yield
formulas.meaning: Even though no coupons are paid, your bond's tax basis rises with earned interest.
formulas.laymanExplanation: Even though no coupons are paid, your bond's tax basis rises with earned interest.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Initial issue $600,000, face redemption $1,000,000 after five years; OID=$400,000. Step 2: The book's semiannually compounded tax calculations produce annual amounts $64,540, $71,482, $79,171, $87,687, $97,120. Step 3: Add annual interest to adjusted issue price: $664,540, $736,022, $815,193, $902,880, $1,000,000. Step 4: Total OID across five years=$400,000, notwithstanding no earlier cash payment.
formulas.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 7 syllabus assigned pp. 301–302. Formula figures from the textbook unless an illustrative variation is identified.

formulas.title: §1274 deferred sale note at below-AFR rate
formulas.formula: First-year economic interest = PV of payments × AFR; OID = economic interest − stated interest
formulas.meaning: A $5m note paying 8% may be treated like a smaller principal plus extra interest if AFR is 10%.
formulas.laymanExplanation: A $5m note paying 8% may be treated like a smaller principal plus extra interest if AFR is 10%.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Nominal note $5m, ten-year term, cash coupon $400k/year (8%), AFR 10%. Step 2: Present value of cashflows=$4,385,543 (book). Step 3: OID=$5m−$4,385,543=$614,457. Step 4: Year 1 interest=10%×$4,385,543≈$438,554; actual coupon=$400,000; accrued OID=$38,554. Step 5: Year 2 base ~$4,424,097 and interest ~$442,410, OID ~$42,410; carry forward compounding/rounding.
formulas.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 7 syllabus assigned pp. 302–303. Formula figures from the textbook unless an illustrative variation is identified.

formulas.title: Market discount on existing bond
formulas.formula: Ordinary market discount at maturity ≈ redemption face − discounted secondary purchase price
formulas.meaning: Buying a low-coupon old bond cheaply can create ordinary income later.
formulas.laymanExplanation: Buying a low-coupon old bond cheaply can create ordinary income later.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Existing bond redemption $1,000; old coupon rate 3% produces $30 annual cash interest. Step 2: New rates 12%, bond trades at $727 with four years remaining. Step 3: Hold to maturity and receive $1,000, giving $273 market discount gain. Step 4: Under §§1276–1278 that discount may be ordinary interest-type income rather than capital gain, subject to technical rules.
formulas.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 7 syllabus assigned pp. 303–304. Formula figures from the textbook unless an illustrative variation is identified.

formulas.title: §483 personal residence seller-financing split
formulas.formula: PV of deferred payment = nominal future payment/(1 + AFR)^years; interest = nominal − PV
formulas.meaning: Money paid five years after sale includes a time-value component treated as interest.
formulas.laymanExplanation: Money paid five years after sale includes a time-value component treated as interest.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Home basis $400,000; buyer promises $1,000,000 lump sum in five years, illustrative 10% rate. Step 2: PV=$1,000,000/1.10^5≈$620,921. Step 3: Unstated interest=$379,079. Step 4: Total difference from $400k basis=$600k, of which $379,079 interest and $220,921 property gain. Step 5: §121 may cover eligible property gain, not imputed interest.
formulas.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 7 syllabus assigned pp. 304. Formula figures from the textbook unless an illustrative variation is identified.

formulas.title: Implicit municipal bond tax and after-tax comparison
formulas.formula: Implicit rate = (taxable yield − tax-exempt yield) / taxable yield
formulas.meaning: An 8% tax-free bond is as attractive as a 10% taxable bond to someone taxed at 20%.
formulas.laymanExplanation: An 8% tax-free bond is as attractive as a 10% taxable bond to someone taxed at 20%.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Taxable yield 10%; exempt yield 8%. Step 2: Implicit tax=(10−8)/10=20%. Step 3: A 30% bracket investor gets 10%×(1−.30)=7% from taxable bond, less than 8% muni. Step 4: A zero-rate investor earns full 10% from taxable bond, more than 8% muni, assuming equal risks.
formulas.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 7 syllabus assigned pp. 304–306. Formula figures from the textbook unless an illustrative variation is identified.

formulas.title: Hypothetical tax arbitrage — limitation required
formulas.formula: After-tax cash gain = exempt interest − deductible interest + tax saved by deduction
formulas.meaning: A fake 'free money' strategy appears if one deducts borrowing interest while exempting investment interest.
formulas.laymanExplanation: A fake 'free money' strategy appears if one deducts borrowing interest while exempting investment interest.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Borrow $1,000,000 at 10% ⇒ pay $100,000 interest. Step 2: Buy tax-exempt bonds yielding 8% ⇒ receive $80,000. Step 3: Pretax net loss −$20,000. Step 4: If borrower wrongly could deduct full $100,000 at 30%, tax saving $30,000, apparent after-tax profit $10,000. Step 5: §265(a)(2) and §148 address this asymmetry; example is counterfactual, not a lawful recommendation.
formulas.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 7 syllabus assigned pp. 308–310. Formula figures from the textbook unless an illustrative variation is identified.

formulas.title: Present value of distant death benefit
formulas.formula: PV = future death benefit/(1 + discount rate)^years
formulas.meaning: A million dollars payable decades from now is worth far less in today's money.
formulas.laymanExplanation: A million dollars payable decades from now is worth far less in today's money.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Hypothetical death benefit $1,000,000, 50 years until expected payment, rate 5%. Step 2: PV=$1,000,000/(1.05)^50≈$87,204; source says 'roughly $80,000' as a stylized estimate. Step 3: A real insurance price also includes mortality variance, loading and expenses; this is a pure time-value illustration, not a valid actuarial quote.
formulas.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 7 syllabus assigned pp. 313–314. Formula figures from the textbook unless an illustrative variation is identified.

formulas.title: §72 annuity exclusion ratio
formulas.formula: Exclusion ratio = investment in contract / expected total return; excluded payment = payment × ratio
formulas.meaning: Each annuity payment may be partly your own money coming back and partly taxable earnings.
formulas.laymanExplanation: Each annuity payment may be partly your own money coming back and partly taxable earnings.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Book's annuitant A pays $100,000 for expected ten payments of $20,000. Step 2: Expected return=$200,000. Step 3: Exclusion ratio=$100,000/$200,000=50%. Step 4: Each $20,000 payment excludes $10,000 of basis and includes $10,000 taxable income, subject to §72's full rules.
formulas.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 7 syllabus assigned pp. 315–317. Formula figures from the textbook unless an illustrative variation is identified.

formulas.title: §1259 short against the box — constructive gain
formulas.formula: Deemed gain on a constructive sale ≈ FMV appreciated position − adjusted basis (subject to §1259)
formulas.meaning: Shorting shares identical to your appreciated stock can trigger taxable profit even if you never sell your original shares.
formulas.laymanExplanation: Shorting shares identical to your appreciated stock can trigger taxable profit even if you never sell your original shares.
formulas.worked: Step 1: Eileen owns 1,000 ABC shares worth $90,000, basis $10,000. Step 2: Borrow and short 1,000 identical shares for $90,000, offsetting her market exposure. Step 3: §1259 can treat position as constructively sold. Step 4: Hypothetical realized gain=$90,000−$10,000=$80,000, subject to precise statutory exceptions and adjustment rules.
formulas.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 7 syllabus assigned pp. 318–320. Formula figures from the textbook unless an illustrative variation is identified.

updates.title: 2026 tax-rate regime
updates.book: The casebook predicts a 39.6% top rate in 2026.
updates.current: 2026 individual top bracket remains 37%; the seven individual rates from 2018 were made permanent by 2025 legislation.

updates.title: 2026 standard deduction
updates.book: The casebook uses 2022 values ($12,950 single; $25,900 joint).
updates.current: 2026 regular standard deduction: $16,100 single or MFS, $32,200 MFJ, $24,150 HOH, before potential additional amounts.

updates.title: 2026 state and local tax limit
updates.book: The casebook states a $10,000 SALT itemized-deduction cap since 2017.
updates.current: For 2026, generally $40,400 (half for MFS), with income-based phase-down and a floor; check statutory and IRS details.

updates.title: Loper Bright and Chevron
updates.book: The casebook describes Mayo/Chevron deference as governing Treasury regulations.
updates.current: Loper Bright (2024) overruled Chevron; courts exercise independent judgment under the APA when resolving statutory meaning.

updates.title: Modern realization doctrine
updates.book: The casebook presents Eisner v. Macomber as a historical constitutional bar to taxing unrealized gains.
updates.current: Moore (2024) upheld a tax on attributed undistributed corporate income but expressly did NOT decide whether realization is constitutionally required in all settings.

updates.title: Like-kind exchange qualifications
updates.book: The land/apartment exchange is presented as likely nonrecognition.
updates.current: §1031 nonrecognition applies only to qualifying like-kind real property held for business/investment, subject to detailed statutory conditions.

updates.title: 2026 gambling-loss deduction under §165(d)
updates.book: Chapter 2 describes deducting wagering losses up to the amount of winnings.
updates.current: For tax years beginning after 2025, allowable wagering loss deduction is limited to 90% of wagering losses and cannot exceed wagering gains; apply year-specific individual rules.

updates.title: 2026 employer meals deduction versus employee exclusion
updates.book: Chapter 2 discusses employer cafeteria deductions historically, alongside §119 exclusions for employee gross income.
updates.current: Beginning with amounts paid or incurred after 2025, §274(o) generally disallows specified employer deductions for §119 meals, subject to exceptions. Do not confuse employer deduction with employee §119 exclusion.

updates.title: Post-Gaylor Establishment Clause methodology
updates.book: The separately supplied 2019 Gaylor opinion analyzes §107(2) using contemporaneous Lemon-related Establishment Clause doctrine.
updates.current: Kennedy v. Bremerton (2022) rejected the Lemon/endorsement approach in favor of historical practices and understandings. The §107(2) statutory exclusion and Gaylor's ultimate result should not be conflated with the historical test it applied.

updates.title: Outcome after the assigned 2018 McKenney government brief (independently verified)
updates.book: Assigned five-page handout: government's Sept. 6, 2018 opening appeal brief arguing the accountants' $800,000 settlement should be taxable. The handout does not include the court's opinion.
updates.current: The Eleventh Circuit's Sept. 1, 2020 opinion reversed summary judgment for the taxpayers on exclusion of the $800,000. Assuming without deciding that Clark was correctly decided and could apply to transaction-structuring malpractice, the taxpayers failed to prove entitlement to an exclusion or its amount. This is supplemental research, NOT part of the attached 2018 advocacy excerpt.

updates.title: 2026 miscellaneous itemized deductions
updates.book: In a Chapter 1 note, the 2023 casebook describes the 2018–2025 suspension of §67 miscellaneous itemized deductions, including many unreimbursed employee expenses.
updates.current: Public Law 119-21 (2025) made the disallowance of miscellaneous itemized deductions subject to the former 2% floor permanent beginning with 2026 tax years, with specific educator-expense treatment. Do not assume the suspended category returned in 2026.

updates.title: Section 168(k) bonus depreciation — 2025 law update
updates.book: The 2023 assigned book discusses bonus depreciation declining year by year beginning in 2023.
updates.current: IRS Notice 2026-11 confirms permanent 100% bonus depreciation for eligible property acquired after Jan.19,2025 under P.L.119-21, subject to terms. This is outside textbook current-law verification; source pp163–164 remain historical.

updates.title: Section 448 2026 inflation adjusted cash-method limit
updates.book: The casebook gives historical $25m §448 gross-receipts threshold.
updates.current: The 2026 §448(c) inflation adjusted test is $32m average annual gross receipts for the three prior taxable years, subject to aggregation/exception rules.

updates.title: Moore (2024) and the constitutional realization question
updates.book: The 2023 casebook debates whether realization is constitutionally necessary and analyzes Macomber and modern realization doctrine.
updates.current: Moore (2024) held that shareholders can be taxed on undistributed income realized by an entity and attributed to them in a pass-through-style tax, but expressly reserved whether realization is always constitutionally required. NOT a reproduced syllabus opinion.

updates.title: Retirement required minimum distributions after SECURE 2.0
updates.book: The 2023 casebook uses an old 70½ required-distribution age.
updates.current: Current IRS guidance describes age 73 and age 75 cohorts under SECURE 2.0, plus designated Roth account distinctions; test year of birth and account type.

updates.title: Student loan CODI exclusion — 2026 §108(f)(5) amendment
updates.book: The assigned 2023 textbook describes a broad §108(f)(5) student-loan discharge income exclusion applicable in tax years 2021–2025.
updates.current: P.L.119-21 amended §108(f)(5) for post-2025 discharges to specified death/total and permanent disability cases, including an SSN-on-return condition; service-based exceptions elsewhere in §108(f) may still apply. Do not apply 2021–25 broad rule to ordinary 2026 income-driven forgiveness.

updates.title: Qualified principal-residence mortgage CODI exclusion — 2026 date
updates.book: The casebook states that certain qualified principal-residence loan discharges could qualify for §108 exclusion through 2025.
updates.current: §108(a)(1)(E) generally requires discharge before Jan.1,2026 or a written arrangement entered into before that date; §108(h) imposes substantive limitations and basis reduction.

topics.title: Chapter 1 — Introduction
topics.description: Conceptual gateway: the tax system, the tax calculation, tax planning, administration, and legal sources.

entries.title: The five questions that organize federal tax
entries.summary: What is taxed? How much? When? At what rate? And who pays?
entries.details: Use the entire course as one conceptual pipeline. The tax base identifies taxable income; timing determines the year; character and filing status influence rates; entity classification identifies the taxpayer; compliance rules determine reporting and dispute procedures. Source: conceptual synthesis of Chapter 1.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 1–33
entries.legalExplanation: Organize federal income-tax analysis in a sequence: (1) identify the taxpayer and receipts; (2) classify includible gross income and exclusions under §61 and related provisions; (3) calculate above-the-line adjustments under §62 and taxable income under §63; (4) determine character and timing; (5) apply progressive rate schedules and credits; and (6) reconcile payments and consider compliance requirements. This is a study map drawn from Chapter 1, not a single statutory test.
entries.laymanExplanation: On a tax exam, ask five big questions: what did the person get, who should pay tax on it, when does the tax event happen, what rate applies, and what adjustments or credits change the final bill?

entries.title: Tax base
entries.summary: The amount to which the tax-rate structure applies; for individuals, generally taxable income.
entries.details: Tax is not ordinarily imposed on all cash received. Begin with gross income, account for AGI deductions and additional deductions, apply rates to taxable income, then apply eligible credits and payments.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 11–15
entries.laymanExplanation: The tax base is the amount the government uses to figure out your tax. Think of it as the number the tax rate is applied to.
entries.legalExplanation: A tax base is the amount to which rates are applied. Under the personal federal income tax, taxable income is the relevant base, after inclusions, exclusions and legally allowable deductions have been determined. Do not confuse this tax base with gross receipts or economic income.

entries.title: The calculation pipeline
entries.summary: Gross income → AGI → taxable income → preliminary tax → credits → tax due/refund.
entries.details: 1. Determine inclusions and exclusions. 2. Gross income less adjustments/above-the-line deductions = AGI. 3. AGI less applicable below-the-line deductions = taxable income (subject to other statutory adjustments). 4. Apply tax rates and relevant special computations. 5. Apply tax credits. 6. Compare liability with withholding/estimated payments.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 11–16, 28
entries.legalExplanation: For an individual, start with gross income under §61 and exclusions, then subtract §62 above-the-line deductions to determine AGI. Under §63, subtract the applicable standard deduction or allowable itemized deductions and other applicable adjustments to arrive at taxable income. Apply rates and special computations, then credits, prepayments and withholding to find the final liability or refund. Each subtraction requires statutory eligibility.
entries.laymanExplanation: Think of a funnel. Start with money and benefits counted as income, subtract allowed deductions, apply tax rates, then subtract credits and amounts already paid.

topics.assignmentSource: Tax syllabus: Week 1, Chapter 1 pp. 1–33

topics.title: A. Why Income Taxes Matter
topics.description: Distribution, progressivity, economic incentives, lawyering, and tax policy.

entries.title: Income tax as collective cost allocation
entries.summary: Taxation allocates the financial burdens of government and reflects social-policy choices.
entries.details: The chapter frames taxation as part of the social contract: how costs should be shared and how much taxpayers should retain. The tax base and deductions embody value judgments as well as revenue needs.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 1–2
entries.legalExplanation: The casebook treats taxation as a way to share the costs of collective government activity. This is social and political background, not a rule authorizing a particular tax. Policy choices shape tax bases, rates, credits, and the distribution of burdens; statutory enactment is required to impose the actual income tax.
entries.laymanExplanation: Taxes pay for things society does together. The political disagreement is about how much each person should contribute.

entries.title: Progressive, proportional, regressive
entries.summary: Progressive: average rate rises with income; proportional: constant; regressive: falls.
entries.details: Classify tax systems using AVERAGE TAX RATE, not whether higher-income taxpayers pay more total dollars. The individual federal income tax is generally progressive; payroll and excise taxes often have regressive features.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 3–5, 16–17
entries.laymanExplanation: Progressive means higher earners pay a higher percentage on average. Proportional means everyone pays the same percentage. Regressive means lower earners pay a higher percentage of their income.
entries.legalExplanation: A tax system is called progressive, proportional or regressive by examining average tax rates as income increases. Progressive means the tax/income ratio rises; proportional means the ratio is constant; regressive means the ratio falls. Larger total dollar payments by wealthy taxpayers alone do not prove that a tax is progressive. The reading uses historical CBO 2018 distributional data to contrast income, payroll and excise taxes.
entries.examApplication: Compare the average rate at low, middle and high income. Does the percentage of income paid rise, stay constant, or fall? Do not rely on dollar liability alone.
entries.examTrap: A taxpayer can pay more dollars at a lower average tax rate. Progressivity depends on percentages.

entries.title: Negative income-tax liability
entries.summary: Refundable credits can produce net payments to an eligible taxpayer.
entries.details: The casebook describes negative average individual income-tax rates among lower-income quintiles in its 2018 data. Credits such as the EITC are central. Distinguish refundable-credit payments from merely withholding overpayments.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 3–5, 15
entries.laymanExplanation: Sometimes tax credits are worth more than the income tax you owe. If the credit is refundable, the government may pay you the difference.
entries.legalExplanation: Refundable credits can exceed a taxpayer's income-tax liability and create a net government payment. The earned income tax credit is an example in the reading. Negative net income-tax liability differs from simply receiving back excess wages withheld from a positive tax bill. It does not necessarily mean negative tax liability across every federal tax category.

entries.title: Federal revenue and distribution data — historical
entries.summary: The casebook uses FY 2021 revenue and 2018 tax-burden data as historical illustrations.
