entries.details: FY 2021: individual income tax 51%; corporate income tax 9%; payroll/social insurance 32% of total federal revenues (source Table 1-1). In 2018 the individual income-tax average rate ranged from −12% in the lowest quintile to 15.4% in the top quintile (Table 1-2). These are dated snapshots, not current estimates.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Tables 1-1 through 1-3 (historical data)
entries.legalExplanation: Table 1-1 reports 2021 federal revenue: individual income taxes $2,044 billion (51%), corporate income taxes $372 billion (9%), payroll/social-insurance $1,314 billion (32%), excise $75 billion (2%), estate/gift $27 billion (1%), other $214 billion (5%), total $4,046 billion. Table 1-2 reports 2018 average individual-income-tax rates of −12.0%, −2.1%, 2.2%, 5.9% and 15.4% across ascending quintiles; overall federal average tax rates were 0.0%, 8.1%, 12.8%, 16.7% and 24.4%. Table 1-3 shows the top quintile's pretax-income share grew from 46.0% in 1980 to 55.2% in 2018. These figures illustrate historical distribution; they are not 2026 rates.
entries.laymanExplanation: The old tables show where federal tax money came from and how much different income groups paid. They're snapshots of past years, not tax rates to use on today's return.

entries.title: Income effect vs. substitution effect
entries.summary: Income effect: need to replace lost disposable income; substitution: after-tax incentives change choices.
entries.details: Income tax may cause someone to work more to replace lost take-home pay (income effect) or work less because leisure becomes relatively attractive (substitution effect). Theory alone does not identify which dominates for a particular taxpayer.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 6–7
entries.legalExplanation: An income effect arises because tax reduces disposable resources, potentially inducing someone to earn more to restore their spending power. A substitution effect arises because tax changes relative returns: taxable work may become less attractive relative to untaxed leisure or nonmarket activity. These forces can move labor supply in opposite directions; the casebook warns that theory alone does not determine the net result.
entries.laymanExplanation: A tax might make someone work more because they need to replace lost income, or work less because keeping free time now feels better than earning taxed wages. Both can happen.

entries.title: Tax expenditures and behavioral incentives
entries.summary: Deductions, exclusions, and credits can subsidize activities through the tax system.
entries.details: For example, homeowner and charitable tax provisions may encourage particular spending. A $6 million government grant and a $6 million tax reduction may confer similar benefits even though framed differently in political debate.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 7–8
entries.legalExplanation: Tax preferences can be understood as implicit subsidies because deductions, exclusions, and credits reduce the tax paid by favored activities. The source compares a $6 million direct subsidy with an equivalent tax reduction for a firm owing $10 million: both may leave a $4 million net payment, given the assumed facts. Distinguish this policy analogy from the legal calculation of a particular deduction.
entries.laymanExplanation: Instead of giving people a cash grant to encourage something, the government can lower their tax bill if they do it. That tax break changes incentives.

entries.title: Distributional effects without explicit race classifications
entries.summary: Facially race-neutral deductions can have uneven impacts given differences in income and wealth.
entries.details: The chapter examines how itemizing and homeowner tax benefits can be unevenly distributed. Keep separate: (1) disparities linked to income distribution and (2) differences that may remain among groups with comparable income or wealth. Treat the book’s demographic statistics as historical.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 8–9
entries.legalExplanation: Formally facially neutral provisions can generate disparate benefits when income, homeownership or itemization patterns differ across groups. The reading distinguishes (1) differences produced through the distribution of income and wealth and (2) possible differential effects at similar income levels. Its demographic figures describe dated empirical observations and are not legal eligibility elements.
entries.laymanExplanation: A tax rule doesn't need to name a racial group to have different average effects across groups. Existing differences in income, housing and wealth can affect who benefits.

entries.title: Tax implications in general legal practice
entries.summary: Tax planning affects property transfers, settlements, business entities, compensation, and family law.
entries.details: Lawyers must spot when a proposed transaction has tax consequences, even if tax is not their specialty. Legal complexity creates incentives to structure transactions to comply and reduce liability.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 6
entries.legalExplanation: The reading emphasizes tax issue-spotting for attorneys across practice areas: property sales, leases and financing, divorce settlements, entity choice, compensation structures and damages settlements may trigger income-tax consequences. This is practical professional context, not a governing rule.
entries.laymanExplanation: Even when you're not a tax lawyer, your client's divorce, settlement, property sale, business formation or job contract might have tax consequences worth spotting.

entries.title: Quintile and average tax burden
entries.summary: A quintile is one of five equal-sized groups sorted by income; the reading compares average tax rates across income quintiles.
entries.details: The 2018 CBO table groups households by income fifths and compares tax burdens across tax types; it is historical empirical evidence, not a tax statute.
entries.laymanExplanation: A quintile is just 20% of the people after you line them up by income. Comparing five groups helps show who carries more tax.
entries.legalExplanation: The 2018 CBO table groups households by income fifths and compares tax burdens across tax types; it is historical empirical evidence, not a tax statute.
entries.source: Assigned Week 1, Bankman/Shaviro/Stark/Scharff, Federal Income Taxation, 19th ed., Ch. 1, printed pp. 4–6

entries.title: Tax expenditure
entries.summary: A statutory tax preference, such as a deduction, exclusion, or credit, that can subsidize behavior through foregone tax revenue.
entries.details: The reading compares a $6 million direct government grant with a $6 million reduction in a taxpayer's bill. Similar net economic benefits can look different politically and be administered differently.
entries.laymanExplanation: A tax break can work a lot like the government giving someone money. Instead of sending a check, it lets the person keep more of what they would otherwise owe.
entries.legalExplanation: The reading compares a $6 million direct government grant with a $6 million reduction in a taxpayer's bill. Similar net economic benefits can look different politically and be administered differently.
entries.source: Assigned Week 1, Bankman/Shaviro/Stark/Scharff, Federal Income Taxation, 19th ed., Ch. 1, printed pp. 7–8

topics.assignmentSource: Tax syllabus: Week 1, Chapter 1 pp. 1–33

topics.title: B. U.S. Income Tax History
topics.description: Origins, Pollock, the Sixteenth Amendment, and the mass income tax.

entries.title: Tariffs and excise taxes
entries.summary: Tariffs tax cross-border goods; excise taxes target particular products or services.
entries.details: Before the modern income tax, the federal government depended heavily on tariffs and excise taxes. Both affect prices and burden distribution differently from individual income taxes.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 9–10
entries.laymanExplanation: Tariffs are taxes on goods brought in from abroad. Excise taxes target particular goods or activities, such as fuel.
entries.legalExplanation: Tariffs are taxes on cross-border trade in goods. Excise taxes generally fall on specified goods or activities. The federal government historically relied heavily on tariffs and excises before the permanent modern individual income tax.

entries.title: Historical authority: Pollock v. Farmers' Loan & Trust Co. (1895)
entries.summary: The Court invalidated the 1894 income tax based on direct-tax apportionment concerns.
entries.details: Facts: Challenge to federal tax on rents, dividends, and interest. Issue: whether the tax contravened constitutional apportionment requirements for direct taxes. Holding: the Court invalidated the income-tax law. Why it matters: it prompted a constitutional solution—the Sixteenth Amendment. The textbook gives the historical constitutional account.

legalWarning.label: SUPERSEDED — HISTORICAL
legalWarning.reason: The Sixteenth Amendment (1913) removed the apportionment obstacle for taxes on income. Pollock is studied to explain why the Amendment was adopted, not as the current rule restricting income taxation.
legalWarning.authority: Sixteenth Amendment; Moore v. United States (2024)

entries.legalExplanation: The Supreme Court treated the 1894 tax on rents, dividends and interest as violating direct-tax apportionment requirements and invalidated the law after finding the provisions inseverable. This is historical constitutional context. The Sixteenth Amendment subsequently permitted unapportioned federal income taxes, so Pollock's apportionment objection is not a current general bar to income taxation. This case is cited/discussed in text, not reproduced as an assigned judicial opinion.
entries.laymanExplanation: The Supreme Court once blocked a federal income tax because of constitutional apportionment rules. The Sixteenth Amendment later removed that obstacle for taxes on income.

entries.title: Sixteenth Amendment (1913)
entries.summary: Congress may tax incomes from any source without apportionment among the states.
entries.details: It responded to the direct-tax obstacle identified in Pollock and enabled the modern federal income tax. The definition of income and the limits of congressional taxing power remain subjects of doctrine and litigation.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 10
entries.laymanExplanation: The Sixteenth Amendment lets Congress impose federal income taxes without dividing the tax bill among states according to population.
entries.legalExplanation: The Sixteenth Amendment provides Congress power to lay and collect taxes on income from whatever source derived without apportionment among states or regard to census enumeration. It does not independently specify every includible receipt or eliminate statutory exclusions, which must be analyzed under the Code.
entries.examTrap: The amendment removes the apportionment barrier for income taxes; it does not tell you all items are included in taxable income.

entries.title: Evolution from class tax to mass tax
entries.summary: Civil War income taxes → 1894 tax and Pollock → 1913 amendment → WWI growth → WWII mass tax.
entries.details: 1861 first Civil War income tax; 1894 progressive revival; 1895 Pollock; 1913 Sixteenth Amendment; WWI sharply expanded rates; WWII brought broad population coverage. Later Congress repeatedly revised brackets, rates, and deductions.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 9–11
entries.legalExplanation: The reading traces the Civil War tax, repeal and tariff reliance, the 1894 income tax and 1895 Pollock decision, the Sixteenth Amendment of 1913, high wartime rates, and the World War II expansion from a narrow 'class tax' to a broader 'mass tax.' These developments are useful background, not tax rates to use for today's calculations.

legalWarning.label: 2026 PROJECTION OUTDATED
legalWarning.reason: The 2023 casebook predicted that the 37% top individual bracket would revert to 39.6% in 2026. Congress made the existing seven individual rates, including 37%, permanent in Public Law 119-21 (2025). Treat historical tax-rate figures as examples, not current schedules.

entries.laymanExplanation: At first, the federal income tax mostly targeted wealthy people. After World War II it covered a much broader part of the population.

topics.assignmentSource: Tax syllabus: Week 1, Chapter 1 pp. 1–33

topics.title: C. Core Tax Terminology and Doctrines
topics.description: The chapter’s most exam-useful material: the calculation pipeline and major classifications.

entries.title: IRC § 61 — Gross income
entries.summary: Gross income starts with a broad inclusion rule: income from whatever source derived, absent an exclusion.
entries.details: Examples listed by the chapter: wages, salary, interest, dividends and rents. The tax-law concept differs from economic income because Congress excludes some receipts. Verify exclusion provisions before determining the tax base.
entries.source: IRC § 61; Bankman et al. pp. 11–12
entries.examApplication: When a taxpayer receives a payment, begin with § 61's broad inclusion principle. Determine whether it is an economic gain, then look for a statutory exclusion or other limiting rule.
entries.examTrap: Do not assume that a receipt is exempt because it is unusual, punitive, or received outside employment; identify a legal basis for exclusion.
entries.laymanExplanation: Start by assuming that money or other valuable things you receive may count as income. Then check whether a specific tax-law rule says otherwise.
entries.legalExplanation: Section 61(a) broadly defines gross income as all income from whatever source derived and provides a nonexclusive list. Wages, interest, dividends and rents are examples. Other Code provisions govern special inclusions and exclusions, and neither economic intuition nor a descriptive label alone determines statutory taxability. Examine the specific facts and any applicable exclusion.

entries.title: Gross receipts versus gross income
entries.summary: Gross receipts are cash sales proceeds; inventory gross income generally subtracts cost of goods sold.
entries.details: For merchandising businesses, gross income from inventory sales means gross profit rather than gross cash receipts. Inventory costs recovered through COGS are not the same as personal deductions.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 12–13
entries.laymanExplanation: A shop might collect $100 selling something it bought for $70. The $100 is gross receipts; after subtracting the item's cost, its gross profit is $30.
entries.legalExplanation: Gross receipts are the entire amount a business takes in from sales, while for inventory sales the merchandise cost is recovered in determining gross income. The textbook's two $20 hammers yield $40 gross receipts, but $24 cost of goods sold, leaving $16 gross profit/inventory gross income. Separate COGS from operating-expense deductions.
entries.examApplication: Calculate gross receipts and cost of goods sold separately. For two hammers at $20 sales price and $12 cost each, 2×$20=$40 receipts; 2×$12=$24 COGS; gross profit=$16.
entries.examTrap: Gross receipts and taxable income are not interchangeable; COGS differs from a personal below-the-line deduction.

entries.title: Adjusted gross income — AGI
entries.summary: Gross income less applicable §62 adjustments/above-the-line deductions = AGI.
entries.details: AGI is an intermediate statutory measure, NOT the individual’s final tax base. Deductions below AGI, including eligible standard or itemized deductions, take the taxpayer toward taxable income.
entries.source: IRC § 62; Bankman et al. pp. 13–14
entries.examApplication: Start with gross income and subtract the qualifying deductions identified in § 62 to compute AGI; only afterward consider applicable below-the-line deductions.
entries.examTrap: AGI and taxable income are not the same number.
entries.laymanExplanation: AGI is an intermediate number on the way to taxable income: take gross income and subtract certain deductions that the law lets you take before the next stage.
entries.legalExplanation: Adjusted gross income under §62 generally equals gross income less specified deductions that are allowed in arriving at AGI. The source calls AGI a 'way station'; it is used for subsequent tax calculations and limitations, not generally the final tax base. Only qualifying statutory items belong above the line.

entries.title: Taxable income — § 63
entries.summary: Taxable income is the tax base after permissible deductions from gross income/AGI.
entries.details: Conceptual sequence: AGI, then allowed below-the-line deductions (normally the standard deduction OR itemized deductions, plus other relevant statutory amounts). A taxpayer generally does not claim both standard and itemized deductions.
entries.source: IRC § 63; Bankman et al. pp. 13–15
entries.laymanExplanation: Taxable income is the amount left after the deductions the law allows. It's the number used to apply the income-tax rates.
entries.legalExplanation: Under §63, taxable income for individuals generally begins with gross income less legally allowable deductions, commonly computed from AGI minus the appropriate standard or itemized deductions. Additional provisions, limitations and special rules affect the amount. The resulting taxable income is the base to which income-tax rate schedules are applied before credits.
entries.examApplication: Ask whether a payment is included in gross income, whether a deduction is above or below AGI, whether itemizing beats the standard deduction, and whether a credit is available.
entries.examTrap: Do not double-claim standard and itemized deductions. Use figures for the specified tax year, not 2022 amounts in an old example.

entries.title: Above-the-line and below-the-line
entries.summary: Above-line reduces gross income to AGI; below-line reduces AGI to taxable income.
entries.details: These are practitioner shorthand, not formal statutory terms. The distinction matters because AGI influences limits and other tax computations; above-line deductions can be more advantageous.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 13–14
entries.laymanExplanation: Above-the-line deductions are taken before AGI is calculated. Below-the-line deductions generally come afterward, when going from AGI to taxable income.
entries.legalExplanation: Above-the-line and below-the-line are practical shorthand for deductions taken respectively before and after calculation of AGI. They do not appear as controlling Code labels. Above-the-line deductions generally remain available regardless of itemizing; many below-the-line personal deductions depend on itemization and statutory thresholds.

entries.title: Deduction versus credit
entries.summary: Deduction reduces taxable income; credit reduces tax liability dollar for dollar, subject to its rules.
entries.details: Approximate value of a marginal deduction = amount × applicable marginal rate (only if fully usable and not crossing rate brackets or phased-out benefits). A nonrefundable credit helps only to extent of eligible tax liability; refundable credits can yield a payment.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 15–16
entries.examApplication: When given a $1,000 deduction at 30%, approximate the tax benefit as $300; a fully usable $1,000 tax credit can reduce the bill by $1,000. Check deductibility, limitations and phaseouts.
entries.examTrap: A tax credit is not multiplied by the marginal tax rate the way a deduction typically is.
entries.laymanExplanation: A deduction reduces how much income gets taxed. A credit reduces the tax bill itself. A $1,000 credit usually saves more than a $1,000 deduction.
entries.legalExplanation: A deduction subtracts an allowed amount from the tax base, so its incremental tax saving ordinarily depends on the relevant marginal tax rate. A credit reduces computed tax directly, dollar for dollar as permitted. A $100 deduction at a 37% marginal rate may save $37, while a fully usable $100 credit reduces tax by $100. The source distinguishes refundable and nonrefundable credits.

entries.title: Exclusion, exemption, deduction
entries.summary: An exclusion is not counted as income; a deduction is subtracted; exemption may describe tax-free taxpayers or receipts.
entries.details: Gifts under § 102 and certain other receipts are cited as examples of statutory exclusions. An exclusion of $50 and inclusion followed by a usable $50 deduction can have comparable current-year tax-base effects, but other rules may make them differ.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 15–16
entries.laymanExplanation: An exclusion keeps something out of income in the first place. A deduction subtracts an allowed amount later. 'Exemption' is a separate tax-law term whose meaning depends on the provision.
entries.legalExplanation: An exclusion removes an item from gross income. A deduction subtracts an allowable expense or amount after inclusion. 'Exemption' can be used informally for tax-favored status, but may also denote a specific statutory mechanism. Assuming equal deductibility and no collateral effects, excluding $50 and deducting the same $50 after inclusion can produce the same liability; whether they do depends on applicable limits.

entries.title: Progressive tax brackets are layered
entries.summary: Only the income in a higher bracket is taxed at its higher marginal rate.
entries.details: If hypothetical tax rates are 20% on the first $50,000 and 40% above $50,000, $50,010 taxable income creates $10,004 tax—not 40% of the full $50,010. This is a stylized illustration, not actual federal rate tables.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 16–17
entries.examApplication: Apply each marginal rate only to the taxable income falling inside its bracket.
entries.examTrap: Moving into a higher bracket does not retroactively subject all lower-bracket income to that higher rate.
entries.laymanExplanation: Only the part of your income that falls inside a higher tax bracket gets that bracket's higher rate—not your entire income.
entries.legalExplanation: Progressive rates are applied marginally: divide taxable income among brackets and multiply each layer by its own rate. In the book's artificial two-rate illustration, $50,010 of taxable income yields $50,000 × 20% + $10 × 40% = $10,004; $60,000 yields $14,000. Neither example is a federal rate schedule for 2026.

entries.title: Marginal vs. average tax rate
entries.summary: Marginal rate taxes the next dollar; average rate equals tax liability ÷ chosen income measure.
entries.details: A taxpayer can face a 40% marginal bracket while having an average rate near 23% in the book’s hypothetical $60,000 example. Apply the marginal rate to incremental income or a fully usable deduction within that bracket.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 17–18
entries.laymanExplanation: Your marginal rate tells you the rate on your next dollar of taxable income. Your average rate is your total tax divided by an appropriate income measure.
entries.legalExplanation: The marginal rate is the rate affecting the taxpayer's next taxable dollar; the average rate is total tax divided by a stated measure of income. Using the casebook's hypothetical, tax is $14,000 on $60,000 taxable income under 20%/40% brackets: average rate 23.33%, marginal rate 40%. A deduction affecting only the top bracket generally saves its amount multiplied by the marginal rate.
entries.examApplication: Use the chapter's hypothetical: tax=$50,000×20%+$10,000×40%=$14,000; average=$14,000/$60,000=23.33%; marginal=40%.

entries.title: Statutory vs. effective tax rate
entries.summary: Statutory reflects legal bracket schedule; effective may account for broader income and phaseouts.
entries.details: An effective marginal rate can exceed the stated marginal bracket where a refundable credit or benefit is phased out as income rises. Always identify what counts in both numerator (tax) and denominator (income).
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 17–18
entries.laymanExplanation: The statutory rate is the percentage stated in the tax brackets. The effective rate tries to show what tax actually costs after other rules such as credits and phaseouts.
entries.legalExplanation: A statutory rate comes from the rate structure enacted in the Code. 'Effective' can refer to a broader measure of actual tax burden, including a denominator based on economic rather than taxable income, or an effective marginal burden including lost benefits during credit phaseouts. Always specify the denominator and which taxes/benefits are counted.
entries.examApplication: If a credit is phased out by $0.20 per extra $1 of earnings, add the phaseout effect to the statutory incremental burden to find an effective marginal rate, where appropriate.

entries.title: Ordinary income versus capital gain
entries.summary: Capital gain arises from sale/exchange of capital assets; not every capital gain gets preferential rates.
entries.details: Capital asset definition (§ 1221) generally includes investment stock but excludes, among other things, inventory and property held mainly for sale to customers. Long-term means held MORE than one year; one year or less is short-term. Preferential rates concern net capital gain after the required netting and other restrictions.
entries.source: IRC §§ 64, 1221, 1222; Bankman et al. pp. 19–20
entries.laymanExplanation: Paychecks and many business earnings are ordinary income. Profits from selling certain investments may be capital gains, which can be taxed differently.
entries.legalExplanation: Ordinary income includes gains or receipts not receiving special capital-gain treatment. Under §§1221–1222, a capital gain generally arises from sale or exchange of a capital asset, but preferential treatment depends on holding period and statutory net capital gain. Short-term gains generally enter ordinary rate computation; merely labeling gain 'capital' does not guarantee a reduced rate.
entries.examApplication: Classify the asset under §1221, compute realized gain, determine holding period, net capital gain/losses, then identify which portion gets special rates.
entries.examTrap: Capital gain is not always long-term, and not all capital gain qualifies for preferential rates.

entries.title: Capital loss limitations
entries.summary: For individuals, net capital losses generally offset capital gains plus up to $3,000 of ordinary income annually.
entries.details: The chapter notes loss limitations under §1211. Separate capital losses from business expense deductions under §162 and general losses under §165; carryover and other limits are addressed later.
entries.source: IRC §§ 1211, 165; Bankman et al. pp. 19–20
entries.examApplication: When a taxpayer sells capital assets at gains and losses, net capital gains and losses before applying the applicable individual capital-loss limit.
entries.examTrap: Do not treat a capital loss as an unlimited offset against ordinary income.
entries.laymanExplanation: Losing money on investments doesn't mean you can always subtract the entire loss from your salary. Tax law places limits on capital losses.
entries.legalExplanation: Section 1211 generally limits capital loss use: individual net capital losses may offset capital gains, plus no more than $3,000 of other income in a year ($1,500 for married filing separately), with carryovers under related rules. Distinguish capital-loss netting from trade/business deductions under §162 and other loss deductions under §165.

entries.title: Business expenses versus losses
entries.summary: Expenses are ordinary operating costs; losses reflect shortfalls on property/transactions and use different rules.
entries.details: Section 162 allows ordinary and necessary business expenses subject to statutory limits; § 165 governs important loss deductions. The labels matter because they follow separate legal tests.
entries.laymanExplanation: An expense is money spent to operate a business. A loss can arise when a property or transaction ends up worth less than its tax cost; different deduction rules apply.
entries.legalExplanation: Section 162 permits deductions for ordinary and necessary business expenses, subject to limits. Section 165 addresses certain losses, including those from dispositions and other qualifying events. A periodic cost of operating a business and an economic loss on property may both reduce income but have distinct legal predicates and limitations.

entries.title: Cash method versus accrual method
entries.summary: Cash: generally recognize income when received and expenses when paid; accrual: generally when earned/incurred.
entries.details: The book illustrates Year 1 services and Year 2 payment. Timing of inclusion and deduction can differ by accounting method and by special limitations. The capital-expenditure requirement applies even to cash-method taxpayers.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 20–21
entries.examApplication: For services performed Year 1 but billed and paid Year 2, cash method generally uses Year 2; accrual method generally points to Year 1 if all applicable conditions are met.
entries.examTrap: The cash method does not let you deduct land or machinery immediately merely because you paid cash.
entries.laymanExplanation: Under the cash method, payment timing generally matters. Under the accrual method, earning the income or incurring the expense generally matters—even when cash moves later.
entries.legalExplanation: Under the cash method, an item generally enters income when actually or constructively received and a deduction generally follows payment, subject to restrictions. Under the accrual method, income is generally included when earned and liabilities may be deducted when the relevant all-events and economic-performance tests are met. The casebook's accountant performs $500 work in Year 1 but is paid Year 2: cash treatment generally points to Year 2; accrual to Year 1, if requirements are satisfied.

entries.title: Capital expenditure versus current expense
entries.summary: A long-lived asset’s acquisition cost ordinarily cannot simply be expensed immediately.
entries.details: Land basis is usually recovered on disposition; depreciable machinery generally receives cost recovery over time, subject to statutory accelerated-depreciation/expensing provisions. Do not treat every cash purchase as a current deduction.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 20–22
entries.laymanExplanation: Buying office supplies and buying a building are treated differently. The building usually has to be capitalized, with its cost recovered over time or on sale rather than all at once.
entries.legalExplanation: Capital expenditures acquire or improve assets whose costs generally are recovered through basis, depreciation or later disposition, rather than automatically as current §162 expenses. The source contrasts $400,000 of land (normally retained in basis) with $50,000 tractor and $100,000 machinery (potentially recoverable under depreciation rules). Special expensing provisions can modify timing.
entries.examApplication: Buying land for $400,000 or machinery for $100,000 is not automatically a current deductible expense. Determine capitalization, depreciation and any statutory expensing election.

entries.title: Basis and adjusted basis
entries.summary: Basis is the taxpayer's tax investment in property (often its cost); adjusted basis reflects required increases and decreases, such as improvements and depreciation.
entries.details: Improvements generally increase basis; depreciation generally reduces basis. Basis supports cost recovery and the measurement of gain or loss when property is disposed of.
entries.source: IRC §§ 1012, 1016; Bankman et al. pp. 21–22
entries.examApplication: Purchase an asset for $100, improve it by $20, take $5 depreciation: adjusted basis=$100+$20−$5=$115 (assuming all adjustments apply). A $150 sale would yield $35 realized gain before special rules.
entries.examTrap: Depreciation can reduce adjusted basis even when the asset's market price has increased.
entries.laymanExplanation: Basis is the tax system's record of what you invested in an asset. Buy something for $100 and improve it for $20: the adjusted basis may be $120, before other adjustments.
entries.legalExplanation: Basis generally begins with acquisition cost under §1012; adjusted basis reflects applicable increases, such as qualifying capital improvements, and reductions, such as depreciation allowed or allowable, under §1016. Under §1001 the amount realized on a disposition is compared to adjusted basis to determine realized gain or loss. The source uses basis to prevent recovery of capital from being taxed as new income.

entries.title: Realization versus recognition
entries.summary: Realization identifies a triggering gain/loss event; recognition asks whether it enters current taxable income.
entries.details: An exchange or sale ordinarily realizes gain. A nonrecognition provision can defer some or all gain. Every recognized gain ordinarily follows a realization event, but not every realized gain is immediately recognized. For §1031 after 2017, qualifying like-kind exchange rules concern real property held for investment or business use—not all exchanges.
entries.source: IRC §§ 1001, 1031; Bankman et al. p. 22
entries.alert: Current-law qualification: §1031 is limited to qualifying real-property exchanges; the book’s land-for-apartment illustration requires statutory conditions.
entries.examApplication: Buy land for $1m, exchange it once worth $5m for like-kind rental property. First determine the $4m realized gain; only then consider §1031 nonrecognition and conditions.
entries.examTrap: Realized does not automatically equal recognized; §1031 requires qualifying real property held for business/investment.
entries.laymanExplanation: Realization is when something happens, like a sale, that turns a paper gain into a tax event. Recognition asks whether the tax law actually makes you report that gain now.
entries.legalExplanation: Realization refers to a taxable-event trigger such as disposition; mere market appreciation normally remains unrealized. Recognition determines whether realized gain or loss is currently taken into account after statutory nonrecognition rules. The book gives $1 million-basis land worth $5 million, later exchanged for a $5 million apartment building: $4 million realized gain, potentially deferred under §1031 if the exchange qualifies. Since 2018 §1031 applies to eligible real-property exchanges, subject to detailed conditions; not all swaps are tax-free.

entries.title: Sole proprietorship and partnerships
entries.summary: Sole proprietor reports directly; partnerships generally pass taxable income and losses through to partners.
entries.details: The partnership files an information return but generally does not pay entity-level federal income tax. Owners separately report their distributive shares under partnership rules, not necessarily cash received.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 22–23
entries.laymanExplanation: A sole proprietor and a partner generally report business income through individual returns, though partnerships have their own reporting rules.
entries.legalExplanation: For a sole proprietor, business receipts and deductions generally enter the owner's federal income-tax calculation directly. Partnerships file informational returns and generally pass distributive shares of tax items to partners rather than paying the regular entity-level income tax. Reporting is not necessarily postponed until cash is distributed.

entries.title: LLCs, S corporations, C corporations
entries.summary: Tax treatment depends on classification: pass-through forms differ from C-corporation entity taxation.
entries.details: The casebook simplifies LLCs as partnerships, but real classification can vary: one-member LLCs may be disregarded, multi-member LLCs often default to partnerships, and eligible LLCs can elect corporate treatment. C corporations generally pay entity-level tax; dividends can be taxed again to shareholders. S corporations generally pass through income under eligibility restrictions.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 22–23
entries.alert: Textbook simplification: do not assume every LLC is taxed as a partnership.
entries.laymanExplanation: Different business forms can lead to different tax bills. A corporation may pay tax itself, while some LLCs and S corporations pass income through to owners.
entries.legalExplanation: A C corporation generally pays income tax as a separate legal entity, and distributed earnings may be taxed again to shareholders. An S corporation generally passes income through to eligible owners, subject to entity-type and eligibility constraints. The casebook treats LLCs as partnership analogues for introductory purposes; in practice the federal classification depends on membership and elections.

entries.title: Tax treatment of trusts
entries.summary: Trusts can serve as conduits but may also have their own income-tax liability.
entries.details: Trustee holds property for beneficiaries; tax depends on income accumulation/distribution and trust classification. Chapter 1 provides only an orientation, not the detailed trust rules.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 23
entries.laymanExplanation: A trust holds and manages assets for beneficiaries. Depending on its rules and distributions, tax may be paid by the trust or by beneficiaries.
entries.legalExplanation: A trustee holds and administers assets for beneficiaries. Depending on the trust category, distribution and accumulation, income may be taxed to the trust or its beneficiaries. Chapter 1 gives only a conceptual introduction and does not supply full Subchapter J rules.

entries.title: Nominal gain versus real gain
entries.summary: Inflation can produce taxable nominal gains even where purchasing power has not increased.
entries.details: Illustration: $100 cost grows to $105 with 5% inflation; $5 nominal gain need not represent real economic improvement. Tax basis is generally not inflation-indexed, while brackets and certain dollar thresholds are adjusted under statutory rules.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 23–24
entries.laymanExplanation: If something rises in price only because everything has become more expensive, your paper profit may not represent a real increase in purchasing power.
entries.legalExplanation: Nominal gain is measured in dollars without adjusting for changes in purchasing power; real gain measures inflation-adjusted improvement. In the example, an asset bought for $100 and sold for $105 after 5% inflation has $5 nominal gain but essentially no real purchasing-power gain. Federal income-tax basis is not generally indexed simply because prices rose.

entries.title: Bracket creep and inflation indexing
entries.summary: Without inflation adjustment, rising nominal income can push taxpayers into higher brackets without real growth.
entries.details: Congress indexed specified tax brackets and amounts to inflation; the book identifies §§1(f) and 151(f) and use of chained CPI. Indexing is distinct from adjusting a taxpayer’s investment basis for inflation.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 24
entries.legalExplanation: Bracket creep occurs when nominal income rises with inflation, potentially pushing taxpayers into higher rate brackets despite unchanged real purchasing power. The book explains inflation indexing of brackets and certain dollar amounts and the shift to chained CPI. This is separate from (generally unavailable) inflation indexing of property tax basis.
entries.laymanExplanation: If inflation doubles your paycheck but also doubles all prices, you aren't necessarily better off. Tax brackets need to adjust too, or your rate could rise without any real income growth.

entries.title: Cost of goods sold (COGS)
entries.summary: The inventory cost recovered before a seller determines gross income from selling merchandise.
entries.details: In inventory transactions, gross income from sales is generally gross receipts minus properly measured cost of goods sold. COGS is conceptually distinct from an ordinary personal itemized deduction. In the textbook's example, two $20 hammers costing $12 each yield $40 receipts − $24 inventory cost = $16 gross income.
entries.laymanExplanation: When a shop sells something, it doesn't make a profit on all the cash it collects. It first subtracts what it paid for the product.
entries.legalExplanation: In inventory transactions, gross income from sales is generally gross receipts minus properly measured cost of goods sold. COGS is conceptually distinct from an ordinary personal itemized deduction. In the textbook's example, two $20 hammers costing $12 each yield $40 receipts − $24 inventory cost = $16 gross income.
entries.source: Assigned Week 1, Bankman/Shaviro/Stark/Scharff, Federal Income Taxation, 19th ed., Ch. 1, printed pp. 12–13

entries.title: Standard deduction or itemized deductions — §63
entries.summary: Eligible individuals generally reduce AGI using the applicable standard deduction OR allowable itemized deductions, subject to statutory limitations; they cannot simply add both.
entries.details: In computing taxable income, compare the allowed standard deduction with allowable itemized deductions. Itemized amounts are useful only insofar as they exceed the standard deduction. The 2022 thresholds and $10,000 state/local tax deduction cap in the printed source are historical, not 2026 limits. Special rules apply to filing status and other categories.
entries.laymanExplanation: You normally get to choose one: take a fixed deduction provided by law, or add up qualifying itemized expenses. Choose whichever actually saves more, subject to the law.
entries.legalExplanation: In computing taxable income, compare the allowed standard deduction with allowable itemized deductions. Itemized amounts are useful only insofar as they exceed the standard deduction. The 2022 thresholds and $10,000 state/local tax deduction cap in the printed source are historical, not 2026 limits. Special rules apply to filing status and other categories.
entries.source: Assigned Week 1, Bankman/Shaviro/Stark/Scharff, Federal Income Taxation, 19th ed., Ch. 1, printed pp. 14–15

legalWarning.label: USE CURRENT TAX-YEAR LIMITS
legalWarning.reason: The textbook uses 2022 standard deduction and SALT limit figures. 2026 limits differ: for 2026, the regular standard deduction is $16,100 for single filers, $32,200 for joint filers; the general SALT cap is $40,400, subject to income-based reduction and other statutory conditions.
legalWarning.authority: IRS 2026 inflation adjustment guidance and 2026 Form 1040-ES correction

entries.title: Standard deduction
entries.summary: An amount allowed under §63 that reduces taxable income without proving a full set of itemized expenses.
entries.details: The standard deduction depends on filing status, tax year, and special eligibility rules. The 2022 standard deduction amounts quoted in the 2023 casebook are dated. Determine the applicable year before computing liability.
entries.laymanExplanation: It's a default amount the government lets many taxpayers subtract instead of keeping receipts for every eligible itemized expense.
entries.legalExplanation: The standard deduction depends on filing status, tax year, and special eligibility rules. The 2022 standard deduction amounts quoted in the 2023 casebook are dated. Determine the applicable year before computing liability.
entries.source: Assigned Week 1, Bankman/Shaviro/Stark/Scharff, Federal Income Taxation, 19th ed., Ch. 1, printed pp. 14–15

legalWarning.label: USE CURRENT TAX-YEAR LIMITS
legalWarning.reason: The textbook uses 2022 standard deduction and SALT limit figures. 2026 limits differ: for 2026, the regular standard deduction is $16,100 for single filers, $32,200 for joint filers; the general SALT cap is $40,400, subject to income-based reduction and other statutory conditions.
legalWarning.authority: IRS 2026 inflation adjustment guidance and 2026 Form 1040-ES correction

entries.title: Itemized deduction
entries.summary: A separately allowed deductible expense that an individual claims instead of using the standard deduction, subject to applicable statutory limits.
entries.details: Typical examples in the reading include qualified mortgage interest, charitable contributions, certain medical expenses, and certain state/local taxes. The amount legally deductible depends on the tax year, category limits, income limits, and whether the taxpayer itemizes. The reading's $13,000 mortgage-interest example uses a historical $12,950 standard deduction.
entries.laymanExplanation: Itemizing means listing eligible costs one by one. It's usually only worthwhile if the allowed total beats your standard deduction.
entries.legalExplanation: Typical examples in the reading include qualified mortgage interest, charitable contributions, certain medical expenses, and certain state/local taxes. The amount legally deductible depends on the tax year, category limits, income limits, and whether the taxpayer itemizes. The reading's $13,000 mortgage-interest example uses a historical $12,950 standard deduction.
entries.source: Assigned Week 1, Bankman/Shaviro/Stark/Scharff, Federal Income Taxation, 19th ed., Ch. 1, printed pp. 14–15

legalWarning.label: USE CURRENT TAX-YEAR LIMITS
legalWarning.reason: The textbook uses 2022 standard deduction and SALT limit figures. 2026 limits differ: for 2026, the regular standard deduction is $16,100 for single filers, $32,200 for joint filers; the general SALT cap is $40,400, subject to income-based reduction and other statutory conditions.
legalWarning.authority: IRS 2026 inflation adjustment guidance and 2026 Form 1040-ES correction

entries.title: Refundable versus nonrefundable tax credits
entries.summary: A nonrefundable credit generally offsets income tax owed; a refundable credit can generate a payment in excess of that liability if its statutory conditions are met.
entries.details: After finding preliminary liability, credits reduce tax. The book uses the EITC as an example of a refundable credit that may yield negative net income-tax liability; a nonrefundable credit generally does not produce a payment beyond the applicable tax.
entries.laymanExplanation: A nonrefundable credit can bring your tax bill down to zero. A refundable credit may also pay you the difference if it's larger than the tax you owe.
entries.legalExplanation: After finding preliminary liability, credits reduce tax. The book uses the EITC as an example of a refundable credit that may yield negative net income-tax liability; a nonrefundable credit generally does not produce a payment beyond the applicable tax.
entries.source: Assigned Week 1, Bankman/Shaviro/Stark/Scharff, Federal Income Taxation, 19th ed., Ch. 1, printed pp. 15–16

entries.title: Capital asset — §1221
entries.summary: Property treated as a capital asset under §1221, subject to statutory exclusions such as inventory held primarily for sale to customers.
entries.details: Capital status is a threshold issue for determining capital gain or loss character. Investor-held stocks generally can qualify; inventory held for ordinary customer sales generally does not. Having something valuable or long-lived does not by itself establish capital-asset treatment.
entries.laymanExplanation: Stocks you buy as investments are often capital assets. The products a business keeps on shelves to sell customers generally aren't.
entries.legalExplanation: Capital status is a threshold issue for determining capital gain or loss character. Investor-held stocks generally can qualify; inventory held for ordinary customer sales generally does not. Having something valuable or long-lived does not by itself establish capital-asset treatment.
entries.source: Assigned Week 1, Bankman/Shaviro/Stark/Scharff, Federal Income Taxation, 19th ed., Ch. 1, printed pp. 19–20

entries.title: Short-term versus long-term holding period
entries.summary: Capital gain or loss on a capital asset held for more than one year is generally long-term; one year or less is short-term.
entries.details: §1222 distinguishes short-term and long-term gains and losses. Preferential rates generally depend on net capital gain after statutory netting, not simply the word 'capital' on any disposition. Keep separate the property's character and the period held.
entries.laymanExplanation: Sell an investment after six months and it's normally short-term; sell it after more than a year and it's generally long-term.
entries.legalExplanation: §1222 distinguishes short-term and long-term gains and losses. Preferential rates generally depend on net capital gain after statutory netting, not simply the word 'capital' on any disposition. Keep separate the property's character and the period held.
entries.source: Assigned Week 1, Bankman/Shaviro/Stark/Scharff, Federal Income Taxation, 19th ed., Ch. 1, printed pp. 19–20

entries.title: Net capital gain
entries.summary: A technical amount relevant to preferential tax rates, determined through the statutory netting of long-term capital gain and specified losses.
entries.details: Not every capital gain receives the reduced tax rates. The reading explains that 'net capital gain' depends on net long-term capital gain in excess of net short-term capital loss after applying statutory netting provisions. Review §1222 before calculating preferential treatment.
entries.laymanExplanation: Just because you sold an investment at a profit doesn't automatically mean the special low tax rate applies. You have to look at the type of gain, how long you held it, and other capital losses.
entries.legalExplanation: Not every capital gain receives the reduced tax rates. The reading explains that 'net capital gain' depends on net long-term capital gain in excess of net short-term capital loss after applying statutory netting provisions. Review §1222 before calculating preferential treatment.
entries.source: Assigned Week 1, Bankman/Shaviro/Stark/Scharff, Federal Income Taxation, 19th ed., Ch. 1, printed pp. 19–20

entries.title: Depreciation and cost recovery
entries.summary: A system for recovering the cost of eligible long-lived business property through deductions over time, subject to statutory acceleration and expensing rules.
entries.details: The reading contrasts nondepreciable land, whose cost is ordinarily recovered upon disposition, with a business tractor or manufacturing machine, which generally has depreciation/cost-recovery deductions. Allowed or allowable depreciation generally reduces adjusted basis; §§167–168 address major cost-recovery rules.
entries.laymanExplanation: A business machine lasts for years, so tax law often spreads its cost across multiple years instead of subtracting the entire purchase price immediately.
entries.legalExplanation: The reading contrasts nondepreciable land, whose cost is ordinarily recovered upon disposition, with a business tractor or manufacturing machine, which generally has depreciation/cost-recovery deductions. Allowed or allowable depreciation generally reduces adjusted basis; §§167–168 address major cost-recovery rules.
entries.source: Assigned Week 1, Bankman/Shaviro/Stark/Scharff, Federal Income Taxation, 19th ed., Ch. 1, printed pp. 21–22

entries.title: Pass-through taxation
entries.summary: Business income and certain losses are generally reported by owners rather than taxed at the partnership or S-corporation entity level.
entries.details: Partnerships file information returns but generally pass income or loss through to partners for federal income-tax purposes. Eligible S corporations also pass items through under their own rules. Owner inclusion may occur even before cash is distributed.
entries.laymanExplanation: The business calculates its earnings, but the owners—not the business itself—typically report those earnings on their own taxes.
entries.legalExplanation: Partnerships file information returns but generally pass income or loss through to partners for federal income-tax purposes. Eligible S corporations also pass items through under their own rules. Owner inclusion may occur even before cash is distributed.
entries.source: Assigned Week 1, Bankman/Shaviro/Stark/Scharff, Federal Income Taxation, 19th ed., Ch. 1, printed pp. 22–23

entries.title: Corporate double taxation
entries.summary: A C corporation generally pays income tax at the entity level, and shareholders may pay tax again when it distributes dividends.
entries.details: The reading describes C corporations as separate taxpayers, distinct from pass-through partnerships and S corporations. A corporation's retained income can raise share value but a shareholder generally does not realize gain from price appreciation until a disposition.
entries.laymanExplanation: A corporation may pay tax on its profit, then its owners may pay another tax when it sends them that profit as dividends.
entries.legalExplanation: The reading describes C corporations as separate taxpayers, distinct from pass-through partnerships and S corporations. A corporation's retained income can raise share value but a shareholder generally does not realize gain from price appreciation until a disposition.
entries.source: Assigned Week 1, Bankman/Shaviro/Stark/Scharff, Federal Income Taxation, 19th ed., Ch. 1, printed pp. 23

topics.assignmentSource: Tax syllabus: Week 1, Chapter 1 pp. 1–33

topics.title: D. Conversion, Deferral & Time Value
topics.description: Tax planning concepts and must-know compounding/present-value calculations.

entries.title: Conversion of income character
entries.summary: Recharacterizing ordinary-return activity as eligible long-term capital gain can reduce the applicable rate.
entries.details: The chapter’s start-up founder example shows value created largely by labor but potentially realized as capital gain on sale of ownership interest. Complex anti-conversion provisions may override simplistic characterizations.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 24–25
entries.laymanExplanation: Tax planning sometimes tries to change the legal category of income—for example, whether a gain is ordinary or capital—because different categories may have different rates.
entries.legalExplanation: Conversion refers to tax planning that transforms what would economically look like a return to labor or other ordinary-income activity into receipts treated as capital gain, potentially qualifying for different rates. The reading's founder who builds a company with personal labor and later sells shares illustrates the motivation. The proper classification depends on statutory character rules and transaction facts.

entries.title: Deferral of tax
entries.summary: Delay recognition/payment and keep funds invested in the interim.
entries.details: Deferral may increase after-tax wealth when other variables are held constant and returns are positive. It is not automatically advantageous when future tax rates differ; compare investments and tax rates across both periods.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 25–26
entries.laymanExplanation: Paying tax later can be valuable because you get more time to use or invest the money before paying it.
entries.legalExplanation: Tax deferral postpones current recognition or payment so funds remain available to earn returns. The source distinguishes deferral of an asset's appreciated gain until sale, and tax-favored retirement investment where contributions and earnings can accumulate before later taxation. A constant tax rate and positive return favor deferral in the simplified model, but changing rates or returns may change the comparison.

entries.title: Buy, borrow, die — strategy
entries.summary: Appreciated investments may grow untaxed, borrowing can provide cash, and death may adjust basis.
entries.details: The chapter ties nonrealization of appreciation, nontaxable loan proceeds, and §1014 basis step-up for many inherited assets into one strategy. This is a conceptual description subject to limits, exceptions, and future law changes.
entries.source: IRC §1014; Bankman et al. p. 25
entries.legalExplanation: The 'buy, borrow, die' strategy links appreciation without sale (no ordinary realization), cash borrowing secured by appreciated assets (loan proceeds generally offset by genuine repayment obligation), and basis rules for qualifying inherited property under §1014. The reading describes a possible step-up in basis at death and the resulting effect on built-in gain. Special exceptions and alternative regimes may limit the outcome.
entries.laymanExplanation: The idea is to hold investments while they appreciate, borrow against them instead of selling, and potentially pass them on at death with a tax basis adjustment. Important legal limits still apply.

entries.title: Compound future value
entries.summary: Future value = present investment × (1 + return)^number of periods.
entries.details: For an initial $10,000 growing at 10% per year for ten years, book illustration ≈ $25,937 before tax. Distinguish untaxed growth inside a deferral arrangement from after-tax annual returns.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 26–27
entries.laymanExplanation: Future value estimates how much an investment grows when each period's earnings stay invested and earn more earnings.
entries.legalExplanation: Compound growth uses FV = PV × (1 + r)^n for constant annual rate r and n years. The reading's retirement example: $10,000 × (1.10)^10 ≈ $25,937, before the 40% withdrawal tax under the simplified deferral assumptions. The formula assumes returns reinvested and constant periodic interest.

entries.title: Present value (discounting)
entries.summary: Present value = future amount ÷ (1 + discount rate)^periods.
entries.details: At 10% for 10 years, the multiplier is ≈ 0.3855 (the table rounds to .386). The textbook’s Table 1-5 provides a range of rates and periods, but the formula permits direct calculation.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 26–27
entries.laymanExplanation: Present value asks how much money today is equivalent to a larger amount promised in the future.
entries.legalExplanation: Discount future cash with PV = FV/(1+r)^n. Table 1-5 gives the present-value factor 0.386 for 10 years at 10%; a $10,000 future receipt therefore has a rounded present value of $3,860, versus the direct-calculation result of approximately $3,855.43. The book's factors are approximations and do not create a legal tax rule.

entries.title: After-tax compounding without deferral
entries.summary: Initial after-tax principal = principal × (1 − tax rate); annual after-tax growth uses return × (1 − tax rate).
entries.details: The chapter compares an immediate 40% tax and annual taxation of 10% yields with delayed taxation. This is a simplified model that assumes a constant rate and full annual taxation of investment returns.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 26
entries.laymanExplanation: If taxes are collected from investment earnings every year, less money remains invested and compounding may be reduced.
entries.legalExplanation: Under the textbook's simplified model with $10,000 gross funds, a 40% immediate tax leaves $6,000 to invest; 10% interest taxed annually at 40% leaves a 6% after-tax growth rate. Ten-year result = $6,000(1.06)^10 ≈ $10,745. By contrast, prefunded deferral permits $10,000(1.10)^10(0.60) ≈ $15,562 after the tax paid at withdrawal. Twenty-year results are approximately $19,243 without deferral and $40,365 with deferral. These are fixed-rate comparisons only.
entries.examApplication: Compute both after-tax terminal amounts at 10 and 20 years using the source's 10% return and 40% tax assumptions; compare, then discuss how a different future rate changes the result.
entries.examTrap: Deferred tax at a higher future marginal rate may negate the modeled advantage.

topics.assignmentSource: Tax syllabus: Week 1, Chapter 1 pp. 1–33

topics.title: E. Compliance, Audits & Litigation
topics.description: Self-assessment, assessment procedures, penalties and forum choice.

entries.title: Self-assessment and payment reconciliation
entries.summary: Taxpayers calculate liability; withholding and estimated payments are credited toward that liability.
entries.details: The IRS administers returns, matching, audits, and collections. After computing tax and credits, compare tax owed against taxes already paid to determine remaining balance or refund.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 28
entries.laymanExplanation: You usually calculate and report your own tax on a return. Withholding and estimated tax payments reduce what remains to pay, or may create a refund.
entries.legalExplanation: The personal federal income tax primarily uses annual self-assessment: the taxpayer determines income and deductions, files the return, and compares computed liability with withholding and estimated tax installments already paid. Excess prepayments generally result in a refund; an underpayment results in tax due. Separate filing and information-reporting obligations support IRS enforcement.

entries.title: Audit and deficiency
entries.summary: Audit is closer IRS scrutiny; deficiency is an asserted amount of underpaid tax.
entries.details: The general assessment period discussed by the textbook is three years, subject to major exceptions. Interest typically accrues on underpayments; penalties may also apply. The IRS often resolves disputes administratively.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 28–29
entries.laymanExplanation: An audit is an IRS check of your return. A deficiency is the additional tax the IRS says you owe.
entries.legalExplanation: An audit is a closer IRS examination of a return. The textbook introduces a general three-year period for the IRS to assert a deficiency, with statutory exceptions including certain omitted income and false or fraudulent returns. An underpayment may accrue statutory interest separately from civil penalties; the actual interest rate is set under Code provisions rather than remaining fixed at one percentage.

entries.title: Tax litigation forum choice
entries.summary: Tax Court generally permits qualifying prepayment deficiency challenges; refund suits generally follow payment.
entries.details: Tax Court: no jury, specialist judges, appeal to regional circuit. Federal district court: refund litigation after payment, jury potentially available, regional circuit appeal. Court of Federal Claims: refund litigation after payment, Federal Circuit appeal. Procedural requirements and deadlines are important and not fully covered in the introductory summary.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 29
entries.laymanExplanation: The court you use for a tax dispute matters. Some cases can be contested in Tax Court before paying the proposed deficiency; refund cases generally involve paying first.
entries.legalExplanation: Tax Court offers a common prepayment deficiency forum for eligible taxpayers with a valid notice and timely petition; it conducts bench trials with specialized tax judges and appeals usually to the appropriate geographic circuit. In contrast, ordinary refund suits in district courts and the Court of Federal Claims generally require paying and satisfying refund-claim prerequisites. District court may have a jury; Court of Federal Claims appeals to the Federal Circuit. These are introductory comparisons and do not replace procedural statutes.
entries.examApplication: Choose Tax Court for an appropriate prepayment deficiency challenge, or a paid-refund forum after meeting jurisdictional and claim prerequisites. Explain court/jury/appeal differences.
entries.examTrap: A refund case and a deficiency petition have different payment, jurisdictional and timing requirements.

entries.title: Accuracy-related civil penalties
entries.summary: The casebook describes a 20% penalty for specified negligence/substantial-understatement underpayments.
entries.details: The chapter notes substantial authority, adequate disclosure/reasonable basis, and reasonable-cause/good-faith rules that may limit penalties. Multiple overlapping 20% grounds generally do not simply stack. Check current §6662/§6664 and exact facts.
entries.source: IRC §§ 6662, 6664; Bankman et al. pp. 29–30
entries.laymanExplanation: Tax mistakes can trigger civil penalties, not just extra tax. The applicable penalty and possible defenses depend on what went wrong.
entries.legalExplanation: Under §6662, negligence and substantial-understatement grounds can produce a 20% accuracy-related penalty on the portion of underpayment attributable to the specified ground. The reading discusses reduction based on substantial authority or adequately disclosed positions with reasonable basis and potentially reasonable-cause/good-faith protection under §6664. The same portion of an underpayment does not automatically incur multiple 20% penalties for overlapping grounds.
entries.examApplication: Identify the statutory penalty ground and potentially qualifying substantial-authority, disclosure or reasonable-cause defense; do not merely multiply any error by 20%.

entries.title: Failure-to-file, failure-to-pay, and fraud penalties
entries.summary: The chapter lists monthly filing/payment penalties and a 75% civil-fraud penalty.
entries.details: As a basic introductory reference: failure to file is generally 5% per month up to 25%; failure to pay generally 0.5% per month up to 25%, with statutory interactions and exceptions. Civil fraud generally can produce a 75% penalty on the fraud portion. Actual computation depends on relevant rules and dates.
entries.source: IRC §§ 6651, 6663; Bankman et al. p. 30
entries.laymanExplanation: Filing late, paying late, and deliberately committing fraud are different violations with different penalties.
entries.legalExplanation: The textbook introduces generally applicable late-filing penalties of 5% per month (up to 25%) and late-payment penalties of 0.5% per month (up to 25%), subject to statutory adjustment and interaction. Fraud-related civil penalties can reach 75% of the tax underpayment attributable to fraud. Identify the precise taxable event, deadline, return status and statutory exceptions before performing a penalty calculation.

entries.title: Criminal tax evasion
entries.summary: Willful tax evasion can create felony exposure in addition to civil sanctions.
entries.details: The casebook contrasts civil and criminal enforcement and describes a six-year limitations period for specified tax offenses. Criminal liability requires the relevant statutory elements and mental state.
entries.source: IRC §7201; Bankman et al. p. 30
entries.laymanExplanation: Criminal tax evasion is more than getting a tax number wrong: it involves intentional conduct to evade tax under the governing criminal requirements.
entries.legalExplanation: Federal criminal tax evasion under §7201 requires willful attempted evasion or defeat of a tax imposed under the Code or its payment; the source describes criminal sanctions and a six-year criminal limitations period for specified offenses. Criminal tax liability has distinct intent and proof requirements beyond ordinary civil deficiency or negligence.

entries.title: Tax underpayment, deficiency, and assessment
entries.summary: An underpayment concerns unpaid tax; a deficiency is a statutorily defined additional liability asserted through deficiency procedures; assessment formally records the IRS's tax claim.
entries.details: For exam purposes identify the proposed deficiency, assessment, possible administrative review, interest and payment procedure. The Chapter 1 introductory discussion simplifies these distinctions; full statutory definitions and notice procedures appear elsewhere in the Code.
entries.laymanExplanation: A deficiency notice means the IRS believes you owe more than your return showed. Assessment is the government's formal recording of a tax amount for collection.
entries.legalExplanation: For exam purposes identify the proposed deficiency, assessment, possible administrative review, interest and payment procedure. The Chapter 1 introductory discussion simplifies these distinctions; full statutory definitions and notice procedures appear elsewhere in the Code.
entries.source: Assigned Week 1, Bankman/Shaviro/Stark/Scharff, Federal Income Taxation, 19th ed., Ch. 1, printed pp. 28–29

entries.title: Substantial understatement and penalty defenses
entries.summary: A substantial understatement may trigger §6662 accuracy-related penalties, but the Code recognizes specified substantial-authority, disclosure, and reasonable-cause rules.
entries.details: The textbook introduces a 20% accuracy-related penalty and identifies circumstances relevant to reducing the understatement or qualifying for reasonable-cause/good-faith protection. Tax year, taxpayer type, applicable authority, reasonable basis, and disclosure must be assessed before deciding penalty liability.
entries.laymanExplanation: Making a big tax mistake can carry an extra penalty. But the law may treat a reasonable, disclosed position differently from careless reporting.
entries.legalExplanation: The textbook introduces a 20% accuracy-related penalty and identifies circumstances relevant to reducing the understatement or qualifying for reasonable-cause/good-faith protection. Tax year, taxpayer type, applicable authority, reasonable basis, and disclosure must be assessed before deciding penalty liability.
entries.source: Assigned Week 1, Bankman/Shaviro/Stark/Scharff, Federal Income Taxation, 19th ed., Ch. 1, printed pp. 29–30

topics.assignmentSource: Tax syllabus: Week 1, Chapter 1 pp. 1–33

topics.title: F. Sources of Federal Tax Law
topics.description: Hierarchy and practical use of tax statutes, regulations, case law, IRS guidance.

entries.title: Statutory authority — start with the Internal Revenue Code
entries.summary: Federal income taxes require statutory authority. Begin with Code text and then review applicable regulations, cases, and administrative guidance.
entries.details: Read the controlling provision, definitions, cross-references, and exceptions. Follow regulations, binding case law, and pertinent IRS guidance, while considering how judicial doctrines deal with substance over form.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 30–31
entries.legalExplanation: Federal income-tax liability begins with enacted Code provisions. Statutory definitions, cross-references and exclusions should be reviewed first; then applicable regulations, judicial decisions and published IRS guidance. The reading stresses that courts also use substance-over-form reasoning and law-like doctrines where statutory language is incomplete or susceptible to manipulation.
entries.laymanExplanation: When a tax question comes up, start with the Internal Revenue Code. Then look at the detailed regulations, court opinions and IRS guidance that help explain it.
entries.examApplication: When researching a tax question, cite the applicable Code section first; analyze its definitions and exceptions before turning to Treasury regulations and cases.

entries.title: Legislative history and JCT
entries.summary: Committee reports and Joint Committee on Taxation materials help explain statutory purposes.
entries.details: Tax-writing committees: House Ways and Means and Senate Finance. JCT staff work on legislative analysis and official revenue estimates; JCT 'blue books' summarize legislation after enactment. These are aids to interpretation, not substitutes for enacted law.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 31
entries.legalExplanation: Legislative history can help interpret uncertain provisions. House Ways and Means and Senate Finance committee reports may explain complex drafting compromises; Joint Committee on Taxation staff assists and prepares revenue estimates and 'blue books' summarizing enacted laws. These explanatory documents are not themselves statutes.
entries.laymanExplanation: Congress writes tax statutes, but committee reports and JCT explanations can tell you what lawmakers were trying to accomplish. They explain the law; they aren't laws themselves.

entries.title: Treasury regulations under §7805
entries.summary: Treasury issues regulations interpreting and implementing the Code.
entries.details: The textbook discusses Mayo (2011) and Chevron deference as the then-governing doctrine. CURRENT-LAW UPDATE: Loper Bright (2024) overruled Chevron; courts independently interpret law under the APA. A delegation to an agency can remain legally relevant; the old automatic ambiguity-triggered Chevron rule is not current.
entries.source: IRC §7805; Mayo Foundation v. United States (2011); Loper Bright v. Raimondo (2024)
entries.alert: OUTDATED IN CASEBOOK: Chevron deference was overruled in 2024.
entries.laymanExplanation: Treasury regulations are detailed rules issued by Treasury that help explain how the Internal Revenue Code operates.
entries.legalExplanation: Section 7805 authorizes Treasury to issue regulations for Code enforcement, and particular provisions may specifically delegate regulatory tasks. Income-tax regulations generally use the '1.' number series and proposed regulations ordinarily undergo applicable notice-and-comment procedures. The casebook's description of Chevron deference after Mayo reflects the doctrine as it stood in 2011; the Supreme Court's Loper Bright decision (2024) overruled Chevron's mandatory ambiguity-based deference, while statutory delegations may still matter.
entries.examApplication: Start with a Code section, then the regulation, then relevant binding case law; if Chevron is invoked from the casebook, state that Loper Bright later changed judicial interpretive deference.
entries.examTrap: Do not write that a court must follow any reasonable Treasury interpretation simply because the statute is ambiguous; that is the overruled Chevron approach.

entries.title: Revenue Rulings and Revenue Procedures
entries.summary: Rev. Rul. expresses IRS legal position on a fact pattern; Rev. Proc. addresses administration/procedures.
entries.details: Both are IRS guidance, generally less authoritative than duly issued Treasury regulations and judicial precedent. Their practical importance is substantial, but authority and reliance depend on the specific type and context.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 32
entries.laymanExplanation: Revenue rulings explain the IRS's position on how law applies to facts. Revenue procedures generally explain processes and administrative rules.
entries.legalExplanation: Revenue Rulings express the IRS's published position on how a law applies to a given set of facts; Revenue Procedures describe IRS administrative practices and processes. They are important to practitioners but do not have the same status as Code text or properly promulgated Treasury regulations.
entries.examApplication: Classify the source of guidance in a tax research question. Do not treat an unpublished PLR as general binding authority.

entries.title: Private Letter Rulings (PLRs)
entries.summary: IRS written advice to a particular taxpayer generally may not be cited as precedent by others.
entries.details: PLRs can reveal the Service’s likely approach but do not create general binding law. Distinguished from published Revenue Rulings.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 32–33
entries.laymanExplanation: A private letter ruling is the IRS answering a particular taxpayer's question. Other taxpayers generally cannot treat that letter as binding precedent.
entries.legalExplanation: A PLR responds to a specific taxpayer's factual ruling request. Although letter rulings may illuminate IRS analysis, under §6110(k)(3) a written determination generally cannot be used or cited as precedent by other taxpayers. The reading differentiates PLRs from public Revenue Rulings stating an IRS position with broader applicability.

entries.title: Tax Court decisions and IRS acquiescence
entries.summary: Tax Court has regular and memorandum decisions; IRS may announce acquiescence or nonacquiescence.
entries.details: Acquiescence signals internal acceptance of a ruling for similar cases; nonacquiescence signals continued disagreement and possible relitigation. Neither itself reverses binding judicial precedent.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 33
entries.laymanExplanation: Tax Court decisions interpret tax law. The IRS may say whether it accepts a particular decision's reasoning for similar cases.
entries.legalExplanation: The Tax Court publishes regular opinions and memorandum decisions, and the IRS sometimes announces whether it acquiesces or nonacquiesces in adverse opinions. Acquiescence indicates an administrative willingness to follow the decision in similar matters; nonacquiescence indicates disagreement and possible relitigation, subject to binding appellate rulings. The source's Golsen footnote explains the importance of the circuit of appeal.

entries.title: Cited authority: Mayo Foundation (2011) — old Chevron framework
entries.summary: Historical: applied Chevron framework to Treasury regulations.
entries.details: The textbook uses Mayo to describe the then-prevailing standard. It is useful for historical understanding, but Chevron was overruled in Loper Bright (2024).
entries.source: Assigned textbook p. 32 (Mayo citation only); current-law note: Loper Bright (2024).
entries.alert: Historical doctrinal treatment; not a statement of the current Chevron standard.

legalWarning.label: FRAMEWORK OVERRULED
legalWarning.reason: Mayo applied Chevron deference to Treasury regulations. Loper Bright (2024) overruled Chevron's mandatory deference framework. This does not mean every holding previously relying on Chevron was automatically overturned; Mayo is useful for tracing the former approach.

entries.sourceRole: Case cited or discussed in assigned Chapter 1; no reproduced opinion, so not a dedicated case brief.
entries.legalExplanation: Mayo Foundation (2011) was cited by the casebook as applying Chevron-style agency deference to Treasury tax regulations. The subsequent Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo (2024) decision overruled that mandatory deference framework. The case is mentioned here as an example, not reproduced as an assigned judicial opinion, so it belongs in supporting doctrine with an updated-law warning.
entries.laymanExplanation: The textbook describes a time when judges often deferred to reasonable Treasury interpretations of unclear statutes. The Supreme Court changed that approach in 2024, so don't memorize the old standard as current law.

entries.title: Cited authority: Eisner v. Macomber (1920)
