entries.legalExplanation: The tax benefit doctrine generally requires attention to whether an earlier deduction reduced tax and whether recovery in a later year is inconsistent with the circumstances supporting that deduction. The p.77 lost-envelope hypothetical is a preview; full doctrinal development appears later in the course.

entries.title: Clark fairness paradox
entries.summary: One reimbursed overpayer is better off than an uncompensated overpayer, but merely equal to a taxpayer who never overpaid.
entries.details: The text uses this to illustrate how tax rules define the relevant transaction and may leave some economic inequities.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 76
entries.legalExplanation: Clark's note compares an overpayer who received compensation (Akira), a similarly situated unreimbursed overpayer (Benito), and a taxpayer who was correctly advised (Cora). Whether the recovery is excluded depends on the choice of baseline. This is normative analysis, not a simple mechanical statutory rule.
entries.laymanExplanation: If an accountant repays someone who overpaid taxes, that person is now better off than someone whose accountant never repays them—but only as well off as someone whose taxes were done correctly in the first place.

entries.title: Actual tax liability versus tax overpayment
entries.summary: An actual tax liability is tax legally owed on the transactions undertaken; an overpayment is tax paid beyond that liability. Do not equate a potentially better tax strategy with an overpayment.
entries.details: In the government's 2018 McKenney brief, the McKenneys agreed with the IRS in a closing agreement that they owed approximately $2.2 million additional taxes for 2000–2005. They later obtained an $800,000 settlement from their accounting firm. The government argued that this recovered part of taxes actually owed, not tax they had overpaid through erroneous return preparation. The brief distinguishes an actual historical transaction from hypothetical, more favorable tax planning; these are the government's arguments, not the court's decision.
entries.examApplication: Compare Clark: Did the accountant cause payment beyond the taxpayer's actual legally correct tax, or did the taxpayer pay tax actually owed on the chosen transaction and later receive money from the accountant?
entries.examTrap: Tax that could have been avoided through a different transaction is not automatically an overpayment of tax actually owed. Keep the party's argument separate from a judicial holding.
entries.source: Assigned 'McKenny brief handout (1).pdf', five pages: government's redacted opening brief, Eleventh Circuit No. 18-10810, filed Sept. 6, 2018 (original appellate-brief pp. 21–24). This is government advocacy, not a judicial opinion.
entries.sourceRole: Definition and exam distinction derived from the government's assigned brief, not an attributed court holding.
entries.laymanExplanation: There is a difference between paying too much tax by mistake and paying the correct tax on a deal that turned out to be a bad tax-saving idea.
entries.sourceWeek: Week 3 — separately assigned McKenney government brief

entries.title: Old Colony principle — third-party payment of a taxpayer's tax
entries.summary: When another party pays a taxpayer's legally owed federal income tax on the taxpayer's behalf as a benefit, the discharge of that liability can constitute taxable income.
entries.details: The government's McKenney brief invoked Old Colony Trust Co. v. Commissioner, 279 U.S. 716 (1929), to argue that an accountant's settlement effectively reimbursing valid tax obligations should be included under §61. The handout does not reproduce the Old Colony judicial opinion, so Old Colony remains supporting cited authority, not a dedicated case brief. Whether a particular damages recovery is taxable also requires analysis of what the payment replaces.
entries.examApplication: Identify the underlying taxpayer liability and what a third-party payment actually reimburses. Contrast legal discharge or reimbursement of taxes owed with replacement of an amount paid unnecessarily because of a negligent filing choice.
entries.examTrap: Do not apply Old Colony automatically to all malpractice recoveries; Clark's actual-overpayment facts and the nature of the claimed loss may matter.
entries.source: Assigned 'McKenny brief handout (1).pdf', five pages: government's redacted opening brief, Eleventh Circuit No. 18-10810, filed Sept. 6, 2018 (original appellate-brief pp. 21–24). This is government advocacy, not a judicial opinion.
entries.sourceRole: Legal principle cited in the government's assigned brief; the case opinion is not reproduced in the handout.
entries.laymanExplanation: If your employer or another person pays a tax bill you actually owe for you, that can be the same as receiving money to pay it yourself.

entries.title: Assigned supplemental advocacy — United States' brief in McKenney
entries.summary: The government argued an $800,000 accountant-malpractice settlement was taxable because it reimbursed valid tax liabilities, unlike the excess tax payment in Clark.
entries.details:
DOCUMENT TYPE: Government's redacted opening appellate brief filed September 6, 2018, not a judicial opinion.

FACTS AS ARGUED: Joseph and Amy McKenney used S corporations owned by an ESOP to structure consulting and dealership income. After examination, they signed a closing agreement accepting an IRS determination concerning an abusive ESOP transaction and acknowledged approximately $2.2 million in additional taxes for 2000–2005. They later settled malpractice claims against Grant Thornton for $800,000.

GOVERNMENT'S POSITION: The $800,000 replaced part of tax liabilities the taxpayers actually owed, and thus was income under §61 and Old Colony Trust. It distinguished Clark because Clark involved an accountant reimbursing tax actually overpaid. It also argued that tax consequences should follow transactions actually entered, not hypothetical restructuring that would have saved tax.

LIMITATION: These are arguments made by one litigant. The excerpt does not contain judicial findings or a court's holding. A 2020 court decision is separately linked in the current-law notes.
entries.examApplication: Exam comparison: Clark taxpayer overpaid due to erroneous filing advice; McKenney taxpayers' accountant advised transaction design and the government treated the additional tax on that actual transaction as legally owed. Explain why that difference matters for characterizing the settlement, while keeping the source's advocacy status clear.
entries.examTrap: Never cite the 2018 brief itself as the Eleventh Circuit's holding. The brief includes one party's characterization of the facts and the law.
entries.source: Assigned 'McKenny brief handout (1).pdf', five pages: government's redacted opening brief, Eleventh Circuit No. 18-10810, filed Sept. 6, 2018 (original appellate-brief pp. 21–24). This is government advocacy, not a judicial opinion.

entries.title: Recovery of capital versus return on capital
entries.summary: Getting original investment back is generally not income; earnings or proceeds beyond recoverable basis may be income.
entries.laymanExplanation: Lending someone $500 and being repaid $500 isn't a $500 profit. Extra interest is a separate gain.
entries.legalExplanation: The general recovery-of-capital principle distinguishes return of one's tax investment from income earned on it. Under gain computations, amount realized is reduced by allocated/adjusted basis, with separate treatment for dividends, rents, interest and other returns.
entries.details: The general recovery-of-capital principle distinguishes return of one's tax investment from income earned on it. Under gain computations, amount realized is reduced by allocated/adjusted basis, with separate treatment for dividends, rents, interest and other returns.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, textbook pp. 68–69; Week 3 syllabus-assigned.

entries.title: Textbook's pre-2026 wagering-loss rule — historical

This is historical textbook analysis. Current-law notes separately explain the subsequent 2026 90% limitation. Do not silently rewrite the book's historical statement.
