topics.assignmentSource: Tax syllabus: Week 3, Chapter 2 pp. 68–102

topics.title: E. Personal & Business Injury Recoveries
topics.description: Character of damages, §104(a)(2), deferred settlements and constitutional questions.

entries.title: Business lost-profit damages are income
entries.summary: Amounts recovered to replace profits that would have been taxable are generally included in income.
entries.details: Settlement or insurance proceeds can be analyzed by what they replace; punitive damages also generally fall within §61.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 78
entries.laymanExplanation: If a business gets money to replace profits it missed out on, the payment is generally treated much like the profits would have been.
entries.legalExplanation: Damages replacing taxable business profits are generally income just as the underlying lost earnings would have been. The reading treats the recovery when received as income and distinguishes it from compensation for destruction of an asset with recoverable basis.

entries.title: Damages for destroyed business property — basis recovery
entries.summary: Recovery for damaged or destroyed property generally produces gain to the extent proceeds exceed adjusted basis; §1033 may permit qualifying deferral.
entries.details: Example from reading: $700,000 recovery for a building with $600,000 basis results in $100,000 gain absent qualifying nonrecognition.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 78
entries.laymanExplanation: If a destroyed building had $600,000 of tax basis and you receive $700,000 for it, the extra $100,000 can be gain, unless another rule postpones recognizing it.
entries.legalExplanation: Damages for damaged or destroyed business property can be a capital recovery; measure any gain by amount recovered minus applicable adjusted basis. The source's building example: $700,000 received for an asset with $600,000 basis creates potential $100,000 realized gain, before testing §1033 deferral.

entries.title: IRC §1033 — Involuntary conversions
entries.summary: Qualifying proceeds from destroyed or condemned business/investment property may receive nonrecognition when reinvested in eligible replacement property under statutory conditions.
entries.details: The reading uses it for compensation for a destroyed building; examine detailed replacement requirements in statutory text.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 78
entries.laymanExplanation: When qualifying property is destroyed or taken and you use the proceeds to buy suitable replacement property, tax law may let you delay reporting the gain.
entries.legalExplanation: Section 1033 provides nonrecognition rules for certain involuntary conversions of business/investment property into money when statutorily qualifying replacement property is obtained within the relevant time and conditions. The text illustrates replacement of a destroyed building; do not assume merely receiving insurance is automatically exempt.

entries.title: IRC §104(a)(2) — Physical injury or sickness damages
entries.summary: Qualifying damages (other than punitive damages) received on account of personal physical injuries or physical sickness are excluded from gross income.
entries.details: Applies to qualifying damages whether recovered by suit or agreement and in lump-sum or periodic form; the causal link to physical injury/sickness is critical.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 79
entries.examTrap: Nonphysical injury, reputational harm, or ordinary emotional distress does not by itself satisfy §104(a)(2). Punitive damages remain taxable.
entries.laymanExplanation: Money received as damages because of a physical injury or physical sickness can be tax-free, but punitive damages and many purely emotional-distress awards are different.
entries.legalExplanation: Section 104(a)(2) excludes qualifying damages received on account of personal physical injuries or physical sickness, other than punitive damages. The 1996 change restricted the exclusion and raised the question of nonphysical distress. Murphy II and Perez teach that the causal nature and legal source of payment matter more than whether a person suffered distress or pain.

entries.title: Compensatory versus punitive damages
entries.summary: Compensatory damages replace an identified loss; punitive damages are imposed as punishment or deterrence.
entries.details: For tax consequences examine the origin and purpose of payment, any statutory exclusion, and whether a return of capital is involved.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 79
entries.laymanExplanation: Compensatory damages aim to repay a loss. Punitive damages are an additional amount meant to punish the wrongdoer.
entries.legalExplanation: Compensatory damages restore or substitute for a specified loss, such as lost profits or personal injury; punitive damages add punishment/deterrence beyond compensation. Taxation depends on what is replaced and statutory exclusions; Glenshaw Glass includes punitive amounts absent exclusion, and §104(a)(2) expressly carves punitive amounts out.

entries.title: Origin of the claim
entries.summary: The factual and legal nature of the underlying claim that gives rise to damages.
entries.details: Distinguish recoveries for lost profits, destroyed property, physical personal injury, and reputation/emotional harms.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 79
entries.laymanExplanation: To classify lawsuit money for tax purposes, ask: 'What was this payment really for?' Lost wages, damaged property, and physical injury can have different tax outcomes.
entries.legalExplanation: The 'origin of the claim' looks at the actual right, injury or event for which damages were paid to classify tax consequences. A payment replacing wages or business profits, property value, physical pain and suffering, and reputational damage can be governed by different inclusion and basis rules.

entries.title: Murphy v. United States (Murphy II)
entries.summary: The D.C. Circuit held the award did not fall within §104(a)(2)'s physical-injury exclusion, was included in §61 gross income, and could constitutionally be taxed; the judgment was affirmed.
entries.details: The supplied text reproduces a judicial opinion, so this is a dedicated case brief.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), reproduced judicial opinion, Chapter 2 pp. 80–88.
entries.facts: Marrita Murphy recovered damages through an administrative whistleblower case against a former employer, including awards for emotional distress and reputational injury. She sought a refund of the income tax paid on those nonphysical-injury damages. On rehearing, the D.C. Circuit considered both the statute and Congress's taxing power.
entries.issue: Does §104(a)(2) exclude damages for emotional distress or reputational harm without a qualifying physical injury? If not, does §61 include those damages and may Congress constitutionally tax them?
entries.holding: On rehearing, the D.C. Circuit held the nonphysical-injury recovery was not excluded by §104(a)(2), fell within gross income under §61, and was constitutionally taxable; the taxpayer's challenge failed.
entries.reasoning: The 1996 amendment ties the §104(a)(2) exclusion to physical injury or physical sickness, and reputational/emotional harm alone does not qualify. The court read §61 broadly and reasoned the tax on the award was an excise on receipt/transaction rather than an unapportioned direct tax on property ownership. The prior Murphy I decision was vacated.
entries.rule: Nonphysical personal-injury damages are generally included under §61 absent another exclusion; §104(a)(2) is limited to qualifying physical injury/sickness damages (other than punitive), and Murphy II sustained taxation of its award as an excise.
entries.exam: Separate statutory analysis (§104, §61) from constitutional analysis (direct tax/apportionment). Do not substitute historical Murphy I for the rehearing holding.
entries.examApplication: Separate statutory analysis (§104, §61) from constitutional analysis (direct tax/apportionment). Do not substitute historical Murphy I for the rehearing holding.
entries.laymanExplanation: A whistleblower received damages for emotional harm and damage to reputation, not physical injury. The appeals court ruled the money was taxable and that Congress could tax it.
entries.examTrap: Emotional distress is not automatically a qualifying 'physical injury' solely because it causes bodily symptoms; analyze the precise statutory/regulatory conditions.
entries.sourceRole: Week 3 assigned judicial opinion (reproduced in textbook)

entries.title: Direct tax and apportionment
entries.summary: The Constitution requires certain direct federal taxes to be apportioned by population among states, subject to the Sixteenth Amendment for income taxes.
entries.details: Murphy II discusses Article I and distinguishes taxes on property ownership from taxes on transactions or activities.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 85
entries.laymanExplanation: For some taxes, the Constitution requires each state's tax share to follow its population. Federal income taxes have an important constitutional exception.
entries.legalExplanation: Article I requires certain direct taxes to be apportioned among states by population, while the Sixteenth Amendment removes apportionment for taxes on incomes. Murphy II distinguished a direct tax on owned property from an excise on a transaction or activity and sustained the tax on its damages award.

entries.title: Article I taxing power and constitutional limits
entries.summary: Congress has broad Article I power to lay taxes; direct taxes require apportionment except to the extent the Sixteenth Amendment permits unapportioned income taxes.
entries.details: The reproduced Murphy II excerpt reasons that taxing its award can be an excise on a transaction, satisfying the constitutional framework.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 85
entries.laymanExplanation: Congress has broad power to tax, but constitutional limits can affect particular taxes. The classification of the tax matters.
entries.legalExplanation: Congress has broad powers under Article I to impose income, excise and other taxes, subject to constitutional limitations. Murphy II reasoned the specific tax on receipt of nonphysical-injury damages was a constitutionally permissible excise, even when the taxpayer argued the amount was not income within the Sixteenth Amendment's meaning.

entries.title: Perez v. Commissioner
entries.summary: No. The payments were taxable compensation, not excludable damages for personal physical injury.
entries.details: The supplied text reproduces a judicial opinion, so this is a dedicated case brief.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), reproduced judicial opinion, Chapter 2 pp. 89–94.
entries.facts: Perez agreed with a fertility clinic to undergo hormone injections, medical monitoring, and multiple egg retrieval procedures to supply her eggs for others. She received $20,000 under written arrangements for undergoing the process, which involved pain, risk and physical intervention.
entries.issue: Were contractual payments for willingly undergoing egg-donation retrieval processes excludable 'damages' received on account of physical injury under §104(a)(2)?
entries.holding: No. The Tax Court held the $20,000 was taxable compensation, not qualifying personal physical-injury damages.
entries.reasoning: Perez voluntarily agreed to medical procedures in return for payment. Although they caused physical pain and risk, the clinic did not compensate a wrongful injury through damages; it paid consideration for contractually agreed actions. The post-1996 regulation's removal of a 'tort or tort-type' formal claim requirement did not make all compensation for painful activities damages.
entries.rule: Contract payments for voluntary services or procedures do not become §104(a)(2) injury damages merely because the services are physically invasive or painful.
entries.exam: Distinguish a settlement for a compensable physical injury from contractual pay for willingly performing a physically difficult activity.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish a settlement for a compensable physical injury from contractual pay for willingly performing a physically difficult activity.
entries.laymanExplanation: A woman was paid to go through an egg-retrieval process. The court said this was payment under a voluntary contract, not tax-free injury damages.
entries.examTrap: Pain alone does not show damages; identify the legal source and character of the payment.
entries.sourceRole: Week 3 assigned judicial opinion (reproduced in textbook)

entries.title: Structured settlement
entries.summary: A legal settlement that pays qualified damages over time rather than as a single lump sum.
entries.details: The textbook explains that qualifying periodic payments for physical injuries may receive special tax treatment, creating a timing advantage.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 94
entries.laymanExplanation: A structured settlement pays lawsuit compensation over time instead of in a single check.
entries.legalExplanation: A structured settlement spreads payments for an injury claim across time, often funded through an annuity or obligation of an assignee. The timing and character of the recovery, and the claimant's rights to immediate cash, affect tax analysis. The book focuses on qualifying physical-injury payments under §104(a)(2).

entries.title: Periodic payments for personal physical injury
entries.summary: Under §104(a)(2), qualifying physical-injury damages may be excludable whether paid in a lump sum or periodic payments.
entries.details: Structured settlements require careful analysis of entitlement and economic control; the reading highlights favorable treatment of certain deferred-payment components.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 94
entries.laymanExplanation: Qualifying physical-injury compensation may remain excluded even when paid in installments, subject to the applicable rules.
entries.legalExplanation: A qualifying personal physical-injury recovery can be excludable under §104(a)(2) whether received all at once or in periodic payments, assuming the statutory conditions are satisfied. The source contrasts immediate lump-sum funds invested by the claimant with fixed structured payments administered through a settlement vehicle.

entries.title: Policy rationale for physical injury exclusion
entries.summary: Compensation arguably restores lost physical well-being rather than creating a net economic gain.
entries.details: The text contrasts physical with emotional/reputational injuries and asks why nominally similar compensation can be taxed differently.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 79
entries.legalExplanation: The book contrasts compensatory recovery for physical injury with nonphysical harm. If an award restores a person's situation after an accident, an exclusion might seem fair, but comparison against someone equally injured without an award can suggest the opposite. This is policy rationale, not a substitute for §104's text.
entries.laymanExplanation: Should injury compensation be tax-free because it only repairs what you lost? The book compares someone who is paid damages with someone who suffers the same injury but gets nothing.

entries.title: IRC §104(a)(2) — distinguish physical and nonphysical injury awards
entries.summary: Qualifying physical-injury damages may be excluded; damages for purely nonphysical harm generally do not qualify under §104(a)(2).
entries.laymanExplanation: Money for a broken leg may qualify for a tax exclusion. Money for damage to your reputation usually doesn't qualify simply because it was emotionally painful.
entries.legalExplanation: The 1996 amendment limits §104(a)(2) to damages received on account of personal physical injuries or physical sickness (other than punitive damages). The award's purpose and causation matter. The reading's Murphy II and Perez opinions emphasize statutory text and the nature of the claim.
entries.details: The 1996 amendment limits §104(a)(2) to damages received on account of personal physical injuries or physical sickness (other than punitive damages). The award's purpose and causation matter. The reading's Murphy II and Perez opinions emphasize statutory text and the nature of the claim.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, textbook pp. 78–94; Week 3 syllabus-assigned.
entries.examTrap: The word 'injury' by itself isn't enough; determine whether the source of the payment is a qualifying physical injury or sickness.

entries.title: Damages received on account of injury
entries.summary: For §104, whether damages were received 'on account of' a qualifying injury is a causal question, not merely a label on a settlement.
entries.laymanExplanation: Ask what the check is actually paying for. Is it compensation because the person was physically injured, or payment for something else?
entries.legalExplanation: The text analyzes compensation for lost business profits, harm to property, physical personal injury, emotional distress, reputational harm and voluntary contractual bodily services. Their tax treatments differ because the origin and reason for payment differ.
entries.details: The text analyzes compensation for lost business profits, harm to property, physical personal injury, emotional distress, reputational harm and voluntary contractual bodily services. Their tax treatments differ because the origin and reason for payment differ.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, textbook pp. 79–94; Week 3 syllabus-assigned.

entries.title: Qualified structured settlement / periodic payments
entries.summary: A qualifying personal physical-injury settlement may pay amounts over time, with §104(a)(2) addressing qualifying periodic awards.
entries.laymanExplanation: Instead of one check today, an injured person might get monthly payments for years. The tax outcome depends on the nature of the damages and how the deal is structured.
entries.legalExplanation: The reading describes structured settlements as periodic damage payments with favorable treatment under §104(a)(2) for qualifying physical injury or sickness. Contractual control, the purchaser or assignee's role, and payment design can affect tax consequences. Distinguish this from taxable investment income earned after an unrestricted lump-sum payment.
entries.details: The reading describes structured settlements as periodic damage payments with favorable treatment under §104(a)(2) for qualifying physical injury or sickness. Contractual control, the purchaser or assignee's role, and payment design can affect tax consequences. Distinguish this from taxable investment income earned after an unrestricted lump-sum payment.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, textbook pp. 94–95; Week 3 syllabus-assigned.

topics.assignmentSource: Tax syllabus: Week 3, Chapter 2 pp. 68–102

topics.title: F. Illegal Income
topics.description: Taxability of unlawful gains, claims of right and restitution.

entries.title: Illegal proceeds may be taxable gross income
entries.summary: Unlawful gains can constitute gross income under §61, even if the recipient may later be required to repay them.
entries.details: James v. United States is referenced for the general principle: receipt without consensual recognition of an obligation to repay and without restriction can be taxable.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 96
entries.examTrap: Illegal character of income does not remove it from §61.
entries.laymanExplanation: You don't get an income-tax exemption because the money came from something illegal. Stolen or embezzled money can be taxable.
entries.legalExplanation: Illegal gain is not outside §61 solely because obtaining it was unlawful. James v. United States is cited for treating embezzlement proceeds as income when the recipient acquires funds without consensual repayment obligation or meaningful restrictions. The later possibility of restitution does not itself erase current inclusion.

entries.title: Claim of right
entries.summary: A taxpayer's practical dominion over funds, without an acknowledged limitation or consensual obligation to repay, may support current inclusion.
entries.details: The source compares typical embezzlement proceeds against loans or prompt secured repayment arrangements.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 97
entries.laymanExplanation: If you receive money and can use it as your own without accepting a genuine duty to return it, tax law may treat you as having income right now.
entries.legalExplanation: Under the claim-of-right principle, receipt of money under a claim of free use and without consensual acknowledgment of a repayment obligation may count as current income even when the taxpayer might later have to restore it. Compare genuine borrowing with theft or embezzlement.

entries.title: Obligation to repay
entries.summary: A recognized duty to return money, relevant to whether receipt is a taxable accession to wealth or nonincome borrowing.
entries.details: Do not mistake a purely subjective intention to repay for a legally and factually supported borrowing obligation.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 97
entries.laymanExplanation: Borrowing money usually isn't income because you have a real obligation to pay it back. An empty promise to repay may not be enough.
entries.legalExplanation: A loan principal normally does not enrich the borrower because a genuine corresponding liability to repay arises. Gilbert's exceptional result turned on immediate secured obligations, reasonable expectation of repayment, contemporaneous notice and restrictions on use; an after-the-fact promise does not settle taxability.

entries.title: Gilbert v. Commissioner
entries.summary: The Second Circuit reversed the Tax Court; under its unusual facts, the withdrawals were not income when acquired.
entries.details: The supplied text reproduces a judicial opinion, so this is a dedicated case brief.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), reproduced judicial opinion, Chapter 2 pp. 95–99.
entries.facts: Gilbert, president of Bruce corporation, caused unauthorized withdrawals totaling $1,958,000 for stock margin calls, repaid $5,000 and executed notes for $1,953,000. He promptly disclosed the withdrawals to certain officers and counsel and gave Bruce security over assets then worth more than the money owed. The board accepted the collateral but refused to ratify the withdrawals; later repayment efforts collapsed.
entries.issue: Did these unauthorized corporate withdrawals constitute taxable embezzlement income under James despite a recognized repayment duty and prompt overcollateralization?
entries.holding: The Second Circuit reversed the Tax Court. On these unusual facts, Gilbert did not realize taxable income when he withdrew the funds because they functioned as a genuinely secured obligation to repay.
entries.reasoning: Gilbert intended to return the funds, believed corporate approval would follow, promptly informed officers and counsel, issued demand notes, and subjected assets exceeding the liability to creditor control. The court distinguished typical embezzlement, where there is no contemporaneous consensual recognition of repayment obligation or restrictions on use.
entries.rule: James does not automatically make every unauthorized withdrawal income; a narrow exception may apply where genuine contemporaneous repayment obligation, reasonable expectation of repayment, anticipated consent and prompt adequate security are shown.
entries.exam: Compare a conventional unsecured theft/embezzlement with Gilbert's immediate secured loan-like transaction; identify consent, intent, collateral, timing and actual freedom to use funds.
entries.examApplication: Compare a conventional unsecured theft/embezzlement with Gilbert's immediate secured loan-like transaction; identify consent, intent, collateral, timing and actual freedom to use funds.
entries.laymanExplanation: A company executive took money without permission but promptly gave real security and acknowledged repayment. The court treated those unusual facts differently from ordinary embezzlement.
entries.examTrap: A belated note or subjective promise to repay stolen money is not enough to create Gilbert's exceptional result.
entries.sourceRole: Week 3 assigned judicial opinion (reproduced in textbook)

entries.title: James v. United States (supporting citation)
entries.summary: The textbook cites James for the general taxability of embezzled funds.
entries.details: James is referenced within Gilbert; it is not a separately reproduced assigned opinion in the supplied pages.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 97
entries.legalExplanation: James v. United States is mentioned in Gilbert for the rule that embezzled money can constitute income. Wilcox, earlier excluding such receipts because of a duty to restore them, was overruled by James; the chapter's reference cases should remain supporting citations, not dedicated opinion briefs.
entries.laymanExplanation: The law generally taxes money stolen or embezzled, even if the thief has to repay it later. This cited Supreme Court case helps explain that point.

entries.title: James and Wilcox — supporting historical authorities
entries.summary: The textbook explains that James v. United States overruled Wilcox's prior exclusion of embezzlement receipts; they are citations in the Gilbert notes, not reproduced opinions.
entries.laymanExplanation: Stolen money can count as taxable income. Older Supreme Court decisions disagreed, but the later rule generally includes embezzled proceeds.
entries.legalExplanation: The book notes that James v. United States, 366 U.S. 213 (1961), displaced Commissioner v. Wilcox, 327 U.S. 404 (1946), which had excluded embezzled money based on an obligation to restore it. Gilbert distinguishes certain secured withdrawals from typical embezzlement. No extra case briefs should be generated for James or Wilcox.
entries.details: The book notes that James v. United States, 366 U.S. 213 (1961), displaced Commissioner v. Wilcox, 327 U.S. 404 (1946), which had excluded embezzled money based on an obligation to restore it. Gilbert distinguishes certain secured withdrawals from typical embezzlement. No extra case briefs should be generated for James or Wilcox.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, textbook pp. 98–100; Week 3 syllabus-assigned.

topics.assignmentSource: Tax syllabus: Week 3, Chapter 2 pp. 68–102

topics.title: G. Gain on Sale of a Home
topics.description: Section 121 home-sale gain exclusion and limitations.

entries.title: IRC §121 — Principal residence exclusion
entries.summary: A qualifying taxpayer may exclude up to $250,000 of gain on sale of a principal residence, or generally $500,000 for qualifying joint filers.
entries.details: General rule: taxpayer owned and used the property as principal residence for at least two years during the five-year period ending at sale; subject to frequency, filing and other conditions.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 100
entries.elements: Ownership and principal residence use: generally 2 of the 5 years before sale. Standard cap: $250,000; qualifying MFJ cap: $500,000.
entries.examTrap: A vacation property does not qualify merely because it is owned for two years; the principal-residence use requirement matters.
entries.laymanExplanation: When you sell your main home, the law may let you leave a large portion of the profit out of income tax if you meet ownership and living-in-the-home requirements.
entries.legalExplanation: Section 121(a) generally requires both ownership and use of a home as a principal residence for periods totaling at least 2 years during the 5 years before sale. The ordinary gain exclusion is capped at $250,000 for qualifying individual filers. Analyze whether the use and ownership tests were met and whether other special rules apply.

entries.title: IRC §121 — Joint-return conditions
entries.summary: A $500,000 exclusion for qualifying married joint filers generally requires meeting joint-return, use, ownership and other statutory requirements.
entries.details: The reading notes that both spouses must satisfy the use test, while the ownership condition can be satisfied under the statutory joint-filer rules.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 101
entries.laymanExplanation: A married couple filing jointly may qualify for a higher home-sale exclusion, but they must satisfy extra conditions.
entries.legalExplanation: Section 121(b)(2) allows up to $500,000 exclusion for qualifying married joint filers, generally requiring that either spouse meet ownership conditions and both meet use requirements plus other conditions. The source separately mentions surviving-spouse treatment under §121(b)(4).

entries.title: IRC §121 — Once-every-two-years limit
entries.summary: A taxpayer generally cannot claim the full §121 exclusion if it was used on a different sale within the preceding two years.
entries.details: The reading discusses reduced exclusions when sales arise from qualifying changes in employment, health, or certain unforeseen circumstances.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 101
entries.laymanExplanation: You generally cannot use the full main-home sale exclusion every year. The law usually requires a two-year gap, with some exceptions.
entries.legalExplanation: Section 121 generally prevents an eligible taxpayer from using the full exclusion for another residence sale within the preceding 2 years. Section 121(c) can allow a reduced exclusion for certain moves involving work, health or unforeseen circumstances. Calculate the appropriate tax-year cap and exceptions.

entries.title: Principal residence
entries.summary: The home that serves as the taxpayer's main residence for purposes of §121's use requirement.
entries.details: This characterization is factual and distinct from owning a secondary home or investment property.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 100
entries.laymanExplanation: Your principal residence is the place that actually functions as your main home, not just any house you own.
entries.legalExplanation: Principal residence means the property used as the taxpayer's main home, not merely any owned property, for purposes of §121. Facts about actual residence and occupancy matter, and vacation or investment properties do not qualify just because they appreciate.

entries.title: Taxable gain after §121 exclusion
entries.summary: Taxable gain = max(0, realized home-sale gain − allowable §121 exclusion).
entries.details: Textbook example: single taxpayer's $100,000-basis residence sold for $400,000; realized gain $300,000, $250,000 excluded, $50,000 taxable (assuming full eligibility).
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 101
entries.examApplication: Compute realized gain first, then determine §121 eligibility and exclusion limit.
entries.laymanExplanation: First calculate profit from selling your home. Then subtract the part the law lets you exclude. The remaining amount may be taxable.
entries.legalExplanation: For an eligible principal-residence sale, first calculate realized gain as amount realized less adjusted basis, then subtract the exclusion allowed under §121, keeping taxable gain no lower than zero. Book example: sale $400,000, basis $100,000 → $300,000 realized gain; single-filer $250,000 exclusion → $50,000 taxable.

entries.title: Pre-1997 home-sale gain rules
entries.summary: Former §1034 allowed rollover-style gain deferral on reinvestment in another home; prior §121 had a one-time older-taxpayer exclusion.
entries.details: These rules are repealed and appear in the reading only to explain the current §121 regime.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 102

legalWarning.label: REPEALED PRE-1997 LAW
legalWarning.reason: The old §1034 rollover provision and previous one-time home-sale exclusion were superseded by the 1997 enactment of current §121.

entries.legalExplanation: Before 1997, a repealed §1034 rollover rule and older one-time §121 exclusion treated qualifying home sales differently. The current regime derives from Congress's 1997 redesign; these are purely historical notes, not controlling exam computations.
entries.laymanExplanation: There used to be different rules for selling your house. The old system was repealed and replaced in 1997, so it is background rather than an exam rule today.

entries.title: IRC §121(c) — reduced exclusion for qualifying early home sales
entries.summary: When a taxpayer fails the ordinary ownership/use or frequency rules, a reduced maximum exclusion may apply for qualifying employment, health or unforeseen-circumstance reasons.
entries.laymanExplanation: If you must move for a new job after living in your home only one year, you might still exclude part of the profit rather than losing the entire break.
entries.legalExplanation: The reading illustrates a single taxpayer transferred to a new office after one year who may qualify for a proportional $125,000 ceiling instead of the full $250,000. §121(c) requires identifying the qualifying reason and determining a statutory reduced amount; do not assume every early sale qualifies.
entries.details: The reading illustrates a single taxpayer transferred to a new office after one year who may qualify for a proportional $125,000 ceiling instead of the full $250,000. §121(c) requires identifying the qualifying reason and determining a statutory reduced amount; do not assume every early sale qualifies.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, textbook pp. 101–102; Week 3 syllabus-assigned.
entries.examApplication: For eligible single filer using a main home one year, the book gives a $125,000 reduced cap (half of $250,000) for a qualifying job transfer, not a generally unrestricted exclusion.

entries.title: IRC §121(b)(4) — qualifying surviving spouse
entries.summary: A surviving spouse may qualify for the $500,000 home-sale gain limit for a sale within two years of the other spouse's death, if statutory requirements are met.
entries.laymanExplanation: If someone's spouse dies, they may still have a limited period to use the higher married-couple home-sale exclusion when selling the house.
entries.legalExplanation: The source notes §121(b)(4), which permits a qualifying surviving spouse to receive a $500,000 limit for a sale within two years after the spouse's death when requisite ownership/use and other conditions are met.
entries.details: The source notes §121(b)(4), which permits a qualifying surviving spouse to receive a $500,000 limit for a sale within two years after the spouse's death when requisite ownership/use and other conditions are met.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, textbook pp. 101; Week 3 syllabus-assigned.

topics.assignmentSource: Tax syllabus: Week 3, Chapter 2 pp. 68–102

entries.title: Imputed income
entries.summary: Nonmarket value derived from one's own work or use of one's own property is generally not taxable.
entries.laymanExplanation: Fixing your own car saves you money, but you do not report imagined mechanic wages.
entries.legalExplanation: The source distinguishes imputed income from market exchange. The primary categories are self-provided household labor and the rental value of living in owner-occupied housing. This economic benefit ordinarily is not included under §61.
entries.details: The source distinguishes imputed income from market exchange. The primary categories are self-provided household labor and the rental value of living in owner-occupied housing. This economic benefit ordinarily is not included under §61.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Week 3 assigned pp. 112–114

entries.title: Psychic income
entries.summary: Subjective happiness or pleasure is not measured as taxable income.
entries.laymanExplanation: Enjoying a sunset or an extra vacation week does not create a separate tax charge.
entries.legalExplanation: Psychic income reflects subjective satisfaction or enjoyment, unlike market-measurable consumption. The source explains that taxing leisure would be intrusive and administratively impracticable.
entries.details: Psychic income reflects subjective satisfaction or enjoyment, unlike market-measurable consumption. The source explains that taxing leisure would be intrusive and administratively impracticable.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Week 3 assigned pp. 114–116

entries.title: In-kind income
entries.summary: Property or services received as market compensation generally constitute income, despite the absence of cash.
entries.laymanExplanation: A lawyer who gets house painting in exchange for legal work may have taxable income even though no money changes hands.
entries.legalExplanation: Gross income under §61 includes income realized in money, property, or services. Noncash employer benefits may be excluded under specific statutes such as §§119 and 132.
entries.details: Gross income under §61 includes income realized in money, property, or services. Noncash employer benefits may be excluded under specific statutes such as §§119 and 132.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Week 3 assigned pp. 114–116

entries.title: Private sphere versus public sphere
entries.summary: Private transactions generally occur within the household; public transactions involve market exchanges with others.
entries.laymanExplanation: Babysitting your own child is different from providing childcare to a stranger in exchange for repairs.
entries.legalExplanation: The source distinguishes market-based labor and property exchanges from household and self-provision activity. Tax consequences can differ sharply even where the economic benefit is similar.
entries.details: The source distinguishes market-based labor and property exchanges from household and self-provision activity. Tax consequences can differ sharply even where the economic benefit is similar.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Week 3 assigned pp. 111–112

entries.title: Imputed rental value of a home
entries.summary: An owner-occupant benefits by not paying rent to another landlord; that hypothetical rent is not ordinarily taxed.
entries.laymanExplanation: If you live in the house you own, the IRS does not normally charge you income tax on imagined rent to yourself.
entries.legalExplanation: The source compares investing $1 million in bonds and paying rent with buying a home to occupy. Bond interest is taxable; owner-occupied housing value is not included as imputed rent. This creates an asymmetric tax preference.
entries.details: The source compares investing $1 million in bonds and paying rent with buying a home to occupy. Bond interest is taxable; owner-occupied housing value is not included as imputed rent. This creates an asymmetric tax preference.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Week 3 assigned pp. 113–114

entries.title: Barter and reciprocal services are generally included in gross income
entries.summary: When two people trade valuable services, each generally has income equal to the fair market value received.
entries.laymanExplanation: A babysitter trades $100 in childcare for $100 of painting; both may have $100 of income.
entries.legalExplanation: Under Reg. §1.61-2(d)(1), services paid for with property or other services are generally valued at FMV. Self-service without a negotiated market exchange is treated differently; personal consumption costs typically are not deductible.
entries.details: Under Reg. §1.61-2(d)(1), services paid for with property or other services are generally valued at FMV. Self-service without a negotiated market exchange is treated differently; personal consumption costs typically are not deductible.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Week 3 assigned pp. 115–117

entries.title: Revenue Ruling 79-24 — reciprocal services and art-for-rent
entries.summary: Both sides of taxable barter transactions include the fair market value of services, property, or rental use received.
entries.laymanExplanation: A lawyer swaps legal work for painting; an artist exchanges artwork for apartment rent. Both sides receive taxable value.
entries.legalExplanation: The assigned revenue ruling applies §61 and Reg. §1.61-2(d)(1). Situation 1: legal and painting services are exchanged; each includes FMV received. Situation 2: the apartment owner includes FMV of art and the artist includes rental value. It is an IRS ruling, not a judicial opinion.
entries.details: The assigned revenue ruling applies §61 and Reg. §1.61-2(d)(1). Situation 1: legal and painting services are exchanged; each includes FMV received. Situation 2: the apartment owner includes FMV of art and the artist includes rental value. It is an IRS ruling, not a judicial opinion.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Week 3 assigned pp. 116–117

entries.title: Barter exchange reporting — §6045
entries.summary: Organized barter exchanges may have information-reporting duties; casual swaps of similar services on a noncommercial basis receive separate treatment.
entries.laymanExplanation: A service-credit trade club may report its members' trades to the IRS; informal neighbors helping each other can be different.
entries.legalExplanation: The source cites §6045 and Reg. §1.6045-1(a)(4), which excludes arrangements solely for informal noncommercial exchange of similar services from the defined reporting barter exchange. Reporting and inclusion are separate questions.
entries.details: The source cites §6045 and Reg. §1.6045-1(a)(4), which excludes arrangements solely for informal noncommercial exchange of similar services from the defined reporting barter exchange. Reporting and inclusion are separate questions.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Week 3 assigned pp. 117–118

entries.title: Implicit tax and tax capitalization
entries.summary: Tax-favored investments can command higher prices and lower pretax yields as investors compete for tax savings.
entries.laymanExplanation: You might accept a 6% tax-free municipal bond return instead of a 10% taxable bond return; the yield difference is the hidden cost of the break.
entries.legalExplanation: The source uses §103 municipal bonds to demonstrate implicit taxation and tax capitalization. A 10% taxable return versus 6% tax-free comparable return implies 40% reduced yield by this simplified comparison. This is not a tax payment to the Treasury.
entries.details: The source uses §103 municipal bonds to demonstrate implicit taxation and tax capitalization. A 10% taxable return versus 6% tax-free comparable return implies 40% reduced yield by this simplified comparison. This is not a tax payment to the Treasury.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Week 3 assigned pp. 118–119
entries.examApplication: Implicit tax = (10% − 6%)/10% = 40%; assume comparable risk, maturity and market pricing.

entries.title: Substitute taxation
entries.summary: Tax law may limit the payor's deductions rather than directly including a hard-to-value benefit in the recipient's income.
entries.laymanExplanation: Instead of tracking every free lunch an employee eats, the law might deny some of the employer's expense deduction.
entries.legalExplanation: The source uses consumer furniture assembly and employer-provided meals to illustrate compensating for untaxed private or fringe benefits by taxing an easier-to-observe side of the exchange. This is a policy design mechanism, not a generally applicable statutory inclusion test.
entries.details: The source uses consumer furniture assembly and employer-provided meals to illustrate compensating for untaxed private or fringe benefits by taxing an easier-to-observe side of the exchange. This is a policy design mechanism, not a generally applicable statutory inclusion test.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Week 3 assigned pp. 119

entries.title: Added leisure versus added compensation
entries.summary: Equal annual salaries generally produce equal reported wage income even when one worker receives more vacation days.
entries.laymanExplanation: Two workers earn $60,000, but one has an extra week off. The salary is the same for income-tax calculation.
entries.legalExplanation: Paid leisure changes effective hourly pay, but tax law generally does not separately impute a taxable dollar value for foregone possible work during additional vacation days.
entries.details: Paid leisure changes effective hourly pay, but tax law generally does not separately impute a taxable dollar value for foregone possible work during additional vacation days.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Week 3 assigned pp. 115–116

entries.title: Why private benefits are ignored
entries.summary: Privacy, valuation, enforceability and behavioral consequences complicate taxing the private sphere.
entries.laymanExplanation: The government does not inspect your home repairs or measure your happiness, even though those can make you better off.
entries.legalExplanation: The book emphasizes stay-at-home labor, self-provision, owner-occupied housing, and tax preference effects. This is supplementary policy rather than an exam rule.
entries.details: The book emphasizes stay-at-home labor, self-provision, owner-occupied housing, and tax preference effects. This is supplementary policy rather than an exam rule.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Week 3 assigned pp. 111–119

topics.title: A. Value Outside the Marketplace
topics.description: Imputed income, in-kind barter, implicit and substitute taxation
topics.assignmentSource: Syllabus Week 3 printed pp. 111–119

topics.title: B. Gifts — §102 and Commissioner v. Duberstein
topics.description: The textbook's Week 3 pp.119–134, plus separately assigned Harris opinion (pp.154–161) kept distinct.

entries.title: IRC §102(a) — recipient exclusion for genuine gifts and bequests
entries.summary: Property acquired by gift, bequest, devise or inheritance is generally excluded from the recipient's income.
entries.laymanExplanation: If your parent gives you a real present out of love, you normally do not pay income tax just for receiving it.
entries.legalExplanation: §102(a) excludes qualifying gifts and inheritances. However, §102 does not turn compensation into a gift merely by label. The casebook contrasts Donna giving Edward $30,000 as a gift (recipient excludes, donor no deduction) with wages for personal services. Gift-tax matters are separate.
entries.details: §102(a) excludes qualifying gifts and inheritances. However, §102 does not turn compensation into a gift merely by label. The casebook contrasts Donna giving Edward $30,000 as a gift (recipient excludes, donor no deduction) with wages for personal services. Gift-tax matters are separate.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 3 pp. 120–123
entries.examApplication: Donna earns $100,000, gives adult son Edward $30,000 out of affection. She has no ordinary personal deduction, and Edward excludes the gift.
entries.examTrap: A purported romantic-partner gift still requires donor motive under Duberstein and does not establish criminal tax willfulness under Harris.

entries.title: Detached and disinterested generosity / donor's motive
entries.summary: The giver's purpose is the central inquiry: generosity and affection favor gift status; expected business return or compensation weighs against.
entries.laymanExplanation: A Cadillac called a present may really be payment if it rewards someone for profitable customer leads.
entries.legalExplanation: Duberstein applies §102's colloquial gift concept to total factual circumstances. Detached/disinterested refers to absence of a commercial exchange, not the donor's indifference. No rigid test substitutes for determining the transferor's intention.
entries.details: Duberstein applies §102's colloquial gift concept to total factual circumstances. Detached/disinterested refers to absence of a commercial exchange, not the donor's indifference. No rigid test substitutes for determining the transferor's intention.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 3 pp. 123–130
entries.examApplication: Review transferor statements, relationship circumstances, requests for services, timing and contemporaneous documents. Contrast gift-classification under Duberstein with criminal willfulness under Harris.

entries.title: Duberstein — gift is a fact-sensitive classification
entries.summary: Gift status under §102 is determined from the overall facts and the transferor's motivation, not merely voluntariness, wording, or formal obligations.
entries.laymanExplanation: Someone can willingly hand you money and still be paying for a job you did.
entries.legalExplanation: A gift need not follow a legal obligation, but absence of legal duty is not conclusive. The donor's intended economic benefit, the recipient's services, contemporaneous correspondence, business deductibility, and surrounding relationships matter. Appellate review generally respects factual findings absent clear error.
entries.details: A gift need not follow a legal obligation, but absence of legal duty is not conclusive. The donor's intended economic benefit, the recipient's services, contemporaneous correspondence, business deductibility, and surrounding relationships matter. Appellate review generally respects factual findings absent clear error.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 3 pp. 123–129

entries.title: IRC §102(c) — employer transfers to employees
entries.summary: An employer's transfer to or for the benefit of an employee generally cannot qualify for the §102(a) gift exclusion.
entries.laymanExplanation: A company generally cannot make your bonus tax-free just by saying it is a gift.
entries.legalExplanation: The 1986 statutory enactment of §102(c) generally overrode the historical Stanton outcome from the consolidated Duberstein case. Specific other exclusions, such as qualifying §74(c) achievement awards, may apply.
entries.details: The 1986 statutory enactment of §102(c) generally overrode the historical Stanton outcome from the consolidated Duberstein case. Specific other exclusions, such as qualifying §74(c) achievement awards, may apply.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 3 pp. 129–130

legalWarning.label: STANTON RULE SUPERSEDED
legalWarning.reason: Congress added §102(c) in 1986 and generally disallowed employer-to-employee gift exclusion, unlike the historical outcome following remand.

entries.examTrap: Do not use Stanton's 1960-era treatment as present-day law for employer bonuses.

entries.title: Tips and service-related gratuities are taxable
entries.summary: Ordinary gratuities received for services are compensation under §61 and Reg. §1.61-2(a)(1).
entries.laymanExplanation: A waiter getting a tip has earned money even if a customer gives it voluntarily.
entries.legalExplanation: The casebook discusses restaurant tips, clergyman marriage fees and casino gaming gratuities. The referenced McCormick and Olk decisions appear only as citations; they are not independently reproduced opinions.
entries.details: The casebook discusses restaurant tips, clergyman marriage fees and casino gaming gratuities. The referenced McCormick and Olk decisions appear only as citations; they are not independently reproduced opinions.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 3 pp. 131

entries.title: IRC §74 — prizes and awards
entries.summary: Most prizes and awards are gross income unless a specific statutory exception is satisfied.
entries.laymanExplanation: Winning a car or cash in a contest is normally taxable.
entries.legalExplanation: §74 includes prizes and awards, with statutory exceptions for certain qualifying donated prizes, and eligible employee achievement awards under §74(c). The receiving taxpayer must establish the conditions for an applicable exception.
entries.details: §74 includes prizes and awards, with statutory exceptions for certain qualifying donated prizes, and eligible employee achievement awards under §74(c). The receiving taxpayer must establish the conditions for an applicable exception.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 3 pp. 131

entries.title: IRC §117 — qualified scholarship amounts
entries.summary: Qualified scholarship funds for degree candidates used for tuition, mandatory fees and required educational materials can be excluded, but service compensation is generally taxable.
entries.laymanExplanation: A tuition scholarship may be tax-free; pay for teaching or research is usually taxable compensation.
entries.legalExplanation: §117's statutory scholarship exclusion is limited to specified educational costs for eligible degree candidates. Amounts received as consideration for services (subject to exceptions elsewhere in statute) are generally not excluded by §117.
entries.details: §117's statutory scholarship exclusion is limited to specified educational costs for eligible degree candidates. Amounts received as consideration for services (subject to exceptions elsewhere in statute) are generally not excluded by §117.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 3 pp. 131–132

entries.title: Bequests versus payment for prior services
entries.summary: A true inheritance is ordinarily excluded; testamentary property promised as consideration for services can be taxable income.
entries.laymanExplanation: If a lawyer works for free in exchange for a promise of money in a will, the later will payment can be taxable compensation.
entries.legalExplanation: The casebook contrasts Wolder (contractually promised bequest for services treated as income), McDonald (appreciation bequest excludable) and Lyeth (will contest proceeds deemed bequest). Those are supporting references only; no separate opinions reproduced in assigned pp111–134.
entries.details: The casebook contrasts Wolder (contractually promised bequest for services treated as income), McDonald (appreciation bequest excludable) and Lyeth (will contest proceeds deemed bequest). Those are supporting references only; no separate opinions reproduced in assigned pp111–134.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 3 pp. 132

entries.title: General welfare exclusion
entries.summary: Some need-based welfare, disaster and victim-relief benefits are administratively treated as outside gross income.
entries.laymanExplanation: Certain government aid payments do not go on your income-tax return even though they give you cash or help.
entries.legalExplanation: The source contrasts general-welfare administrative treatment of qualifying relief with unemployment benefits now included under §85. TANF assistance with work requirements can raise characterization issues, and IRS Notice 99-3 states conditions under which TANF assistance remains welfare rather than wages.
entries.details: The source contrasts general-welfare administrative treatment of qualifying relief with unemployment benefits now included under §85. TANF assistance with work requirements can raise characterization issues, and IRS Notice 99-3 states conditions under which TANF assistance remains welfare rather than wages.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 3 pp. 132–133

entries.title: IRC §85 — unemployment compensation
entries.summary: Unemployment benefits are generally taxable income under §85 absent a specific tax-year exception.
entries.laymanExplanation: Unlike some welfare payments, unemployment checks normally go in taxable income.
entries.legalExplanation: The casebook notes an exceptional temporary 2020 COVID-era exclusion; current general treatment is inclusion under §85 rather than a §102 gift.
entries.details: The casebook notes an exceptional temporary 2020 COVID-era exclusion; current general treatment is inclusion under §85 rather than a §102 gift.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 3 pp. 132–133

entries.title: IRC §86 — taxable portion of Social Security benefits
entries.summary: Depending on combined income, zero to 85% of Social Security benefits can be included in gross income.
entries.laymanExplanation: A person receiving Social Security may owe tax on part of those benefits, not on all of them in every case.
entries.legalExplanation: The casebook outlines a statutory combined-income analysis using AGI, tax-exempt interest and one-half of benefits, with joint-filer threshold amounts $32,000 and $44,000. The full piecewise formula is in §86, and the 85% figure is a maximum portion included, not the rate charged on those benefits.
entries.details: The casebook outlines a statutory combined-income analysis using AGI, tax-exempt interest and one-half of benefits, with joint-filer threshold amounts $32,000 and $44,000. The full piecewise formula is in §86, and the 85% figure is a maximum portion included, not the rate charged on those benefits.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 3 pp. 133–134
entries.examTrap: 85% inclusion is NOT an 85% tax rate; the actual rate depends on taxable-income brackets.

entries.title: Donor versus donee income tax consequences
entries.summary: The donor's tax and deduction are separate from the donee's gift exclusion.
entries.laymanExplanation: When someone gives their adult child $30,000 as a true gift, neither a tax deduction for the parent nor income for the child automatically results.
entries.legalExplanation: In the source's Donna–Edward example, Donna still has $100,000 of earned income with no personal deduction for a $30,000 transfer, while Edward excludes the $30,000 under §102. This is distinct from transfer tax considerations.
entries.details: In the source's Donna–Edward example, Donna still has $100,000 of earned income with no personal deduction for a $30,000 transfer, while Edward excludes the $30,000 under §102. This is distinct from transfer tax considerations.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 3 pp. 121–123
entries.examTrap: A recipient's income-tax exclusion does not resolve any separately applicable donor-side gift or estate tax.

entries.title: Business gift versus compensation
entries.summary: A business-motivated transfer can be a genuine gift, but payment intended to reward or induce services is normally income.
entries.laymanExplanation: A store might send a thank-you present, but paying someone for new customers is compensation even if it comes wrapped as a gift.
entries.legalExplanation: Under Duberstein, business purpose, deduction, and corporate identity are evidence but not automatic legal bars to §102. The notes discuss §274(b)'s $25 business-gift deduction cap as a separate, payor-side rule.
entries.details: Under Duberstein, business purpose, deduction, and corporate identity are evidence but not automatic legal bars to §102. The notes discuss §274(b)'s $25 business-gift deduction cap as a separate, payor-side rule.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 3 pp. 126–131

entries.title: Why the Code excludes gifts despite economic enrichment
entries.summary: Privacy, family unit treatment, and administrative burden motivate gift exclusions.
entries.laymanExplanation: Gifts make people richer, but checking every birthday gift would be intrusive and impractical.
entries.legalExplanation: The source contrasts Haig–Simons broad economic income with §102's statutory exclusion and debates alternatives that might tax the recipient, allow donor deduction, both or neither.
entries.details: The source contrasts Haig–Simons broad economic income with §102's statutory exclusion and debates alternatives that might tax the recipient, allow donor deduction, both or neither.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 3 pp. 119–123

entries.title: Commissioner v. Duberstein (with Stanton v. United States)
entries.summary: The Supreme Court sustained the Tax Court's finding that Duberstein's Cadillac was business remuneration, and remanded Stanton for clearer factfinding.
entries.laymanExplanation: A businessman got a Cadillac after sending useful leads to another business. The Court said calling it a gift wasn't enough. Another payment called a 'gratuity' needed clearer factfinding.
entries.facts: Duberstein gave business acquaintance Berman information about possible customers. Berman insisted on gifting a Cadillac to thank him; the donor's company treated it as a business deduction. Duberstein said he never intended compensation. Separately, a church-related corporation awarded departing employee Stanton a $20,000 payment called a gratuity in appreciation of his years of service; the trial court made only a conclusory gift finding.
entries.issue: What makes a transfer a 'gift' excluded by §102(a), and how should appellate courts review trial-level findings about motive?
entries.holding: Duberstein: The Supreme Court reversed the Sixth Circuit and reinstated the Tax Court's permissible factual determination that the Cadillac was payment for business services, not a gift. Stanton: The Second Circuit judgment was vacated and the matter remanded for adequate findings; the Supreme Court did not hold categorically that his gratuity was a gift.
entries.reasoning: The statutory gift concept relies on the transferor's dominant purpose, not simply voluntariness or lack of duty. Detached/disinterested generosity suggests gift; remuneration or hoped-for economic benefit suggests income. Business deduction and corporate status matter but are not conclusive. The decision largely places the question with the factfinder, with limited appellate reversal for clear error.
entries.rule: For §102(a), examine the transferor's actual intention and whole factual record: affection or detached generosity versus anticipated business benefit or services. Neither labels nor voluntary payment decide by themselves.
entries.exam: Analyze donor intent, services, quid pro quo, reimbursement, business records, and the limits on appellate factual review. Apply §102(c) separately for post-1986 employer-to-employee transfers.
entries.examApplication: A supplier sends a car to a consultant who found customers for the supplier. Assess business motives despite references to a gift; if employment relationship exists, add §102(c).
entries.examTrap: The Court did not announce all corporate transfers are income or all personal transfers are gifts. Stanton's historical ultimate classification is limited by later §102(c).
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., reproduced Supreme Court opinion, assigned Week 3 printed pp.123–129.
entries.sourceRole: Opinion reproduced in syllabus-assigned textbook excerpt — dedicated case brief.

topics.assignmentSource: Week 3 syllabus: Chapter 3 pp111–134 + assigned Harris handout

entries.title: Harris — Gift versus paid services in a personal relationship
entries.summary: A gift reflects the transferor's donative motive; compensation is paid for services, duties, or anticipated economic return.
entries.details: Harris discusses financial and property transfers in a long-term romantic relationship and warns against treating all such payments as necessarily taxable compensation or necessarily gifts. Specific payments for specified services may be different from support and gifts motivated by affection.
entries.source: Assigned 'Harris handout (2).pdf', scanned casebook excerpt, Chapter 3: The Private Sphere and the Public Sphere, printed pp. 154–161. Reference pages: 155–160.
entries.examApplication: Suppose one payment is tied to a specific contractual service and another is an unrestricted present motivated by personal affection. Identify donor intent separately for each transfer.
entries.examTrap: Neither 'romantic relationship' nor 'regular payment' alone supplies a conclusive answer.
entries.laymanExplanation: A friend sending birthday money is different from someone paying you to provide a service. The reason for the transfer matters more than its label.

entries.title: Criminal tax willfulness
entries.summary: A criminal tax conviction for willful nonpayment or nonfiling requires proof of a voluntary, intentional violation of a known legal duty.
entries.details: Harris involves §§7201 and 7203. In the criminal setting, the prosecution must prove the relevant criminal elements, including willfulness, beyond a reasonable doubt. A genuinely unsettled legal duty and a good-faith belief may defeat willfulness even if tax treatment could be contested in civil proceedings.
entries.source: Assigned 'Harris handout (2).pdf', scanned casebook excerpt, Chapter 3: The Private Sphere and the Public Sphere, printed pp. 154–161. Reference pages: 154–160.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish whether money is income for civil tax purposes from whether the recipient knowingly violated a clear legal duty and could be criminally convicted.
entries.examTrap: Uncertainty sufficient to prevent criminal conviction does not automatically mean the disputed receipt is an excluded gift.
entries.laymanExplanation: Criminal tax law generally requires more than a wrong return. The prosecution must prove the person intentionally violated a tax duty they knew they had.

entries.title: Criminal burden of proof versus civil tax determination
entries.summary: The government must establish the charged criminal tax offense beyond a reasonable doubt; civil taxability is a different question.
entries.details: In Harris, the court found the donor's purpose inadequately proved as to Conley and serious uncertainty about the tax classification as to Harris. The court stressed that the criminal law must provide fair warning before it may punish willful nonfiling or evasion.
entries.source: Assigned 'Harris handout (2).pdf', scanned casebook excerpt, Chapter 3: The Private Sphere and the Public Sphere, printed pp. 154–161. Reference pages: 154–160.
entries.examApplication: When a question asks whether a tax charge can support criminal sanctions, discuss donor intent, taxpayer knowledge, and legal clarity separately from the likely civil treatment.
entries.examTrap: Do not transform a reversal for insufficient criminal proof into a positive civil tax holding.
entries.laymanExplanation: A civil tax disagreement and a criminal tax prosecution have different stakes. Proving someone deliberately committed a crime is harder than disputing a tax bill.

entries.title: Letters offered to show belief, not necessarily their truth
entries.summary: A communication can be relevant to the recipient's state of mind without being offered as proof that its factual claims are true.
entries.details: Kritzik wrote Harris affectionate letters and described gifts. The court held the letters were relevant to Harris's good-faith belief about his purpose and therefore should not have been excluded as hearsay solely because the letters might be false. This is a supporting evidentiary point in the Tax opinion, not the central gift definition.
entries.source: Assigned 'Harris handout (2).pdf', scanned casebook excerpt, Chapter 3: The Private Sphere and the Public Sphere, printed pp. 154–161. Reference pages: 156–157.
entries.examApplication: A taxpayer's beliefs and the words communicated to them can matter to criminal willfulness, even when the exact objective truth of the statements is disputed.
entries.laymanExplanation: The donor wrote letters calling the transfers gifts. Even if those words were disputed, the recipient might reasonably believe them, which matters when deciding whether she knowingly committed a tax crime.

entries.title: United States v. Harris (7th Cir. 1991)
entries.summary: The Seventh Circuit reversed the convictions of Harris and Conley and ordered dismissal of their indictments; the government had not shown the criminal tax duty and willfulness needed for convictions.
entries.details: This is a reproduced judicial opinion in the assigned handout, not merely a citation. The handout also includes a separate concurrence by Judge Flaum expressing concern about an overly categorical approach to payments between romantic partners.
entries.source: Assigned 'Harris handout (2).pdf', scanned casebook excerpt, Chapter 3: The Private Sphere and the Public Sphere, printed pp. 154–161. Reproduced opinion 'United States v. Harris,' 942 F.2d 1125, at printed pp. 154–160; Judge Flaum's concurrence and notes through p. 161.
entries.facts: David Kritzik, a wealthy widower, gave Leigh Ann Conley and Lynnette Harris (twin sisters) substantial amounts of money and property during personal relationships. The government alleged they should have reported the transfers as taxable income; both were convicted in separate criminal trials. Conley's prosecution relied on inferences about the donor's intent. Harris attempted to introduce Kritzik's letters describing affection and gifts, but the district court excluded them.
entries.issue: Could the government sustain criminal tax convictions treating these transfers as taxable income when it had not proved donor intent, when Harris's evidence of her good-faith belief was excluded, and when relevant gift-versus-income law did not clearly establish criminal liability?
entries.holding: No. Conley's conviction was reversed because the government had not sufficiently shown Kritzik's intent and her knowledge. Harris's conviction was reversed because relevant letters should have been admitted to show good-faith belief and because the unclear tax law did not give fair warning sufficient for a willful criminal violation. The court ordered dismissal of both indictments.
entries.reasoning: Applying Duberstein, the court identified the transferor's intent as central to the gift inquiry. Gift-tax returns did not establish the nature of all transfers to Conley. For Harris, affectionate letters could affect her belief even if not true, and their exclusion denied evidence central to willfulness. Prior civil Tax Court cases indicated noncriminal gift treatment in comparable personal relationships; the law was too unclear for criminal sanctions. The opinion did not establish a categorical civil tax exemption for transfers between lovers. Judge Flaum concurred in the judgment but criticized the majority's broad language and favored case-by-case donor-intent analysis.
entries.rule: The §102(a) gift inquiry focuses on the transferor's motive under Duberstein; ambiguous civil tax classifications and failures to prove knowledge of a known duty can defeat criminal willfulness. Harris does not conclusively exempt all personal-relationship transfers from civil income tax.
entries.exam: When facing gifts-versus-income questions, analyze donor motive and any quid pro quo. If the hypothetical asks for criminal liability, separately analyze proof of willfulness and clarity of the legal duty. Do not equate absence of criminal liability with a holding that the amount was necessarily a civil-tax gift.
entries.examApplication: A wealthy individual gives recurring money and jewelry to a longtime romantic partner. Assess affection, potential payment for services, donor statements and gift returns. Then, if the recipient failed to file a return, explain why the government must independently show a known tax duty and intentional violation.
entries.examTrap: Harris reversed criminal convictions, not all potential civil tax liabilities. Pair with assigned Duberstein (pp123–129) and §102(c) when relevant.
entries.sourceRole: Dedicated assigned-case brief based on the reproduced judicial opinion in the handout.
entries.laymanExplanation: Two women received substantial money from a wealthy man. The court threw out their criminal tax convictions because the government had not adequately shown the necessary criminal tax violations; it did not say every romantic gift is tax-free.
entries.sourceWeek: Week 3 — separate Harris opinion handout pp154–161.

entries.title: Judge Flaum's concurrence — avoid a categorical gift rule
entries.summary: Judge Flaum agreed criminal convictions should fall but objected to treating all long-term romantic transfers as categorically exempt.
entries.details: The concurrence stresses individualized donor intent under Duberstein and warns that some payments may be compensation for services even within a sustained personal relationship. He joined the judgment because the record was insufficient and the legal standards were uncertain.
entries.source: Assigned 'Harris handout (2).pdf', scanned casebook excerpt, Chapter 3: The Private Sphere and the Public Sphere, printed pp. 154–161. Reference pages: 160–161.
entries.examTrap: This is a concurrence, not a majority holding establishing a bright-line taxable or exempt category.
entries.laymanExplanation: One judge agreed the criminal convictions had to go but warned not to assume that every gift between romantic partners is tax-free. Each transfer still needs a look at why it was given.

entries.title: Section 83 mentioned in the prefatory Duberstein note
entries.summary: The handout's preceding note mentions §83 for property transferred in connection with services.
entries.details: The first handout page (printed p. 154) includes a question about whether §83 changes analysis of a business-motivated transfer. This is a prompt and supporting reference, not an assigned judicial opinion or a developed §83 treatment in the excerpt.
entries.source: Assigned 'Harris handout (2).pdf', scanned casebook excerpt, Chapter 3: The Private Sphere and the Public Sphere, printed pp. 154–161. Reference pages: 154.
entries.laymanExplanation: If property is given in return for work, separate tax provisions may apply to compensation paid with property. The reading mentions this as an extra issue, not a full lesson on §83.

topics.assignmentSource: Separate Harris handout, explicitly assigned Week 3; not textbook pp111–134
