entries.title: IRC §1001 — realized gain or loss
entries.summary: Realized gain or loss generally equals amount realized minus adjusted basis.
entries.laymanExplanation: Sell an asset for $5,000 that has $1,000 basis: your realized gain is $4,000.
entries.legalExplanation: §61(a)(3), §1001(a)-(b), §1011, §1012, and §1016 supply the mechanics; amount realized includes qualifying money and FMV of other property, and adjusted basis accounts for statutory increases/decreases. Recognition can differ under a separate nonrecognition provision.
entries.details: §61(a)(3), §1001(a)-(b), §1011, §1012, and §1016 supply the mechanics; amount realized includes qualifying money and FMV of other property, and adjusted basis accounts for statutory increases/decreases. Recognition can differ under a separate nonrecognition provision.
entries.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 4 assigned printed pp. 134–135.
entries.examApplication: Compute sale proceeds − relevant gain/loss basis before applying any exclusion or nonrecognition.

entries.title: IRC §1015(a) — gifted property generally takes donor's basis
entries.summary: A recipient of gifted property generally takes the donor's adjusted basis to determine gain on a later disposition.
entries.laymanExplanation: Giving your child stock doesn't erase the profit already built into it. Your child usually inherits your tax cost.
entries.legalExplanation: Under §1015(a), the donee typically assumes donor's adjusted basis; the donor's untaxed appreciation remains built in. A special dual-basis limitation applies when FMV at gift is below donor's basis, for determining losses.
entries.details: Under §1015(a), the donee typically assumes donor's adjusted basis; the donor's untaxed appreciation remains built in. A special dual-basis limitation applies when FMV at gift is below donor's basis, for determining losses.
entries.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 4 assigned printed pp. 134–138.
entries.examApplication: Donor bought stock for $1,000, gift-date FMV $2,000, donee sells for $5,000; gain generally $4,000, not $3,000.

entries.title: IRC §1015(a) — dual basis for gifts of loss property
entries.summary: If donor basis exceeds FMV when gifted, donee generally uses donor basis for gain and gift-date FMV for loss.
entries.laymanExplanation: If someone gives you a stock they bought for $2,000 when it's worth only $1,000, you can't claim the donor's full old loss if you sell it for $500.
entries.legalExplanation: The statute prevents shifting built-in loss to the donee. If sale price exceeds donor basis, use donor basis for gain; if it falls below gift-date FMV, use gift-date FMV for loss; if sale proceeds lie between those figures, generally no recognized gain or loss from the basis comparison.
entries.details: The statute prevents shifting built-in loss to the donee. If sale price exceeds donor basis, use donor basis for gain; if it falls below gift-date FMV, use gift-date FMV for loss; if sale proceeds lie between those figures, generally no recognized gain or loss from the basis comparison.
entries.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 4 assigned printed pp. 135, 141.
entries.examTrap: There are TWO bases for depreciated gift property. For sales between the two values, the result ordinarily is neither gain nor loss.

entries.title: Transferred (carryover) basis versus substituted basis
entries.summary: Transferred basis follows the property's former owner's basis; substituted basis derives from basis in another asset or event under statutory rules.
entries.laymanExplanation: A gift recipient generally starts with the donor's tax cost, not today's market price.
entries.legalExplanation: The source distinguishes 'transferred basis' under §7701(a)(43) from 'exchanged/substituted basis' terminology under §7701(a)(42)-(44); practitioners often use 'carryover' broadly. By contrast, §1014 generally resets basis on qualifying property acquired from a decedent.
entries.details: The source distinguishes 'transferred basis' under §7701(a)(43) from 'exchanged/substituted basis' terminology under §7701(a)(42)-(44); practitioners often use 'carryover' broadly. By contrast, §1014 generally resets basis on qualifying property acquired from a decedent.
entries.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 4 assigned printed pp. 134–135.

entries.title: Fair market value on the gift date
entries.summary: The property's market value when donated matters particularly when donor basis exceeds that value.
entries.laymanExplanation: To determine a deductible loss on a later sale, you may need to know exactly what the stock was worth on the day you received it.
entries.legalExplanation: For purposes of §1015(a)'s loss-basis limitation, gift-date FMV serves as the loss basis if it is below donor basis; valuation is not a new fair-market-value gain basis. The chapter questions require checking each potential sale price.
entries.details: For purposes of §1015(a)'s loss-basis limitation, gift-date FMV serves as the loss basis if it is below donor basis; valuation is not a new fair-market-value gain basis. The chapter questions require checking each potential sale price.
entries.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 4 assigned printed pp. 135, 141.

entries.title: Built-in gain and built-in loss
entries.summary: Economic appreciation or depreciation accumulated before a disposition and not yet recognized.
entries.laymanExplanation: A stock bought for $1,000 that's worth $2,500 has $1,500 of profit on paper; that isn't necessarily currently taxed.
entries.legalExplanation: Gifted property with built-in appreciation generally preserves the gain through donor carryover basis. A built-in loss is subject to the distinct FMV-limited loss basis, which prevents loss shifting by gift.
entries.details: Gifted property with built-in appreciation generally preserves the gain through donor carryover basis. A built-in loss is subject to the distinct FMV-limited loss basis, which prevents loss shifting by gift.
entries.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 4 assigned printed pp. 134–138.

entries.title: IRC §1015(d) — basis adjustment for gift tax paid
entries.summary: Certain federal gift tax paid by the donor can increase a donee's basis, with statutory limits for post-1976 gifts.
entries.laymanExplanation: If the giver actually pays gift tax, part of that tax can sometimes raise the recipient's basis.
entries.legalExplanation: The notes identify §1015(d) and its limitation for gifts made after 1977 to gift tax attributable to net appreciation. This is a narrow calculation overlay, not a blanket addition of the entire gift tax.
entries.details: The notes identify §1015(d) and its limitation for gifts made after 1977 to gift tax attributable to net appreciation. This is a narrow calculation overlay, not a blanket addition of the entire gift tax.
entries.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 4 assigned printed pp. 138.

entries.title: IRC §1014 — basis of inherited property
entries.summary: Qualifying property acquired from a decedent generally receives a basis equal to date-of-death FMV or an eligible alternate valuation date.
entries.laymanExplanation: If an heir receives stock worth $500,000 that the decedent bought for $50,000, the heir's starting basis may be about $500,000, subject to statutory exceptions.
entries.legalExplanation: Under §1014 and qualifying estate valuation rules, basis generally steps up or down to FMV at death (or alternate date elected under §2032), often removing previously unrealized appreciation from future income tax. Some property and income-in-respect-of-decedent categories have exceptions.
entries.details: Under §1014 and qualifying estate valuation rules, basis generally steps up or down to FMV at death (or alternate date elected under §2032), often removing previously unrealized appreciation from future income tax. Some property and income-in-respect-of-decedent categories have exceptions.
entries.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 4 assigned printed pp. 139–140.
entries.examTrap: A gift during life typically uses §1015 carryover basis; qualifying property at death generally uses §1014 fair-market-value basis.

entries.title: Lock-in effect and buy-borrow-die
entries.summary: Taxpayers may retain appreciated assets until death for §1014 basis treatment, borrowing rather than selling when cash is needed.
entries.laymanExplanation: Selling appreciated stock may trigger gains tax, so wealthy owners can keep it, borrow against it, and pass it on instead.
entries.legalExplanation: The notes discuss incentives created by §1014 and borrowing against appreciated assets. Loans usually do not themselves create income due to a repayment obligation; holding assets until death can avoid realization before the basis adjustment, subject to tax-law exceptions and financing risks.
entries.details: The notes discuss incentives created by §1014 and borrowing against appreciated assets. Loans usually do not themselves create income due to a repayment obligation; holding assets until death can avoid realization before the basis adjustment, subject to tax-law exceptions and financing risks.
entries.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 4 assigned printed pp. 139–141.

entries.title: Policy debate: forgiven appreciation at death
entries.summary: Basis at death encourages holding appreciated assets and can cause distortion despite allowing estate taxation in some circumstances.
entries.laymanExplanation: A person who never sells a very profitable investment may pay less income tax on its increase than someone who sells during life.
entries.legalExplanation: The source describes the §1014 lock-in incentive, valuation questions, potential estate-tax interaction, and the historically attempted but repealed carryover-basis regime of §1023. This is background, not an operative current-law test.
entries.details: The source describes the §1014 lock-in incentive, valuation questions, potential estate-tax interaction, and the historically attempted but repealed carryover-basis regime of §1023. This is background, not an operative current-law test.
entries.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 4 assigned printed pp. 139–141.

entries.title: Taft v. Bowers
entries.summary: The Supreme Court sustained the statutory rule taxing a donee on gain measured from the donor's cost basis, including appreciation predating the gift.
entries.laymanExplanation: A father bought stock for $1,000, gifted it when worth $2,000, and the recipient sold it for $5,000. The recipient's gain was $4,000, not just the last $3,000 of growth.
entries.legalExplanation: Opinion reproduced in assigned Chapter 3 pp135–137.
entries.details: Opinion reproduced in assigned Chapter 3 pp135–137.
entries.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 4 assigned printed pp. 135–137.
entries.facts: A bought 100 shares of stock for $1,000; by the time he gifted them to B they were worth $2,000. B later sold the stock for $5,000. The tax statute applied A's original cost basis to B; B asserted the first $1,000 of appreciation occurred while A owned it and therefore could not be taxed to B.
entries.issue: Can Congress constitutionally tax the donee on the entire gain measured from the donor's basis, including appreciation during the donor's ownership?
entries.holding: Yes. The Court affirmed that the donee owed tax on $4,000 total realized gain after a $5,000 sale using the original $1,000 basis.
entries.reasoning: The property represented one original capital investment by the donor. The appreciation was not taxed at the moment of gift, but became realized on the donee's later sale. Congress could make a succeeding owner assume the predecessor's tax position; the Sixteenth Amendment did not bar the carryover-basis scheme.
entries.rule: A donee who later sells gifted appreciated property can be taxed on the total appreciation measured against the donor's original basis, not merely the period after receipt.
entries.exam: Compute transferred basis and gain under §1015/§1001. Contrast §1014 at death and the special loss-basis limitation for depreciated gifts.
entries.examApplication: Gift FMV $2,000; donor basis $1,000; donee sale $5,000 -> $4,000 gain.
entries.examTrap: The fact that a gift is excluded under §102 does NOT eliminate the pre-gift appreciation when a donee sells.

entries.title: IRC §1041 — spousal and divorce-related property transfers
entries.summary: No gain or loss generally is recognized on property transfers between spouses or former spouses incident to divorce.
entries.laymanExplanation: If one spouse transfers appreciated shares to the other as part of divorce, the person giving them usually doesn't pay gains tax at that moment.
entries.legalExplanation: Section 1041(a) generally provides nonrecognition for transfers between spouses and former spouses incident to divorce. Section 1041(b) treats the recipient as receiving property by gift and taking transferor's adjusted basis. This was Congress's statutory response to United States v. Davis and normally applies regardless of appreciation or depreciation, with statutory exceptions.
entries.details: Section 1041(a) generally provides nonrecognition for transfers between spouses and former spouses incident to divorce. Section 1041(b) treats the recipient as receiving property by gift and taking transferor's adjusted basis. This was Congress's statutory response to United States v. Davis and normally applies regardless of appreciation or depreciation, with statutory exceptions.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Week 4 assigned printed pp. 142–147
entries.elements: Check transferor and transferee are spouses or former spouses; if former spouses, transfer must be incident to divorce; examine exceptions and transferee's carryover basis.
entries.examTrap: §1041 is generally NOT available to unmarried couples ending their relationship; pre-marriage transfers may need other analysis.

entries.title: IRC §1041(b) — transferee carries over basis
entries.summary: A qualifying recipient spouse generally gets the transferor's adjusted basis instead of fair market value.
entries.laymanExplanation: Receiving $500,000 worth of stock with $50,000 basis doesn't automatically give the recipient $500,000 of new basis.
entries.legalExplanation: Nonrecognition means unrecognized built-in gain or loss persists after transfer. Under §1041(b), the recipient is treated as acquiring the property by gift and receives transferor's adjusted basis, even though the property may be awarded in a contested separation.
entries.details: Nonrecognition means unrecognized built-in gain or loss persists after transfer. Under §1041(b), the recipient is treated as acquiring the property by gift and receives transferor's adjusted basis, even though the property may be awarded in a contested separation.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Week 4 assigned printed pp. 146–147
entries.examApplication: Stock FMV $500,000, donor/transferor basis $50,000: no immediate recognition under qualifying §1041; recipient takes $50,000 basis.

entries.title: Release of marital rights as consideration
entries.summary: Historically, a spouse's surrender of marital rights could be treated as value received in exchange for property.
entries.laymanExplanation: Before today's nonrecognition statute, trading appreciated shares for a spouse's release of property claims could trigger tax.
entries.legalExplanation: Davis treated the husband's transfer of appreciated stock in satisfaction of the wife's inchoate rights under Delaware law as a taxable exchange. Where no direct valuation existed, the Court presumed arm's-length exchanged values to equal the FMV of property transferred. §1041 later superseded the recognition rule for covered transfers.
entries.details: Davis treated the husband's transfer of appreciated stock in satisfaction of the wife's inchoate rights under Delaware law as a taxable exchange. Where no direct valuation existed, the Court presumed arm's-length exchanged values to equal the FMV of property transferred. §1041 later superseded the recognition rule for covered transfers.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Week 4 assigned printed pp. 143–146

entries.title: Historical Davis exchange-valuation presumption
entries.summary: Where an arm's-length exchange lacks observable value of the received rights, exchanged values may be presumed equal to the FMV of the property surrendered.
entries.laymanExplanation: If someone swaps valuable stock for rights that can't easily be priced, the court may estimate what was given up by looking at stock's market value.
entries.legalExplanation: Davis, decided before §1041, measured the husband's realized gain on stock exchanged for wife's marital-right release by using the market value of the transferred stock as the estimated value of rights received. This is historical case analysis, not today's general spousal-transfer recognition rule.
entries.details: Davis, decided before §1041, measured the husband's realized gain on stock exchanged for wife's marital-right release by using the market value of the transferred stock as the estimated value of rights received. This is historical case analysis, not today's general spousal-transfer recognition rule.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Week 4 assigned printed pp. 145–146

legalWarning.label: HISTORICAL DAVIS FRAMEWORK
legalWarning.reason: IRC §1041 now governs qualifying spousal or divorce-related property transfers without gain or loss recognition, subject to statute.

entries.title: Antenuptial (prenuptial) property settlement
entries.summary: An agreement negotiated before marriage allocating property or rights in anticipation of the marriage.
entries.laymanExplanation: If someone transfers stock to a future spouse in exchange for waiving future claims, the transfer may not be treated like a gift.
entries.legalExplanation: The source discusses Farid-Es-Sultaneh's consideration for a stock transfer through surrender of prospective marital rights. Pre-marriage parties may be outside §1041's spouse-to-spouse regime; characterize property received as a genuine gift, exchange, or other transfer based on legal and factual context.
entries.details: The source discusses Farid-Es-Sultaneh's consideration for a stock transfer through surrender of prospective marital rights. Pre-marriage parties may be outside §1041's spouse-to-spouse regime; characterize property received as a genuine gift, exchange, or other transfer based on legal and factual context.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Week 4 assigned printed pp. 147–150

entries.title: Gift-tax classification is not the same as income-tax classification
entries.summary: The meaning of gift for income-tax basis and exclusion can differ from special gift/estate-tax statutory definitions.
entries.laymanExplanation: A transfer can raise a gift-tax question for one person but still be treated as an exchange for income-tax basis purposes.
entries.legalExplanation: Farid-Es-Sultaneh rejects automatically importing the gift-tax rule about full consideration in money or money's worth into the income-tax analysis of a prenuptial transfer. Compare §§1012 and 1015 and the actual rights released.
entries.details: Farid-Es-Sultaneh rejects automatically importing the gift-tax rule about full consideration in money or money's worth into the income-tax analysis of a prenuptial transfer. Compare §§1012 and 1015 and the actual rights released.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Week 4 assigned printed pp. 148–150

entries.title: Unmarried couples and §1041
entries.summary: The spousal nonrecognition rule does not generally extend to formerly cohabiting unmarried partners.
entries.laymanExplanation: A ten-year unmarried couple who splits up doesn't automatically get the same tax treatment as a divorcing married couple.
entries.legalExplanation: The reading raises the policy question whether comparable relief should be available to unmarried couples. Under the statutory text as described, §1041 focuses on transfers between spouses or former spouses incident to divorce.
entries.details: The reading raises the policy question whether comparable relief should be available to unmarried couples. Under the statutory text as described, §1041 focuses on transfers between spouses or former spouses incident to divorce.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Week 4 assigned printed pp. 147

entries.title: Why Congress enacted §1041 after Davis
entries.summary: Prior law made divorce settlements difficult to value and taxed couples differently depending on state marital-property rules.
entries.laymanExplanation: Old tax law could treat dividing property in a divorce like a sale. Congress adopted a clearer rule to avoid that mess.
entries.legalExplanation: Davis created disputes over whether marital rights were ownership or obligations and their market value. Modern §1041 offers nonrecognition and transferred basis for qualifying transfers; historical case opinions remain important for understanding the policy shift.
entries.details: Davis created disputes over whether marital rights were ownership or obligations and their market value. Modern §1041 offers nonrecognition and transferred basis for qualifying transfers; historical case opinions remain important for understanding the policy shift.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Week 4 assigned printed pp. 141–147

entries.title: United States v. Davis
entries.summary: Under pre-§1041 law, the Supreme Court treated a husband's stock transfer to his former wife for release of marital rights as a taxable exchange, with gain measured using FMV.
entries.laymanExplanation: A husband gave appreciated DuPont stock to settle divorce rights. The Supreme Court treated it like a sale that could create taxable profit—but Congress later changed the rule.
entries.legalExplanation: The opinion is reproduced in the assigned pages; its taxable-exchange result is historically superseded for qualifying transfers by §1041.
entries.details: The opinion is reproduced in the assigned pages; its taxable-exchange result is historically superseded for qualifying transfers by §1041.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Week 4 assigned printed pp. 142–146
entries.facts: Thomas Crawley Davis conveyed 1,000 shares of appreciated DuPont stock under a Delaware separation agreement to settle his wife's marital rights. Under state law, the wife had inchoate rights and possible future marital claims but did not hold an ownership interest identical to community property.
entries.issue: Did the husband's stock transfer in settlement of marital rights realize taxable gain, and could the released rights be valued?
entries.holding: The Supreme Court held the transfer was a taxable exchange under the law then in force; the value of marital rights received was reasonably measured by the FMV of stock transferred, and the husband's gain was taxable.
entries.reasoning: Delaware law gave the wife burdens and claims against the husband's property, not the kind of co-ownership making it a mere division of existing property. The court assumed arm's-length equal values in settlement, enabling the amount realized under §1001 to be measured by stock FMV. It sought consistency in taxing growth in appreciated assets when exchanged for valuable rights.
entries.rule: Historical holding: exchange of appreciated property for release of marital rights could cause realization and recognition of gain, measured by FMV of property transferred; §1041 later governs qualifying transactions instead.
entries.exam: First use current §1041 for qualifying spouse/former-spouse incident-to-divorce transfers. If analyzing Davis, identify it as pre-§1041 historical doctrine and explain why the statute replaced the result.
entries.examApplication: Husband transfers $100,000-FMV stock with $40,000 basis in divorce settlement. Under historical Davis exchange, $60,000 realized gain; if §1041 applies, no current gain recognized and spouse carries $40,000 basis.
entries.examTrap: Do not use Davis's historical taxable-exchange holding as controlling for current qualifying §1041 divorce transfers.

legalWarning.label: OVERRIDDEN BY IRC §1041
legalWarning.reason: Congress enacted §1041, generally providing nonrecognition on qualifying transfers between spouses or incident to divorce. The assigned Davis opinion explains the prior rule.

entries.title: Farid-Es-Sultaneh v. Commissioner
entries.summary: The court held an antenuptial stock transfer for release of substantial marital rights was a purchase for income-tax basis, not automatically a gift governed by donor carryover basis.
entries.laymanExplanation: Before a marriage, a wealthy man gave stock in return for his future wife's agreement to give up valuable marital claims. The court treated her as having paid with rights rather than getting a free gift.
entries.legalExplanation: The reproduced assigned opinion distinguishes §1012 cost basis from §1015 gift basis and gift-tax definitions.
entries.details: The reproduced assigned opinion distinguishes §1012 cost basis from §1015 gift basis and gift-tax definitions.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Week 4 assigned printed pp. 147–150
entries.facts: In 1924, S.S. Kresge transferred to his future spouse Farid-Es-Sultaneh shares worth about $800,000 as part of an antenuptial arrangement; she agreed to marry and relinquish support, dower and other valuable marital rights. His basis was about 15 cents per share, FMV near $10 per share at transfer; she later sold part at $19 per share. IRS treated the shares as gifts with donor basis; the Tax Court agreed.
entries.issue: Was the stock received as a §1015 gift using Kresge's low basis, or acquired for fair consideration under an antenuptial agreement and therefore cost basis?
entries.holding: The Second Circuit reversed: the transfer was supported by valuable consideration consisting of marital rights released, making her a purchaser rather than donee for income-tax basis purposes.
entries.reasoning: Income-tax classification does not automatically import estate/gift tax's specialized restrictions on marital-right consideration. The antenuptial contract represented real exchange for valuable rights, and the Court found that the shares were not a completed unconditional gift before the agreement.
entries.rule: For income-tax purposes, a stock transfer in exchange for adequate consideration is not necessarily a §1015 gift merely because gift-tax statutes or the parties' documents call it a gift; historical application required a cost-basis analysis.
entries.exam: Distinguish §1012 cost basis and §1015 carryover basis, classify transfer timing, determine whether §1041 covers the facts and separate income-tax from gift-tax standards.
entries.examApplication: A prospective spouse gives stock in exchange for releasing enforceable marital rights before marriage. Evaluate exchange/consideration and whether current §1041 actually applies.
entries.examTrap: Do not assume all prenups are gifts or automatically protected by §1041 before the parties are married.

legalWarning.label: HISTORICAL PRENUP DECISION
legalWarning.reason: The case predates §1041 and modern divorce-transfer rules. Analyze contemporary spouse status, statutory scope and basis rules before applying it.

entries.title: Post-2018 alimony generally is neither deductible nor included
entries.summary: Under divorce or separation agreements executed after 2018, qualifying alimony payments generally are not deducted by the payor or included by the recipient.
entries.laymanExplanation: After a 2019 divorce, a person paying support generally cannot reduce income tax because of that alimony, and the former spouse receiving it generally doesn't report it as taxable income.
entries.legalExplanation: The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act repealed the former alimony deduction/inclusion system for divorce/separation instruments executed after December 31, 2018. Certain qualifying modifications to pre-2019 instruments also may adopt the new treatment. Statutory year and instrument date are essential; the book's general statement must not be overextended to every old decree.

Certain qualifying modifications to pre-2019 instruments also may adopt the new treatment. Statutory year and instrument date are essential; the book's general statement must not be overextended to every old decree.

entries.examTrap: Do not apply post-2018 alimony treatment automatically to an unmodified pre-2019 divorce instrument.

entries.title: Historic pre-2019 alimony system
entries.summary: Under the prior regime, qualifying alimony generally was deducted by the payor and included by the recipient.
entries.laymanExplanation: The old law used to shift tax liability from the person paying alimony to the person receiving it; a 2017 change generally ended that for newer agreements.
entries.legalExplanation: The casebook contrasts the former §71/§215 arrangement with post-2018 treatment. The effective-date rule depends on when the divorce/separation instrument was executed and whether a later modification expressly invokes the new law.

entries.title: Child-support payments are not deductible or taxable to recipient
entries.summary: Ordinary child support is not deductible by the payor and is not included as income by the recipient.
entries.laymanExplanation: If a parent pays $10,000 in child support, it generally isn't a tax deduction for the parent or taxable income for the other parent.
entries.legalExplanation: The source draws a consistent distinction between child support and pre-2019 alimony. Child support is generally a personal obligation; nonpayment does not automatically create a deductible tax loss for the custodial parent.
entries.details: The source draws a consistent distinction between child support and pre-2019 alimony. Child support is generally a personal obligation; nonpayment does not automatically create a deductible tax loss for the custodial parent.

entries.title: IRC §166(d) — nonbusiness bad-debt deduction requires tax basis
entries.summary: Nonbusiness bad debts may be deductible as short-term capital losses only when wholly worthless and when the taxpayer has basis in the debt.
entries.laymanExplanation: Someone not paying you a promised amount doesn't always mean you can deduct that amount from taxes. You first need a tax investment or other basis in the debt.
entries.legalExplanation: The assigned Diez-Arguelles excerpt applies §166(b),(d): a taxpayer cannot deduct the uncollected child-support obligation when the taxpayer has no basis in that receivable. Expenditures for supporting one's own children do not automatically create a basis in a former spouse's support obligation.
entries.details: The assigned Diez-Arguelles excerpt applies §166(b),(d): a taxpayer cannot deduct the uncollected child-support obligation when the taxpayer has no basis in that receivable. Expenditures for supporting one's own children do not automatically create a basis in a former spouse's support obligation.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 4 assigned pp. 151–153
entries.examTrap: A legally enforceable support claim is not automatically a deductible 'bad debt' without basis.

entries.title: Basis in a receivable / unpaid obligation
entries.summary: To deduct a debt as worthless, the taxpayer ordinarily must have invested tax basis in the debt rather than a mere unpaid expectation.
entries.laymanExplanation: If you were promised $5,000 but never actually paid tax on or invested $5,000 in the receivable, you might have zero deductible basis.
entries.legalExplanation: Section 166(b) measures deduction by adjusted basis. A support arrearage can be legally collectible but still carry no tax basis to the obligee. The source compares paid money, actual lending and merely unrealized expected support.

entries.title: Unpaid child support and equitable-tax concerns
entries.summary: The court acknowledged economic hardship but declined to create a deduction without statutory authorization.
entries.laymanExplanation: Not getting promised child-support money makes life harder, but a judge cannot invent a tax write-off just because the outcome feels unfair.
entries.legalExplanation: The source discusses Perry as an additional supporting case and asks whether a tax deduction would target needy parents effectively. Perry is cited, not reproduced as an assigned opinion in this upload.

entries.title: Diez-Arguelles v. Commissioner
entries.summary: The Tax Court rejected a bad-debt deduction for unpaid child support because the parent had no tax basis in the unpaid obligation.
entries.laymanExplanation: A parent never received the child support her ex-husband legally owed. The court said that missing money was not a deductible bad debt because she had no tax basis in it.
entries.legalExplanation: Opinion excerpt reproduced in assigned Chapter 3 pp151–152.
entries.details: Opinion excerpt reproduced in assigned Chapter 3 pp151–152.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 4 assigned pp. 151–152
entries.facts: Christina Diez-Arguelles divorced Kevin Baxter and was owed $300 monthly child support. He failed to make payments, leaving $4,325 arrears through 1978 and another $3,000 in 1979. Christina and her husband supported the children themselves and claimed the unpaid sums as bad-debt losses, despite repeated unsuccessful collection attempts and court orders.
entries.issue: Could the custodial parent deduct unpaid child-support arrears as nonbusiness bad debts under §166(d) despite having no tax basis in the expected support payments?
entries.holding: No. The Tax Court rejected the deductions because the taxpayer had no basis in the overdue child-support obligations.
entries.reasoning: A nonbusiness bad-debt deduction under §166(d) also requires adjusted basis under §166(b). The taxpayer did not loan money to Baxter or include the promised child-support amounts in taxable income and could not create basis merely by paying the children's ongoing household expenses. A state court judgment did not by itself establish a federal tax basis.
entries.rule: Nonbusiness bad-debt loss deductions require actual adjusted basis in the debt; unreceived child-support obligations cannot be deducted merely because they are legally owed and uncollectible.
entries.exam: Identify a debt, whether it became wholly worthless, and importantly whether the claimant has adjusted basis. Distinguish a loaned and later defaulted amount from unreceived personal-support payments.
entries.examApplication: Parent is owed $7,325 in past-due child support and has no basis in the claim: §166(d) generally provides no deduction for the unpaid amount.
entries.examTrap: A court order and actual household expenses do not automatically create basis in unpaid child support.

entries.title: Tax deferral — postponing income inclusion
entries.summary: Postponing inclusion or accelerating deductions can reduce the present value of tax, and may change the rate that applies.
entries.laymanExplanation: Paying the same tax next year is usually better than paying it now because you can use today's money meanwhile.
entries.legalExplanation: The chapter distinguishes (1) changing marginal tax rates over time and (2) the time value of money. Deferral of a tax liability is beneficial, but postponing actual cash receipt can cost more than the tax deferral saves.

entries.title: Present value and discounting
entries.summary: The value today of a future payment is its future amount divided by compound growth.
entries.laymanExplanation: A $1 tax bill due next year costs less today than $1 due right now if you can earn interest in the meantime.
entries.legalExplanation: Present value = future sum/(1+r)^n for constant periodic discount rate r and n periods. At 10% annual return, a $1 payment due in one year has present value approximately $0.9091. Calculate economic value separately from statutory tax recognition.

entries.title: December 31 versus January 1 timing
entries.summary: Delaying a taxable cash receipt by one day may defer income tax by an entire annual tax year.
entries.laymanExplanation: Getting paid January 1 instead of December 31 can move the whole tax event to the next return.
entries.legalExplanation: With a calendar-year taxable period and a cash method taxpayer whose income is truly received January 1, the annual accounting boundary produces significant tax-payment deferral. Constructive receipt could prevent artificial delays where money was already unrestrictedly available.

entries.title: Traditional IRA — deduction/deferral and later taxation
entries.summary: Qualifying deductible traditional contributions reduce current taxable income, earnings compound inside the account, and taxable withdrawals generally are included later.
entries.laymanExplanation: You save tax now when contributing, but generally pay tax when you take the money out.
entries.legalExplanation: The book compares a deductible IRA investment with Roth accounts. A $15,000 pretax contribution at 33⅓% tax costs $10,000 after the $5,000 tax saving; account earnings accumulate untaxed, while withdrawals generally bear income tax. Eligibility, deductibility and distribution rules are statutory and must be tested.

entries.title: Roth IRA — after-tax contributions and qualified tax-free distributions
entries.summary: Roth contributions generally are not deductible; qualifying earnings and distributions are tax free.
entries.laymanExplanation: You pay tax before putting the money into a Roth IRA, but generally don't pay again when a withdrawal qualifies.
entries.legalExplanation: In the simplified model, the Roth account starts from after-tax funds, grows without current income tax, and qualified distributions are excluded. Restrictions on eligibility, contribution limits and qualified distributions remain applicable.

entries.title: Traditional–Roth equivalence under equal rates
entries.summary: With equal contribution and retirement tax rates and identical investment returns, the two account structures yield equal after-tax proceeds for equal out-of-pocket cost.
entries.laymanExplanation: A traditional IRA's bigger pretax starting amount can exactly offset the tax you pay when withdrawing; the Roth starts smaller but withdrawals are tax-free.
entries.legalExplanation: If pretax investment is X, total multiplier A and rate t constant, traditional ends XA(1−t); equivalent Roth ends X(1−t)A. Both are equal by commutativity. A higher retirement marginal rate favors Roth; a lower retirement rate favors traditional, all else equal.

entries.title: Annual accounting — each taxable year stands separately
entries.summary: Taxable income is measured for fixed annual taxable periods rather than waiting until each transaction's final lifetime profit is known.
entries.laymanExplanation: A business can lose money overall on a project and still owe tax in one year if it receives taxable payments that year.
entries.legalExplanation: Burnet v. Sanford & Brooks confirms that prior-year business expenses and losses do not automatically erase gross receipts recovered in a later taxable year. Statutory NOL mechanisms and other provisions can provide explicit relief.

entries.title: IRC §172 — net operating loss carryforward
entries.summary: An eligible net operating loss from a business may offset future taxable income, subject to statutory limits.
entries.laymanExplanation: A $1 million business loss may reduce tax on next year's profit, but it doesn't necessarily make the next year tax-free.
entries.legalExplanation: The textbook explains that eligible post-2017 NOL carryforwards ordinarily offset no more than 80% of taxable income determined without the NOL deduction, with indefinite carryforward under its stated rules. Identify source, taxable year and any applicable changes or exceptions; §382 limits certain acquisitions.

entries.title: Capitalization, depreciation and expensing
entries.summary: Costs of longer-lived business assets may be deducted over time through depreciation or immediately when an expensing provision applies.
entries.laymanExplanation: A business machine lasts years, so its cost may be spread across several tax years instead of deducted as soon as purchased.
entries.legalExplanation: The matching principle allocates asset cost against future income; §§167–168 provide the statutory recovery framework. ACRS/MACRS may accelerate depreciation relative to economic loss of value. Expensing or bonus depreciation can allow immediate deduction where eligibility rules apply.

entries.title: Matching principle in depreciation
entries.summary: Capital cost should generally be matched against the periods in which an asset produces revenues for the business.
entries.laymanExplanation: A $10,000 machine earning $2,100 each year for five years doesn't truly create a giant first-year operating loss just because it was purchased then.
entries.legalExplanation: Textbook's Acme machine cost $10,000, lasts 5 years with zero salvage and generates $2,100/year. Hypothetical straight-line $2,000 annual depreciation leaves $100/year before other costs; immediate expensing would make year one look artificially poor despite future expected benefits.

entries.summary: The casebook describes a scheduled bonus-depreciation phaseout; later law restored 100% first-year bonus depreciation for qualifying property acquired after January 19, 2025.
entries.laymanExplanation: Some qualifying business assets may now be fully deducted in their first year. The book's old phaseout schedule is outdated.

This annotation is independently verified, not from the textbook.

entries.title: Claim-of-right doctrine — receipt without restriction
entries.summary: An amount received under a claim of right without restrictions on disposition generally is included even if later repayment might be required.
entries.laymanExplanation: If you can keep and use money as your own today, it may be taxable now even if someone later sues you for it.
entries.legalExplanation: The assigned excerpt quotes North American Oil's formulation. Profits controlled by a court-appointed receiver in 1916 were not taxpayer income until paid over following a 1917 judgment; an unrestricted receipt under an asserted right can be included notwithstanding later legal dispute. North American Oil is cited and excerpted in textbook prose, not a standalone reproduced judicial opinion.

entries.title: Custodial funds versus claim-of-right receipts
entries.summary: Money held under an unequivocal obligation to return it is different from income held as one's own.
entries.laymanExplanation: Holding money that you must give back is not the same as being paid for your own work.
entries.legalExplanation: The chapter describes Illinois Power, where statutory/regulatory obligations deprived the utility of beneficial entitlement to rate-increase revenue. A mere deposit into a general account was not dispositive; legal and beneficial rights controlled. This is a cited case, not reproduced judicial opinion.

entries.title: Burnet v. Sanford & Brooks Co.
entries.summary: No. The Supreme Court held the business recovery and interest taxable as gross income in 1920 under the annual accounting regime.
entries.laymanExplanation: A dredging company lost money over several years, then won repayment from the government. The Court said the repayment counts in the year received, not by adding every year of the project together.
entries.details: This judicial opinion is reproduced in the assigned textbook excerpt.
entries.facts: A dredging contractor incurred expenses exceeding payments during a dredging project performed 1913–1915, then sued for breach of contract. In 1920 it recovered $192,577.59 including $176,271.88 compensating previously deducted operating expenses and $16,305.71 interest. It sought to exclude the expense reimbursement because the entire contract ultimately generated no net profit.
entries.issue: May the taxpayer exclude recovery of previously expensed business costs in 1920 because the underlying multiyear contract produced no overall profit?
entries.holding: No. The Supreme Court held the business recovery and interest taxable as gross income in 1920 under the annual accounting regime.
entries.reasoning: Annual returns determine income for fixed periods. Operating expenses deducted in earlier years were not capital invested in property. Congress could tax later-year recoveries notwithstanding prior losses and the transaction's ultimate poor outcome; a lifetime transaction-wide system was not constitutionally required.
entries.rule: Taxable income is generally computed by taxable year; a later recovery of earlier business costs can be gross income even where the entire transaction is unprofitable.
entries.exam: Compare Clark's restoration of capital with Sanford & Brooks's reimbursement of deductible business expenses. Discuss §172 NOL relief separately.
entries.examApplication: Compare Clark's restoration of capital with Sanford & Brooks's reimbursement of deductible business expenses. Discuss §172 NOL relief separately.
entries.examTrap: Do not offset a later year's receipt with prior-year losses automatically, and do not treat an earlier business deduction as unrecovered capital.
entries.source: Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 4 reproduced judicial opinion, assigned printed pp. 159–161

entries.title: Cash method versus accrual method
entries.summary: Cash generally records receipts and paid costs; accrual generally recognizes earned income and fixed liabilities despite later payment.
entries.laymanExplanation: A cash-method worker paid in January usually reports January income; an accrual business may report it when earned in December.
entries.legalExplanation: For federal tax, cash-method income ordinarily enters when received or constructively received and allowable deductions often on payment; accrual method hinges on right to income, fixed liabilities, all-events and economic-performance requirements. Specific provisions can override general timing.

entries.title: IRC §446 — regular accounting method and clear reflection of income
entries.summary: A taxpayer's regular accounting method generally governs, but the IRS may challenge one that does not clearly reflect income.
entries.laymanExplanation: You can't freely invent a bookkeeping method just to move tax bills around.
entries.legalExplanation: Under §446(a), tax accounting ordinarily tracks the regular method used in books. Section 446(b) permits the IRS to require another method when the chosen method does not clearly reflect income. Tax accounting and GAAP may diverge.

entries.summary: Certain entities must use accrual accounting once statutory conditions and inflation-indexed gross-receipts tests apply.
entries.laymanExplanation: Big corporations may not be allowed to wait until customers pay to count earnings.

entries.title: All-events test for accrued liabilities
entries.summary: An accrual-method liability generally cannot be deducted until all events fix liability and its amount is reasonably determinable.
entries.laymanExplanation: Even if you expect to pay workers or a customer later, you can't necessarily deduct an estimated bill now.
entries.legalExplanation: The reading states the liability must be fixed and determinate, and notes General Dynamics' reimbursement claims were not fixed until employees filed them. §461(h)'s economic-performance requirement supplies an additional limit; the General Dynamics opinion is discussed, not reproduced as an assigned case brief.

entries.title: IRC §461(h) — economic performance
entries.summary: A fixed obligation may still be nondeductible until the related service or property is actually provided.
entries.laymanExplanation: You can't usually deduct next year's office rent this year merely because you signed a binding contract.
entries.legalExplanation: §461(h) imposes an economic performance requirement for accrual deductions, generally as services or property are furnished, with statutory/regulatory exceptions. Distinguish this from the separate all-events test.

entries.title: IRC §451(b) — tax income recognition and financial statements
entries.summary: For certain accrual taxpayers, income cannot be recognized later for tax than it is recognized in applicable financial statements, subject to exceptions.
entries.laymanExplanation: If an accrual business reports money as earned to its investors, tax law often won't let it push that income to a later year.
entries.legalExplanation: Section 451(b) coordinates certain income items with applicable financial-reporting recognition. The reading emphasizes that GAAP and taxable income remain distinct, but one limit prohibits tax deferral beyond specified book recognition timing.

entries.title: Accrued receivable and right to payment
entries.summary: Under accrual accounting, the fixed right to earn payment usually determines inclusion, not when cash arrives.
entries.laymanExplanation: If a business has already earned its fee, it may owe income tax on that fee even while waiting for a check.
entries.legalExplanation: Georgia School-Book Depository's 8% commissions accrued when brokerage duties were substantially complete. Delay in paying by the state without genuine legal contingency or insolvency was insufficient to avoid accrual.

entries.title: Contingent right versus doubtful collection
entries.summary: A genuine unresolved condition to earning a receivable differs from mere delay in collecting an earned amount.
entries.laymanExplanation: If you haven't earned the fee yet, you may wait. If you've earned it but the customer is slow, waiting for cash may not delay tax.
entries.legalExplanation: The Georgia School-Book opinion allows narrow exceptions for bona fide contingent rights or proven inability to collect (including debtor insolvency), not general discretion to delay whenever the account is unpaid.
entries.details: The Georgia School-Book opinion allows narrow exceptions for bona fide contingent rights or proven inability to collect (including debtor insolvency), not general discretion to delay whenever the account is unpaid.

entries.title: Prepaid income — general immediate inclusion and statutory deferral
entries.summary: Advance payments often enter taxable income upon receipt even when services will be performed later; qualifying exceptions can defer part.
entries.laymanExplanation: Getting the year's membership dues today may mean tax today, even though you'll provide services next year.
entries.legalExplanation: American Automobile Association upheld IRS rejection of 12-month proration for prepaid on-demand member dues despite acceptable GAAP. Later §§451(c), 455, 456 provide limited statutory deferrals, potentially changing outcome for qualifying payments; do not state AAA means all prepaid income must always be included immediately.
entries.details: American Automobile Association upheld IRS rejection of 12-month proration for prepaid on-demand member dues despite acceptable GAAP. Later §§451(c), 455, 456 provide limited statutory deferrals, potentially changing outcome for qualifying payments; do not state AAA means all prepaid income must always be included immediately.

entries.title: IRC §451(c) — limited advance-payment deferral
entries.summary: Eligible accrual taxpayers may elect to defer qualifying advance payments in accord with statutory limits, generally no later than the next taxable year.
entries.laymanExplanation: A company prepaid for three years of classes might get to postpone some tax, but not spread it across all three years.
entries.legalExplanation: The reading's example under §451(c): $6,000 for 100 dance lessons, 20 delivered in 2024, 40 in 2025, 40 in 2026. Assuming applicable financial-reporting consistency, $1,200 enters 2024 and remaining $4,800 enters 2025, not 2026. Distinguish prepayment allocation from actual service-delivery schedule.

entries.title: IRC §456 — membership organization advance dues
entries.summary: Eligible qualifying membership organizations may elect statutory spreading of prepaid dues for the service period.
entries.laymanExplanation: Congress later created an exception that can let certain member clubs recognize dues over the membership period.
entries.legalExplanation: The notes describe §456 enacted after AAA; it can alter the historical case's result for organizations meeting specific membership and election criteria. §455 separately deals with eligible prepaid periodical subscriptions.

entries.title: Georgia School-Book Depository v. Commissioner
entries.summary: The Tax Court required commissions earned from state-book transactions to be included when the right to payment accrued, despite delay in collection.
entries.laymanExplanation: A textbook broker earned commissions but waited for Georgia to pay. The court said the commissions were already earned, even though cash had not arrived.
entries.details: This judicial opinion is reproduced in the assigned textbook excerpt.
entries.facts: An accrual-basis broker earned 8% commissions arranging, warehousing and distributing schoolbooks for Georgia schools. The state textbook fund, fed by beer excise tax, was short and paid later. The broker reported commissions on state books only when the state settled, though it accrued other book commissions sooner.
entries.issue: Did the commissions accrue when brokerage work was performed or only when the state later paid?
entries.holding: The Tax Court required commissions earned from state-book transactions to be included when the right to payment accrued, despite delay in collection.
entries.reasoning: Substantially all services were completed and entitlement fixed. Delay or lack of current funds did not demonstrate an unresolved condition or reasonable certainty of permanent nonpayment; the state's resources and improving collections supported expected ultimate payment. Broad exceptions would let taxpayers arbitrarily shift years.
entries.rule: Under the accrual method, a fixed, earned right to be paid generally creates income even when payment is delayed. Genuine contingency or proven uncollectibility may justify exception.
entries.exam: Separate whether work has earned the fee (right fixed) from whether the payor is merely late. Compare Hallmark's retention of title (cited in note, not independently reproduced).
entries.examApplication: Separate whether work has earned the fee (right fixed) from whether the payor is merely late. Compare Hallmark's retention of title (cited in note, not independently reproduced).
entries.examTrap: Cash receipt, payment due date and ultimate earned right are not necessarily the same thing.
entries.source: Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 5 reproduced judicial opinion, assigned printed pp. 168–171

entries.title: American Automobile Association v. United States
entries.summary: No. The Court affirmed rejection of the proration and required advance dues to be included in the year received under the applicable law and facts.
entries.laymanExplanation: An auto club took a year's membership fee upfront and wanted to spread income across the months. The Supreme Court let the IRS require it all to be counted when received.
entries.details: This judicial opinion is reproduced in the assigned textbook excerpt.
entries.facts: AAA, an accrual-basis auto club, received prepaid annual dues for road services provided on demand. It recognized dues ratably across the membership term under GAAP and reserved portions for next year. IRS under §446(b) required inclusion of dues in the year received, denying deferral for expected future service costs.
entries.issue: Did AAA's GAAP-consistent ratable method clearly reflect taxable income so IRS was bound to accept it?
entries.holding: No. The Court affirmed rejection of the proration and required advance dues to be included in the year received under the applicable law and facts.
entries.reasoning: Member services were contingent on future demand rather than scheduled specific obligations, and average service estimates did not fix the actual earning of each payment. Legislative context included repeal of permissive deferred-revenue provisions and limited subscriber provisions. Justice Stewart dissented, defending matching and reliable aggregate accounting.
entries.rule: Under the law then applicable, the IRS could reject AAA's deferred reporting of on-demand prepaid dues even when the taxpayer's financial books reasonably spread them over the service period.
entries.exam: Apply current §§451(c) and 456 (if conditions met) before concluding an advance payment must all be included upon receipt.
entries.examApplication: Apply current §§451(c) and 456 (if conditions met) before concluding an advance payment must all be included upon receipt.
entries.examTrap: AAA's historic result was modified for qualifying membership organizations by §456 and other eligible advances by §451(c).
entries.source: Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 5 reproduced judicial opinion, assigned printed pp. 172–176

legalWarning.label: STATUTORY DEFERRAL AVAILABLE
legalWarning.reason: Later IRC §§456 and 451(c) provide limited elective deferral in specified circumstances; the blanket historical AAA result does not control all advances today.

entries.title: Realization versus recognition
entries.summary: Realization usually requires a defined event such as sale or exchange; recognition means including the realized gain in taxable income now.
entries.laymanExplanation: Your stock rising in price is usually untaxed until you sell or exchange it. A special law can delay tax even after that sale or exchange.
entries.legalExplanation: Under §1001 and judicial interpretation, annual price changes alone normally are not taxed. Realization via a disposition precedes a separate question whether nonrecognition statutes apply. The reading presents the doctrine's valuation, liquidity and volatility justifications.

entries.title: Unrealized appreciation and holding gains
entries.summary: An asset may rise in value without triggering a current tax-recognition event.
entries.laymanExplanation: If your property price goes from $100,000 to $150,000, you have a $50,000 paper gain but usually haven't yet generated income tax by holding it.
entries.legalExplanation: Haig–Simons economic income includes changes in net wealth, while the statutory federal income tax generally waits for disposition unless special rules apply. The book raises both fairness and practical administration arguments.

entries.title: Pro rata stock dividend versus cash dividend
entries.summary: A proportional distribution of additional shares may leave a shareholder's fractional ownership and wealth unchanged; cash dividends ordinarily do not.
entries.laymanExplanation: If everyone gets 20% more shares, the pizza isn't bigger—you each have more slices representing the same share.
entries.legalExplanation: Eisner v. Macomber treated the substantially proportionate stock distribution on its facts as no realized gain from capital. The current statutory approach to stock dividends is in §305, with exceptions; Macomber's sweeping income definition was later narrowed in Glenshaw Glass.

legalWarning.label: OLD INCOME TEST LIMITED
legalWarning.reason: Glenshaw Glass rejected Macomber's 'derived from capital or labor' phrase as an exhaustive gross income definition. §§305–307 now govern important stock-dividend tax effects.

entries.title: Stock split and basis allocation
entries.summary: A stock split changes share count and per-share basis but generally not total ownership value.
entries.laymanExplanation: Ten shares becoming twenty doesn't mean your investment doubled; the same original tax basis is spread over more shares.
entries.legalExplanation: The excerpt analyzes why a pro rata stock dividend ordinarily does not generate a real accession to shareholder wealth. Section 305 and related basis provisions govern particular distributions; dividends with alternative forms or changed rights may need separate treatment.

entries.title: Realization doctrine: policy and constitutional development
entries.summary: The historical debate contrasts constitutional realization demands with administrative and economic reasons to wait for sales.
entries.laymanExplanation: Some argue taxing paper gains every year would be hard because prices can change and owners may lack cash. Others say investors can already spend wealth by borrowing.
entries.legalExplanation: The book discusses Eisner v. Macomber and later stock dividend cases, along with the problem of unequal tax rates for wages versus unrealized investment growth. These are secondary doctrinal foundations.
entries.details: The book discusses Eisner v. Macomber and later stock dividend cases, along with the problem of unequal tax rates for wages versus unrealized investment growth. These are secondary doctrinal foundations.

entries.title: Eisner v. Macomber
entries.summary: No. The Supreme Court held that the pro rata distribution did not constitute realized shareholder income on those facts and could not be taxed as income in that manner.
entries.laymanExplanation: The company gave every shareholder more shares in proportion to what they already held. Nobody got a bigger piece of the company, so the Court said this stock dividend wasn't income.
entries.details: This judicial opinion is reproduced in the assigned textbook excerpt.
entries.facts: Macomber held common stock in Standard Oil of California. The corporation issued a pro rata common-stock dividend from accumulated profits, increasing her number of shares but leaving her fractional ownership basically unchanged. The government sought income tax based on a portion of the new shares' par value.
entries.issue: Did a pro rata stock dividend constitute 'income' taxable without apportionment under the Sixteenth Amendment?
entries.holding: No. The Supreme Court held that the pro rata distribution did not constitute realized shareholder income on those facts and could not be taxed as income in that manner.
entries.reasoning: The shareholder had not received assets severed from corporate capital and her proportional ownership remained the same. The Court emphasized realization and distinguished capital from income; dissenting opinions challenged the narrow constitutional conclusion. Subsequent law and §§305–307 address stock dividends, while Glenshaw Glass rejected Macomber's narrow phrase as a complete definition of income.
entries.rule: On its facts, a pure pro rata stock dividend leaving shareholder's substantive ownership unchanged was not a realization of income; later statutory and judicial law constrain broad readings of the opinion.
entries.exam: Check whether the distribution changes shareholders' proportions, gives an election of cash, or qualifies under §305 and exceptions; do not rely on the old capital/labor formulation.
entries.examApplication: Check whether the distribution changes shareholders' proportions, gives an election of cash, or qualifies under §305 and exceptions; do not rely on the old capital/labor formulation.
entries.examTrap: Do not cite Macomber as a universal constitutional prohibition on taxing every unrealized gain. Glenshaw Glass displaced its narrow definition and later cases address realization.
entries.source: Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 5 reproduced judicial opinion, assigned printed pp. 179–186

legalWarning.label: NARROW HISTORICAL HOLDING
legalWarning.reason: Glenshaw Glass treats Macomber's income definition as case-specific; §§305–307 govern stock dividends. Constitutional realization questions are not settled by broad dicta.

entries.title: IRC §§109 and 1019 — leased-property improvements
entries.summary: Certain improvements made by a lessee are excluded from lessor's gross income on termination of lease, without increase in lessor basis.
entries.laymanExplanation: If your tenant improves your building, you may avoid tax when the tenant leaves—but you generally don't get new tax basis in improvements for free.
entries.legalExplanation: The casebook's assigned p196 notes describe §109 exclusion for qualifying improvements not representing rent, paired with §1019's disallowance of basis increase. This can postpone tax rather than permanently eliminate the economic gain. The substantive Bruun opinion on unassigned pp192–195 is not the source of a case brief.
entries.details: The casebook's assigned p196 notes describe §109 exclusion for qualifying improvements not representing rent, paired with §1019's disallowance of basis increase. This can postpone tax rather than permanently eliminate the economic gain. The substantive Bruun opinion on unassigned pp192–195 is not the source of a case brief.

entries.examTrap: The fact improvements are excluded under §109 does not grant the landlord new basis under §1019; §109 does not exclude improvements that are rent.

entries.title: Nonrecourse versus recourse debt
entries.summary: Recourse debt permits personal liability; nonrecourse debt generally looks only to pledged property for repayment.
entries.laymanExplanation: If a loan is nonrecourse, the lender normally can take the collateral but cannot personally pursue the borrower's other assets.
entries.legalExplanation: Woodsam analyzes converting mortgage debt into a nonrecourse obligation and argues about gain when the debt exceeds the property's cost basis. The court holds executing the mortgage is not itself a sale or exchange under the applicable Code.
entries.details: Woodsam analyzes converting mortgage debt into a nonrecourse obligation and argues about gain when the debt exceeds the property's cost basis. The court holds executing the mortgage is not itself a sale or exchange under the applicable Code.

entries.title: Borrowing against appreciated property generally is not realization
entries.summary: Borrowing secured by appreciated property, even nonrecourse debt above basis, ordinarily does not constitute a sale or taxable gain by itself.
entries.laymanExplanation: You can borrow against a house that has increased in value without actually selling the house. The loan money generally isn't sale profit.
entries.legalExplanation: Woodsam held that a mortgage refinancing resulting in nonrecourse obligation did not dispose of the property. Subsequent foreclosure can create a realization event and different amount-realized calculations. A genuine debt has an offsetting repayment obligation; distinguish debt discharge.

Subsequent foreclosure can create a realization event and different amount-realized calculations. A genuine debt has an offsetting repayment obligation; distinguish debt discharge.

entries.title: IRC §1001 — realized gain on sale or other disposition
entries.summary: A sale or exchange of materially different property rights normally produces realized gain or loss before testing recognition exceptions.
entries.laymanExplanation: Selling or exchanging something can 'wake up' the tax system even where you haven't gained any extra cash in the transaction.
entries.legalExplanation: Under §1001, realized gain = amount realized less adjusted basis. Cottage Savings treats exchange of legally distinct mortgage interests as disposition even with broadly similar market economics; a separate §165 or other rule determines deductible losses.
entries.details: Under §1001, realized gain = amount realized less adjusted basis. Cottage Savings treats exchange of legally distinct mortgage interests as disposition even with broadly similar market economics; a separate §165 or other rule determines deductible losses.

entries.title: Material difference in legal entitlements
entries.summary: An exchange is a realization event when the exchanged property embodies legally distinct entitlements under the §1001 test.
entries.laymanExplanation: Two mortgage bundles may be equally valuable but still be different property because they are claims against different borrowers and houses.
entries.legalExplanation: Cottage Savings rejects requiring a large change in market value. Distinct obligors and collateral create materially different legal rights; regulatory-book treatment for thrifts does not determine federal realization.

entries.title: IRC §165 — realizing and deducting a property loss
entries.summary: A genuine loss sustained in a sale or exchange may be deductible when Code conditions and limitations are met.
entries.laymanExplanation: If a lender swaps underwater mortgages for other mortgages and legally gives up the old ones, it might recognize a tax loss.
entries.legalExplanation: Cottage Savings held the mortgage-interest exchange generated realized losses and resolved the §165 issue in favor of deductibility. Distinguish economic losses from realized losses, the deduction timing and potential limitations.

entries.title: Economic similarity versus legal distinctness
entries.summary: For realization, tax law can distinguish assets even where risk and expected return are very similar.
entries.laymanExplanation: Swapping a $100,000 mortgage claim for another $100,000 claim can be a taxable event because the borrower and legal obligations differ.
entries.legalExplanation: Cottage Savings compares FHLBB Memorandum R-49 exchanges designed to be 'substantially identical' for regulator reporting but legally distinct mortgage interests for income-tax realization. This can create realized loss without equivalent GAAP loss recognition.

entries.title: Constitutional realization questions after Macomber
entries.summary: The assigned notes discuss realization as a prominent statutory doctrine and an unsettled broad constitutional debate.
entries.laymanExplanation: The law normally waits until a sale to tax paper gains, but that doesn't necessarily mean the Constitution always requires a sale in every tax.
entries.legalExplanation: The discussion contrasts Eisner's older stock-dividend rationale with broader modern understandings, including cases recognizing income from nontraditional transactions. Do not convert policy theories or superseded dicta into a categorical current constitutional rule.

entries.title: Woodsam Associates, Inc. v. Commissioner
entries.summary: No. The Second Circuit held that the mortgage refinancing was not a sale or other disposition and did not create a prior realization event.
entries.laymanExplanation: The owner borrowed more against property than its original purchase cost, but the court said a nonrecourse mortgage was not a sale.
entries.details: Assigned judicial opinion reproduced in the professor-assigned pages of the 19th-edition textbook.
entries.facts: Mrs. Wood acquired real estate for $296,400, later refinanced and made mortgage debt nonrecourse to herself. The property was later transferred to a closely held company and ultimately foreclosed. The company argued that the earlier conversion of debt to nonrecourse was a taxable disposition, thereby changing basis for its foreclosure loss calculation.
entries.issue: Did executing a nonrecourse mortgage exceeding the property's basis realize gain by disposing of the property for tax purposes?
entries.holding: No. The Second Circuit held that the mortgage refinancing was not a sale or other disposition and did not create a prior realization event.
entries.reasoning: The owner still held the underlying property, notwithstanding debt terms and cash borrowed; statutory realization occurs through sale or disposition, not automatically whenever loan proceeds exceed cost. Subsequent foreclosure was a different realization event.
entries.rule: Nonrecourse borrowing secured by property ordinarily does not itself constitute a §1001 sale or disposition merely because borrowed funds exceed the property basis.
entries.exam: Separate borrowing, debt discharge and foreclosure; explain why substantial liquidity from a loan is not itself a taxable property sale.
entries.examApplication: Separate borrowing, debt discharge and foreclosure; explain why substantial liquidity from a loan is not itself a taxable property sale.
entries.examTrap: Do not equate borrowing money with permanently retaining it free of liability, and don't conclude any nonrecourse loan above basis is automatic income.
entries.source: Reproduced opinion, Tax Week 5, Bankman et al. (19th ed.), printed pp. 197–199
entries.sourceRole: Opinion excerpt, not a mere textbook citation

entries.title: Cottage Savings Association v. Commissioner
entries.summary: Yes. The Supreme Court found the exchanged interests materially different in their legal entitlements, and held the transaction realized losses qualifying for a federal tax deduction on the facts.
entries.laymanExplanation: A lender swapped underwater mortgages for different mortgages of equal value and claimed its loss. The Supreme Court said that swap was a realization event because the legal rights were different.
entries.details: Assigned judicial opinion reproduced in the professor-assigned pages of the 19th-edition textbook.
entries.facts: Cottage Savings, a savings and loan, swapped 90% participation interests in 252 mortgages for participation in 305 other mortgages, both groups worth about $4.5 million. After interest rates increased, old mortgages had declined in value. Financial regulator Memorandum R-49 let thrifts treat certain substantially identical exchanges as having no book loss. Cottage claimed about $2,447,091 loss for tax.
entries.issue: Did the exchange of substantially similar mortgage participation interests count as a disposition producing realized and deductible tax losses?
entries.holding: Yes. The Supreme Court found the exchanged interests materially different in their legal entitlements, and held the transaction realized losses qualifying for a federal tax deduction on the facts.
entries.reasoning: Different mortgage borrowers and homes securing the loans created legally distinct rights even though market characteristics were similar. Federal income-tax realization under §1001 was not controlled by special thrift regulatory accounting. §165's loss requirement was satisfied.
entries.rule: Properties embodying materially different legal entitlements are different enough for §1001 realization upon exchange; economic near-equivalence does not prevent recognition of a disposition.
entries.exam: Identify changed obligors/collateral/contract terms, compute realized loss against adjusted basis, then test §165 and any nonrecognition exception.
entries.examApplication: Identify changed obligors/collateral/contract terms, compute realized loss against adjusted basis, then test §165 and any nonrecognition exception.
entries.examTrap: Do not use 'materially different' to require a big change in FMV, and do not import regulatory GAAP treatment as decisive tax law.
entries.source: Reproduced opinion, Tax Week 5, Bankman et al. (19th ed.), printed pp. 200–206
entries.sourceRole: Opinion excerpt, not a mere textbook citation

topics.title: C. Realization — Debt, Dispositions & Modern Test

entries.title: Nonrecognition versus exclusion
entries.summary: Nonrecognition delays taxing realized gain; exclusion keeps a receipt outside income under a specific rule.
entries.laymanExplanation: Trading investment land for other investment land can postpone taxes, but the old profit often follows you through a low basis.
entries.legalExplanation: The statutory nonrecognition rules postpone current taxation of realized gain by transferring basis or comparable preservation rules. They differ from mere lack of realization and from permanent statutory income exclusions; the source contrasts §1031 and gifts under §1015.
entries.details: The statutory nonrecognition rules postpone current taxation of realized gain by transferring basis or comparable preservation rules. They differ from mere lack of realization and from permanent statutory income exclusions; the source contrasts §1031 and gifts under §1015.

entries.title: IRC §1031(a) — qualifying exchange of like-kind real property
entries.summary: Exchanging qualifying business/investment real estate solely for like-kind business/investment real estate generally defers recognition of gain or loss.
entries.laymanExplanation: Sell investment real estate and swap it for qualifying other real estate in a properly structured exchange; you can often delay the gain tax.
entries.legalExplanation: §1031(a)(1) requires real property held for productive use in a trade or business or for investment and real property of like kind held for qualifying use. Excludes property held primarily for sale and personal-use property. Since 2018, personal property does not qualify; cash/other nonqualifying boot can lead to recognition.
entries.details: §1031(a)(1) requires real property held for productive use in a trade or business or for investment and real property of like kind held for qualifying use. Excludes property held primarily for sale and personal-use property. Since 2018, personal property does not qualify; cash/other nonqualifying boot can lead to recognition.
entries.source: Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), syllabus Week 5 textbook pp. 212–219
entries.elements: Real property given up, qualifying use, real property received, like-kind character, qualifying use after exchange, and no disqualifying dealer/inventory purpose; then check boot and timing.
entries.examTrap: Trading residences, inventory, vehicles, or other personal property is not automatically within §1031.

entries.title: Like-kind real property — nature, not quality
entries.summary: The comparison focuses on the nature or character of real property, not grade, improvements or quality.
entries.laymanExplanation: An unimproved field and an apartment building can often be like-kind real estate even though they look very different.
entries.legalExplanation: Reg. §1.1031(a)-1(b),(c) gives broad real property examples. The casebook reproduces PLR 200203033 evaluating exchange of perpetual conservation easements and fee real estate, conditioned on state-law real-property classification and qualifying investment/business use.

entries.title: Assigned PLR 200203033 — conservation easement exchange
entries.summary: The IRS concluded that on represented facts a perpetual conservation easement could be like-kind to a real-property fee interest, with important conditions.
entries.laymanExplanation: A permanent conservation right might count as real property for an exchange if state law treats it that way.
entries.legalExplanation: The reproduced January 18, 2002 private letter ruling addresses PCE on Old Ranch exchanged for a fee interest in New Ranch subject to PCE. Its conclusion assumes relevant real-property status and qualifying investment/business use; personal residence portion and boot do not automatically qualify. Under §6110(k)(3), the PLR cannot be cited as precedent.
