entries.title: Boot — cash or non-like-kind property received
entries.summary: Receiving cash, nonqualifying property or certain debt relief alongside real estate can trigger recognition despite an otherwise qualifying exchange.
entries.laymanExplanation: If you swap investment buildings but also take $20,000 cash, you may owe tax on part of the profit now.
entries.legalExplanation: The casebook notes §1031(b) gain generally recognized only to the extent of money or other property received when qualifying like-kind real estate is also received, limited by realized gain; losses generally not recognized under §1031(c) in a qualifying exchange. Liabilities require additional analysis.
entries.details: The casebook notes §1031(b) gain generally recognized only to the extent of money or other property received when qualifying like-kind real estate is also received, limited by realized gain; losses generally not recognized under §1031(c) in a qualifying exchange. Liabilities require additional analysis.
entries.source: Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), syllabus Week 5 textbook pp. 215–218

entries.title: IRC §1031(d) — basis preservation in replacement property
entries.summary: Nonrecognition usually carries untaxed appreciation forward through adjusted basis in replacement property.
entries.laymanExplanation: The replacement building's tax basis may be much lower than its market value because you haven't paid tax on the earlier gain yet.
entries.legalExplanation: General like-kind exchange basis starts from old adjusted basis, adjusted for money paid/received, boot and gain recognized. The source explains the tax cost is not erased simply because gain is deferred; compute realized, recognized and deferred gain separately.
entries.details: General like-kind exchange basis starts from old adjusted basis, adjusted for money paid/received, boot and gain recognized. The source explains the tax cost is not erased simply because gain is deferred; compute realized, recognized and deferred gain separately.
entries.source: Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), syllabus Week 5 textbook pp. 215–219

entries.title: Deferred/three-party like-kind exchange
entries.summary: Exchange structures can use intermediaries or multiple participants to meet §1031 conditions when direct counterpart exchange is impractical.
entries.laymanExplanation: You don't necessarily need to find someone who wants your exact property and happens to own the building you want; an intermediary can structure the exchange.
entries.legalExplanation: The assigned text and Figure 4-2 illustrate three-party transactions and qualified intermediaries. Statutory deferred-exchange timing and receipt restrictions are critical; do not treat any ordinary sale followed by repurchase as a §1031 exchange.
entries.details: The assigned text and Figure 4-2 illustrate three-party transactions and qualified intermediaries. Statutory deferred-exchange timing and receipt restrictions are critical; do not treat any ordinary sale followed by repurchase as a §1031 exchange.
entries.source: Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), syllabus Week 5 textbook pp. 217–219

entries.title: Why Congress permits nonrecognition in investment continuity
entries.summary: A qualifying property swap may preserve investment and avoid forcing recognition without new liquidity; tax is often deferred.
entries.laymanExplanation: If you stayed invested in real estate instead of cashing out, Congress sometimes lets you postpone the tax.
entries.legalExplanation: The book raises continuity-of-investment, administrative value, fairness with holders, lock-in mitigation and valuation/liquidity questions. These are policy reasons and not substitutes for checking §1031's statutory elements.
entries.details: The book raises continuity-of-investment, administrative value, fairness with holders, lock-in mitigation and valuation/liquidity questions. These are policy reasons and not substitutes for checking §1031's statutory elements.
entries.source: Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), syllabus Week 5 textbook pp. 211–212

topics.title: D. Statutory Nonrecognition — Like-Kind Exchanges
topics.description: §1031 real-property qualification, boot, basis, triangular/deferred exchanges and assigned IRS ruling.
topics.assignmentSource: Syllabus Week 5 printed pp 211–219

entries.title: Open transaction — unascertainable future consideration
entries.summary: In extremely rare cases, unpredictable future-sale consideration has no ascertainable FMV, allowing basis to be recovered before gain is included.
entries.laymanExplanation: If you sell stock for $120,000 cash plus a promise of mysterious future payments, you might recover your original tax cost before reporting profit—but only in exceptional cases.
entries.legalExplanation: Burnet v. Logan treated a contingent right to payments based on ore mined as not practically valu-able at sale, avoiding speculative immediate gain. Under Reg. §1.1001-1(a), property is almost always treated as having ascertainable FMV; open-transaction treatment is rare and extraordinary. Installment-sale provisions now offer a separate avenue.
entries.details: Burnet v. Logan treated a contingent right to payments based on ore mined as not practically valu-able at sale, avoiding speculative immediate gain. Under Reg. §1.1001-1(a), property is almost always treated as having ascertainable FMV; open-transaction treatment is rare and extraordinary. Installment-sale provisions now offer a separate avenue.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., syllabus Week 6 printed pp. 219–223
entries.examTrap: Do not automatically treat every contingent promissory right as an open transaction. The exception is narrowly confined.

entries.title: Closed transaction versus open transaction
entries.summary: A closed sale generally triggers a current realized gain calculation, including the value of property or debt received even when payment is later.
entries.laymanExplanation: Signing a contract and receiving a usable promissory note can count as completing a sale even without all the cash.
entries.legalExplanation: The closed-transaction approach values all consideration under §1001 and reports gain in the disposition year, subject to §453 installment method and other exceptions. An open transaction defers valuation where rights genuinely lack ascertainable FMV.
entries.details: The closed-transaction approach values all consideration under §1001 and reports gain in the disposition year, subject to §453 installment method and other exceptions. An open transaction defers valuation where rights genuinely lack ascertainable FMV.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., syllabus Week 6 printed pp. 219–229

entries.title: Completed sale versus executory contract
entries.summary: A contract alone generally is not the completed disposition; title, possession, payment obligations and substantial performance help determine sale timing.
entries.laymanExplanation: Promising to sell land in December might not mean the actual sale happens until documents and ownership transfer in January.
entries.legalExplanation: Lucas v. North Texas Lumber and Commissioner v. Segall emphasize actual transfer and unconditional duty to pay, not merely signature or deposit. Analyze title, possession, mutual conditions and substantive performance. Marketable-securities special trade-date rules require separate treatment.
entries.details: Lucas v. North Texas Lumber and Commissioner v. Segall emphasize actual transfer and unconditional duty to pay, not merely signature or deposit. Analyze title, possession, mutual conditions and substantive performance. Marketable-securities special trade-date rules require separate treatment.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., syllabus Week 6 printed pp. 224–227

entries.title: IRC §453 — installment reporting of gain
entries.summary: An eligible installment sale generally recognizes gross profit as qualifying principal payments are received, using a gross-profit ratio.
entries.laymanExplanation: If you sell land in exchange for payments over five years, you may pay tax on portions of the profit as buyers pay, rather than all at once.
entries.legalExplanation: Under §453, for a qualifying seller-financed disposition, gross profit percentage = gross profit / contract price; each installment principal payment generates gain equal to that ratio multiplied by principal received, with interest separately treated as income. Exceptions exclude many dealer, inventory and publicly traded property sales; special §§453A,453B apply.
entries.details: Under §453, for a qualifying seller-financed disposition, gross profit percentage = gross profit / contract price; each installment principal payment generates gain equal to that ratio multiplied by principal received, with interest separately treated as income. Exceptions exclude many dealer, inventory and publicly traded property sales; special §§453A,453B apply.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., syllabus Week 6 printed pp. 227–229
entries.elements: Eligible sale of property, payment after tax year of sale, proper gross profit and contract price, principal versus interest, availability limits and possible interest on deferred tax.
entries.examTrap: The cash method alone does not defer tax on a completed property sale; §453 is a special method and does not apply to losses.

entries.title: Gross profit ratio on installment sale
entries.summary: The fraction of total contract price that represents taxable gross profit, applied to installment payments.
entries.laymanExplanation: If you sell something for $300,000 with $100,000 tax cost, about two-thirds of each principal payment is taxable profit under the simple installment model.
entries.legalExplanation: Under §453's simplified method, gross profit = selling price less adjusted basis and eligible expenses, and gross profit ratio = gross profit / contract price. The casebook uses $100k basis, $300k total price and a five-year varying-payment schedule, assuming adequate separately stated interest.
entries.details: Under §453's simplified method, gross profit = selling price less adjusted basis and eligible expenses, and gross profit ratio = gross profit / contract price. The casebook uses $100k basis, $300k total price and a five-year varying-payment schedule, assuming adequate separately stated interest.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., syllabus Week 6 printed pp. 228

entries.title: Seller financing and debt instruments
entries.summary: A seller finances a buyer by accepting a note or future payments instead of immediate cash.
entries.laymanExplanation: Instead of a bank loan, the buyer owes the seller over time.
entries.legalExplanation: The notes contrast buyer's genuine notes, readily tradable paper, cash equivalents and third-party cash payments. §453(f) may treat specified demand notes or marketable debt as immediate payment, and interest is distinct from capital gain.
entries.details: The notes contrast buyer's genuine notes, readily tradable paper, cash equivalents and third-party cash payments. §453(f) may treat specified demand notes or marketable debt as immediate payment, and interest is distinct from capital gain.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., syllabus Week 6 printed pp. 227–229

entries.title: IRC §453A — interest on large deferred tax obligations
entries.summary: Special rules may impose interest on deferred tax from certain large installment obligations, reducing the deferral's financial benefit.
entries.laymanExplanation: You may be allowed to spread your income tax as a seller receives money, but for large qualifying debts the IRS may charge interest on the delayed tax.
entries.legalExplanation: The source describes §453A's price and $5m outstanding installment obligation thresholds and related interest charge for specified nonfarm property. Verify threshold and eligibility for actual tax year; this is not a blanket denial of installment method.
entries.details: The source describes §453A's price and $5m outstanding installment obligation thresholds and related interest charge for specified nonfarm property. Verify threshold and eligibility for actual tax year; this is not a blanket denial of installment method.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., syllabus Week 6 printed pp. 228–229

entries.title: Burnet v. Logan
entries.summary: No. The Supreme Court permitted the open-transaction treatment on the unusual facts, allowing recovery of basis from receipts before counting taxable profit.
entries.laymanExplanation: A shareholder sold stock for some cash plus uncertain payments based on future ore production. The Court allowed her to recover her original tax investment before reporting profit.
entries.details: Assigned judicial opinion reproduced in the professor-assigned pages of the 19th-edition textbook.
entries.facts: Mrs. Logan had $180,000 basis in mining-company stock. She sold it for $120,000 cash and a contingent promise of future payments depending on ore extracted. The government valued the promise at about $100,000 and wanted $40,000 gain in the sale year. She argued the promise lacked ascertainable FMV and she had not recovered her capital.
entries.issue: Must contingent, unvalu-able future mining payments be included as FMV consideration in the initial sale-year gain calculation?
entries.holding: No. The Supreme Court permitted the open-transaction treatment on the unusual facts, allowing recovery of basis from receipts before counting taxable profit.
entries.reasoning: The obligation depended on indefinite ore production and payment prospects, making immediate valuation highly speculative. Later receipts could be attributed first to restoration of invested capital; current law confines this reasoning to exceptional cases.
entries.rule: Only in rare situations where the value of future rights genuinely cannot be determined can an open transaction permit basis-first cost recovery.
entries.exam: Compare ordinary closed sale or §453 installment payments and explain why merely receiving payment in future years does not make a case like Logan.
entries.examApplication: Compare ordinary closed sale or §453 installment payments and explain why merely receiving payment in future years does not make a case like Logan.
entries.examTrap: Burnet v Logan is an exceptional historical case; Reg. §1.1001-1(a) states property lacking FMV is 'rare and extraordinary.'
entries.source: Reproduced opinion, Tax Week 6, Bankman et al. (19th ed.), printed pp. 219–221
entries.sourceRole: Opinion excerpt, not a mere textbook citation

entries.title: Lucas v. North Texas Lumber Co.
entries.summary: No. The Supreme Court held 1916 created only an executory contract; the sale completed in 1917 when papers and title transferred.
entries.laymanExplanation: A company agreed to sell timberland in December but didn't transfer ownership until January. The Supreme Court taxed the gain in January's year.
entries.details: Assigned judicial opinion reproduced in the professor-assigned pages of the 19th-edition textbook.
entries.facts: A lumber company granted an option to buy timberland in December 1916. Buyer notified it on December 30 that it would close when deeds were prepared, but seller did not tender title, possession or demand price until January 1917. Seller wanted gain in lower-rate 1916; IRS assessed it in 1917.
entries.issue: Did the December option exercise and buyer's readiness to pay complete a taxable land sale during 1916?
entries.holding: No. The Supreme Court held 1916 created only an executory contract; the sale completed in 1917 when papers and title transferred.
entries.reasoning: Buyer was prepared to proceed but seller retained title and possession; the buyer's unconditional present duty to pay had not arisen and no current right to payment was established. Accounting method did not substitute for a completed sale.
entries.rule: A binding executory agreement is not necessarily a completed disposition for income-tax timing; title, possession, performance and payment obligations matter.
entries.exam: Distinguish signing date from actual closing with legal title and ownership; identify year of sale before cash-versus-accrual income timing.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish signing date from actual closing with legal title and ownership; identify year of sale before cash-versus-accrual income timing.
entries.examTrap: Taxability does not always arise on option exercise or contract signature, even under the accrual method.
entries.source: Reproduced opinion, Tax Week 6, Bankman et al. (19th ed.), printed pp. 224–225
entries.sourceRole: Opinion excerpt, not a mere textbook citation

entries.title: Commissioner v. Segall
entries.summary: The Sixth Circuit held the sale occurred in 1932 upon substantive closing and satisfaction of conditions, not at the 1931 agreement date.
entries.laymanExplanation: A merger-style asset deal was signed in 1931, but its mutual exchange obligations only became unconditional in January 1932, so that was the sale year.
entries.details: Assigned judicial opinion reproduced in the professor-assigned pages of the 19th-edition textbook.
entries.facts: Silent Automatic and Timken-Detroit entered a 1931 agreement anticipated to be a tax-free reorganization. The court concluded the transaction was actually a taxable sale. Bills of sale and debentures were to be exchanged January 2, 1932 and mutual performance conditions remained.
entries.issue: When did the taxable asset sale occur, when the agreement was signed in 1931 or when the parties performed exchange obligations in 1932?
entries.holding: The Sixth Circuit held the sale occurred in 1932 upon substantive closing and satisfaction of conditions, not at the 1931 agreement date.
entries.reasoning: The court looked pragmatically at title, possession, substantial performance and the unconditional duty to pay. No single formality alone controlled; the parties intended the exchange obligations to operate as of January 2, 1932.
entries.rule: A sale's year turns on the transaction as a whole, particularly completed transfer and unconditional payment duties, not merely advance agreement.
entries.exam: Apply factors to an executory contract with deposits and future deed delivery; compare Lucas.
entries.examApplication: Apply factors to an executory contract with deposits and future deed delivery; compare Lucas.
entries.examTrap: A buyer's deposit does not, by itself, complete the sale.
entries.source: Reproduced opinion, Tax Week 6, Bankman et al. (19th ed.), printed pp. 225–227
entries.sourceRole: Opinion excerpt, not a mere textbook citation

topics.title: E. Open Transactions, Completed Sales & Installments
topics.description: Burnet v Logan, rare open transactions, sale completion, installment accounting.
topics.assignmentSource: Tax syllabus Week 6, printed pp.219–245 (problem p245) and pp.245–257

entries.title: Constructive receipt — cash available without substantial restriction
entries.summary: A cash-method taxpayer generally includes income made freely available, even without physically collecting it.
entries.laymanExplanation: If your employer lets you take a paycheck today and you deliberately leave it uncollected, it may count as income now.
entries.legalExplanation: Reg. §1.451-2(a) generally treats income as constructively received when credited, set apart or otherwise available to draw on without substantial limitation. Mere right to future promised payment is not constructive receipt when the payer cannot yet be compelled to pay.
entries.details: Reg. §1.451-2(a) generally treats income as constructively received when credited, set apart or otherwise available to draw on without substantial limitation. Mere right to future promised payment is not constructive receipt when the payer cannot yet be compelled to pay.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., syllabus Week 6 printed pp. 229–234
entries.examTrap: The opportunity to negotiate an earlier payment is not the same as already having an unconditional right to demand payment.

entries.title: Bona fide payment deferral vs. constructive receipt
entries.summary: Contractually fixed future due dates can postpone receipt; unrestricted currently payable income cannot always be delayed by request.
entries.laymanExplanation: If you genuinely agree in advance to get paid in January for December work, you may not have December receipt—unless cash was already available.
entries.legalExplanation: Amend involved a bona fide wheat-sale contract with January payment; the Tax Court refused to treat the possible option to make a different sale for immediate cash as taxable receipt of the agreed future payment.
entries.details: Amend involved a bona fide wheat-sale contract with January payment; the Tax Court refused to treat the possible option to make a different sale for immediate cash as taxable receipt of the agreed future payment.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., syllabus Week 6 printed pp. 229–233

entries.title: Economic benefit doctrine — irrevocably funded rights
entries.summary: An irrevocable, vested fund set aside for a taxpayer beyond the payor's creditors can create current taxable economic benefit without physical cash.
entries.laymanExplanation: If prize money is locked in a trust entirely for you, you may be taxable before the trustee sends you the check.
entries.legalExplanation: Pulsifer emphasizes a fixed, nonforfeitable right to Irish sweepstakes winnings held by court. The source contrasts unfunded, unsecured deferred compensation in Minor. Separate economic benefit from constructive receipt.
entries.details: Pulsifer emphasizes a fixed, nonforfeitable right to Irish sweepstakes winnings held by court. The source contrasts unfunded, unsecured deferred compensation in Minor. Separate economic benefit from constructive receipt.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., syllabus Week 6 printed pp. 234–240

entries.title: Vested versus forfeitable rights
entries.summary: Vested rights are no longer conditional on future services or contingencies; forfeitable rights can be lost when conditions fail.
entries.laymanExplanation: A pension benefit that belongs to you even if you quit is vested; one that vanishes if you leave early isn't.
entries.legalExplanation: This is one axis of deferred compensation analysis. The presence of a substantial risk of forfeiture can postpone inclusion where property/funding is involved, subject to §§83 and 409A.
entries.details: This is one axis of deferred compensation analysis. The presence of a substantial risk of forfeiture can postpone inclusion where property/funding is involved, subject to §§83 and 409A.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., syllabus Week 6 printed pp. 234–242

entries.title: Amend v. Commissioner
entries.summary: No. The Tax Court held there was no constructive receipt in 1944 because the agreed payment was not due until January 1945.
entries.laymanExplanation: A farmer sold wheat in 1944 under an agreement requiring payment in January 1945. He wasn't taxed as though he'd already received the money in 1944.
entries.details: Assigned judicial opinion reproduced in the professor-assigned pages of the 19th-edition textbook.
entries.facts: A cash-method wheat farmer agreed with Burrus to deliver wheat from his 1944 crop and be paid under their contract in January 1945, though the buyer might otherwise have bought wheat with immediate cash. The IRS asserted he constructively received the money in 1944.
entries.issue: Did the farmer constructively receive proceeds in 1944 because he could have arranged a different cash-on-delivery contract?
entries.holding: No. The Tax Court held there was no constructive receipt in 1944 because the agreed payment was not due until January 1945.
entries.reasoning: The written/oral sales arrangement fixed future payment timing; the farmer had no unconditional legal right to demand the amount in 1944. Merely being able to make a different immediate-cash bargain is not presently available income.
entries.rule: Constructive receipt requires present ability to obtain funds without substantial limitations; a genuine contract for future payment does not create early receipt.
entries.exam: Check whether an agreement predates accrual of a right to demand income. Compare freely available payment the taxpayer simply refuses to collect.
entries.examApplication: Check whether an agreement predates accrual of a right to demand income. Compare freely available payment the taxpayer simply refuses to collect.
entries.examTrap: The cash method does not mean every future promise is income now, and the potential to negotiate cash does not equal current availability.
entries.source: Reproduced opinion, Tax Week 6, Bankman et al. (19th ed.), printed pp. 229–233
entries.sourceRole: Opinion excerpt, not a mere textbook citation

entries.title: Pulsifer v. Commissioner
entries.summary: Yes. The Tax Court held the minors' nonforfeitable right to the winnings constituted currently taxable economic benefit in the year the fund was set aside for them.
entries.laymanExplanation: Children won sweepstakes money held by an Irish court for them. Because the money was irrevocably theirs, the court taxed it that year although they had not yet taken it out.
entries.details: Assigned judicial opinion reproduced in the professor-assigned pages of the 19th-edition textbook.
entries.facts: Minor petitioners held winning Irish Hospital Sweepstakes tickets. Prize winnings were deposited under supervision of an Irish court for their sole benefit pending action by a guardian. The funds were set aside and not subject to payer creditors; petitioners argued neither actual nor constructive receipt occurred until release.
entries.issue: Did an irrevocable, vested fund created for the taxpayer yield current income under the economic benefit doctrine?
entries.holding: Yes. The Tax Court held the minors' nonforfeitable right to the winnings constituted currently taxable economic benefit in the year the fund was set aside for them.
entries.reasoning: Ownership and security of the award, not merely the ability to physically reach cash, created an absolute, valued benefit. The fund was dedicated to petitioners and beyond reach of the payor; guardian could take required steps to obtain it.
entries.rule: An irrevocably funded and nonforfeitable right held for a taxpayer can constitute current income under the economic-benefit doctrine without actual payment.
entries.exam: Contrast a secured vested prize fund with an employer's unsecured promise to pay a worker later (Minor).
entries.examApplication: Contrast a secured vested prize fund with an employer's unsecured promise to pay a worker later (Minor).
entries.examTrap: Constructive receipt and economic benefit are distinct legal grounds; the absence of physical control doesn't always bar inclusion.
entries.source: Reproduced opinion, Tax Week 6, Bankman et al. (19th ed.), printed pp. 234–235
entries.sourceRole: Opinion excerpt, not a mere textbook citation

topics.title: F. Constructive Receipt & Economic Benefit
topics.description: Cash-basis availability, Amend, trust benefit and Pulsifer.
topics.assignmentSource: Tax syllabus Week 6, printed pp.219–245 (problem p245) and pp.245–257

entries.title: Funded versus unfunded deferred compensation
entries.summary: Funding places assets beyond employer creditors for employee's benefit; unfunded promises remain subject to employer insolvency risk.
entries.laymanExplanation: If your boss just promises to pay later, you bear risk the company runs out of money. A separate protected trust may make the benefit taxable earlier.
entries.legalExplanation: The Minor opinion treats a trust still subject to general employer creditors as unfunded despite bookkeeping arrangements. An employee's vested, funded benefit is generally immediately taxable; the form of rabbi trust and creditors' claims matter.
entries.details: The Minor opinion treats a trust still subject to general employer creditors as unfunded despite bookkeeping arrangements. An employee's vested, funded benefit is generally immediately taxable; the form of rabbi trust and creditors' claims matter.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., syllabus Week 6 printed pp. 237–244

entries.title: Vesting + funding often triggers current income
entries.summary: A vested right to funded compensation ordinarily creates current employee income, even without cash payout.
entries.laymanExplanation: If money is permanently yours and safely set aside, tax law may count it before you take it out.
entries.legalExplanation: The reading's shortcuts: no vesting generally no current income; vesting plus funding or unrestricted constructive receipt triggers inclusion; vesting without funding or constructive receipt often allows deferral. For funded but unvested property, §83(b) election may be relevant.
entries.details: The reading's shortcuts: no vesting generally no current income; vesting plus funding or unrestricted constructive receipt triggers inclusion; vesting without funding or constructive receipt often allows deferral. For funded but unvested property, §83(b) election may be relevant.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., syllabus Week 6 printed pp. 241–251
entries.examTrap: Simply calling an account a 'trust' is not proof of funding; creditor access and beneficiary rights control.

entries.title: IRC §83 — property compensation and risk of forfeiture
entries.summary: Property transferred for services generally becomes taxable when vested, based on value then, unless a valid §83(b) election applies.
entries.laymanExplanation: If you're paid with stock that you lose if you quit, you usually aren't taxed as though you own it outright until it vests—unless you elect earlier taxation.
entries.legalExplanation: The excerpt explains property transferred as compensation, substantial risk of forfeiture, funding, and the §83(b) election to include property at transfer rather than vesting, subject to statutory timing and conditions. Qualified stock options generally follow more specific treatment.
entries.details: The excerpt explains property transferred as compensation, substantial risk of forfeiture, funding, and the §83(b) election to include property at transfer rather than vesting, subject to statutory timing and conditions. Qualified stock options generally follow more specific treatment.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., syllabus Week 6 printed pp. 240–249

entries.title: Section 83(b) election
entries.summary: An election to recognize qualifying restricted-property compensation at transfer rather than later vesting.
entries.laymanExplanation: You can sometimes pay tax when restricted shares are cheap now, hoping later growth won't be compensation taxed on vesting.
entries.legalExplanation: An employee receiving transferred property subject to substantial risk of forfeiture may elect under §83(b) to include value at transfer in the election year; the choice has risks if property is later forfeited and requires timely valid election. Ordinary nontraded NQSOs generally are not treated as §83 property on grant.
entries.details: An employee receiving transferred property subject to substantial risk of forfeiture may elect under §83(b) to include value at transfer in the election year; the choice has risks if property is later forfeited and requires timely valid election. Ordinary nontraded NQSOs generally are not treated as §83 property on grant.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., syllabus Week 6 printed pp. 240–249

entries.title: IRC §409A — strict deferred compensation timing rules
entries.summary: Nonqualified deferred compensation arrangements can impose immediate inclusion, a 20% additional tax and interest-like charges if acceleration or other requirements are violated.
entries.laymanExplanation: Your employer can't casually let you take deferred salary whenever you want without risking major tax penalties.
entries.legalExplanation: Section 409A regulates election/distribution dates, payment acceleration and certain funding structures. The notes list separation from service, disability, death, specified fixed time, change in corporate control, unforeseeable emergency as specified triggers. Noncompliance can cause inclusion before payment plus 20% and additional interest charge. Specialized exceptions apply.
entries.details: Section 409A regulates election/distribution dates, payment acceleration and certain funding structures. The notes list separation from service, disability, death, specified fixed time, change in corporate control, unforeseeable emergency as specified triggers. Noncompliance can cause inclusion before payment plus 20% and additional interest charge. Specialized exceptions apply.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., syllabus Week 6 printed pp. 245–247
entries.examTrap: §409A is separate from constructive receipt and §83; violating it can trigger tax even before the deferred cash actually arrives.

entries.title: Nonqualified employee stock options — tax on exercise spread
entries.summary: Ordinary nontransferable NQSOs generally are not taxed at grant/vesting, but exercise creates ordinary compensation income on the spread.
entries.laymanExplanation: An employee option lets you buy a $450 stock for $200. When you exercise, that $250 bargain per share is usually wage income.
entries.legalExplanation: Under Reg. §1.83-7 and §83(e)(3), typical nontraded NQSOs lack readily ascertainable FMV at grant, so grant and vesting are generally not income events. Exercise triggers ordinary compensation equal to (FMV at exercise − exercise price) × number exercised; employer deduction generally matches.
entries.details: Under Reg. §1.83-7 and §83(e)(3), typical nontraded NQSOs lack readily ascertainable FMV at grant, so grant and vesting are generally not income events. Exercise triggers ordinary compensation equal to (FMV at exercise − exercise price) × number exercised; employer deduction generally matches.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., syllabus Week 6 printed pp. 247–249
entries.examTrap: An ordinary NQSO is not eligible for a §83(b) election upon grant under the book's fact pattern.

entries.title: IRC §83(i) — qualified equity grants
entries.summary: Eligible employees at specified private corporations may elect limited deferral of inclusion for qualifying stock obtained through options or RSUs.
entries.laymanExplanation: Certain private-company employees can delay tax when receiving company stock under a special election.
entries.legalExplanation: The source discusses the 2017 provision for qualified stock at privately held corporations, with up-to-five-year or earlier trigger conditions and detailed eligibility restrictions. It is not universal for every private-company stock award.
entries.details: The source discusses the 2017 provision for qualified stock at privately held corporations, with up-to-five-year or earlier trigger conditions and detailed eligibility restrictions. It is not universal for every private-company stock award.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., syllabus Week 6 printed pp. 248–249

entries.title: IRC §404(a)(5) — employer deduction matched to employee inclusion
entries.summary: For certain nonqualified deferred compensation, employer's compensation deduction generally waits until the employee includes the income.
entries.laymanExplanation: If your employer promises you $10,000 next year, the employer generally cannot take the employee-compensation deduction now if you haven't been taxed yet.
entries.legalExplanation: The excerpt describes a timing-matching rule: deferral benefits the employee but delays employer deduction. Different employer/employee tax rates, exempt employers and certain investments can produce unequal economic results.
entries.details: The excerpt describes a timing-matching rule: deferral benefits the employee but delays employer deduction. Different employer/employee tax rates, exempt employers and certain investments can produce unequal economic results.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., syllabus Week 6 printed pp. 249–251

entries.title: Rabbi trust and general-creditor risk
entries.summary: A trust holding deferred compensation can remain unfunded for tax if its assets are still reachable by employer's general creditors.
entries.laymanExplanation: Money can sit in a trust but still be at risk if the business fails; that risk can help keep compensation untaxed until payout.
entries.legalExplanation: The source describes employer trusts and creditor exposure, contrasting secured, protected employee benefits and unfunded promises. Actual plan documents and beneficiary rights matter more than trust label.
entries.details: The source describes employer trusts and creditor exposure, contrasting secured, protected employee benefits and unfunded promises. Actual plan documents and beneficiary rights matter more than trust label.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., syllabus Week 6 printed pp. 242–245

entries.title: Minor v. United States
entries.summary: No. The Ninth Circuit affirmed that the physician had no currently taxable economic benefit: the unfunded employer promise had not vested as protected taxable property.
entries.laymanExplanation: A doctor's fees were deferred into a trust-like plan, but because the money wasn't actually safe from employer creditors, he wasn't taxed on it yet.
entries.details: Assigned judicial opinion reproduced in the professor-assigned pages of the 19th-edition textbook.
entries.facts: Physician Ralph Minor participated in Snohomish Physicians' deferred compensation plan, reporting only 10% of scheduled fees actually received while 90% was deferred. The employer formed a trust to buy annuities, but the trust's settlor and beneficiary were the employer; doctors had no enforceable title or right to trust assets, which remained exposed to general employer creditors.
entries.issue: Did the deferred fee allocations create a presently taxable economic benefit although the physician had received no cash?
entries.holding: No. The Ninth Circuit affirmed that the physician had no currently taxable economic benefit: the unfunded employer promise had not vested as protected taxable property.
entries.reasoning: The employer retained beneficial trust ownership and its general creditors could reach plan assets. The individual doctor held only a deferred contractual claim; constructive receipt was conceded absent. The court found funding missing without deciding the independent significance of all forfeiture restrictions.
entries.rule: An employer's unfunded, unsecured promise of future compensation generally is not current employee income solely because the employer maintains earmarked assets.
entries.exam: Analyze both vested/forfeitable and funded/unfunded axes, and compare Pulsifer's irrevocable protected trust.
entries.examApplication: Analyze both vested/forfeitable and funded/unfunded axes, and compare Pulsifer's irrevocable protected trust.
entries.examTrap: A trust label alone doesn't establish employee ownership; Minor did not definitively decide every substantial-risk-of-forfeiture issue.
entries.source: Reproduced opinion, Tax Week 6, Bankman et al. (19th ed.), printed pp. 237–240
entries.sourceRole: Opinion excerpt, not a mere textbook citation

topics.title: G. Nonqualified Deferred Compensation
topics.description: Minor, funded/vested benefits, §83, §409A, nonqualified stock options and employer matching.
topics.assignmentSource: Tax syllabus Week 6, printed pp.219–245 (problem p245) and pp.245–257

entries.title: Qualified employee retirement plan — key tax benefits
entries.summary: Eligible employer contributions are generally not taxed to employees immediately; employer deducts them; funds grow tax-deferred until distributions.
entries.laymanExplanation: Your company pays money into a retirement plan now, and generally you pay income tax when taking retirement money out later.
entries.legalExplanation: The source outlines benefits of qualifying pension/profit-sharing/stock bonus plans: immediate deduction to employer, deferred inclusion to employees even with vested rights, tax-sheltered investment growth. Qualified-plan rules are governed by applicable Code provisions and ERISA, with significant limitations.
entries.details: The source outlines benefits of qualifying pension/profit-sharing/stock bonus plans: immediate deduction to employer, deferred inclusion to employees even with vested rights, tax-sheltered investment growth. Qualified-plan rules are governed by applicable Code provisions and ERISA, with significant limitations.

entries.title: Defined-benefit versus defined-contribution plan
entries.summary: Defined-benefit plans promise a specified retirement benefit; defined-contribution plans accumulate funded contributions and investment returns.
entries.laymanExplanation: A traditional pension promises payments based on a formula; a 401(k) is based more on what's invested and how the investments perform.
entries.legalExplanation: The book describes defined-benefit amount based on compensation and years of service, and defined-contribution employer/employee amounts whose final balance depends on investment returns.
entries.details: The book describes defined-benefit amount based on compensation and years of service, and defined-contribution employer/employee amounts whose final balance depends on investment returns.

entries.title: Traditional 401(k) versus Roth 401(k)
entries.summary: Pretax 401(k) contributions defer tax until eligible withdrawal; Roth 401(k) contributions use after-tax money with qualifying tax-free distributions.
entries.laymanExplanation: Traditional: tax break today. Roth: pay tax today, then qualifying retirement withdrawals generally tax-free.
entries.legalExplanation: Under §401(k), elective pretax contributions generally defer employee tax while plan earnings accumulate; Roth designated contributions don't reduce current income tax but qualified distributions can be excluded. The textbook's 2022 dollar contribution limits are historical, not 2026 limits.

entries.title: ERISA and qualified-plan nondiscrimination
entries.summary: Qualified plans must meet tax and retirement-benefit safeguards, including protections against favoring highly paid employees.
entries.laymanExplanation: A business can't generally reserve all the special pension tax breaks for executives and exclude the ordinary staff.
entries.legalExplanation: The source outlines ERISA oversight, employee vesting and Code anti-discrimination requirements aimed at reasonably comparable benefit participation, as well as spousal protections.
entries.details: The source outlines ERISA oversight, employee vesting and Code anti-discrimination requirements aimed at reasonably comparable benefit participation, as well as spousal protections.

entries.title: IRC §72(t) — early distribution additional tax
entries.summary: Certain retirement plan withdrawals before age 59½ incur a 10% additional tax, unless an exception applies.
entries.laymanExplanation: Taking your 401(k) money out early can cost extra taxes on top of ordinary income tax.
entries.legalExplanation: The book explains §72(t)'s 10% additional tax and exceptions for disability, death, specified periodic distributions and qualifying separation circumstances. Determine which plan type and exception actually apply.
entries.details: The book explains §72(t)'s 10% additional tax and exceptions for disability, death, specified periodic distributions and qualifying separation circumstances. Determine which plan type and exception actually apply.

entries.title: Required minimum distributions — modern age differs from casebook
entries.summary: Qualified retirement accounts generally require distributions by statutory ages and schedules; exact age depends on birth year and account type.
entries.laymanExplanation: You usually cannot leave pretax retirement money growing untaxed forever; at some point you must withdraw minimum amounts.
entries.legalExplanation: The 2023 casebook describes an old 70½-year threshold. Subsequent statutory amendments raise applicable ages in many cases and set different Roth treatment. Use governing tax-year and birth-year rules rather than outdated casebook age. CURRENT-LAW ANNOTATION: SECURE 2.0 generally sets an age-73 required beginning age for covered individuals who reach age 73 before 2033 and age 75 for covered later cohorts; plan, Roth and retirement exceptions affect exact dates.

entries.title: IRC §415 — contribution and benefit ceilings
entries.summary: Qualified plan benefits and contributions are subject to statutory and annually adjusted dollar caps.
entries.laymanExplanation: Tax-favored retirement savings aren't unlimited; the IRS places caps depending on plan type.
entries.legalExplanation: The casebook quotes a 2022 dollar ceiling for an annual defined-benefit amount and separately addresses contributions, catch-up amounts and plan eligibility. The amounts are historic examples.

entries.title: Who benefits most from retirement-savings tax preferences?
entries.summary: The book cites historical government estimates that benefits disproportionately accrue to high-income taxpayers.
entries.laymanExplanation: People with more income to save can often take greater advantage of tax-sheltered retirement plans.
entries.legalExplanation: The reading cites 2019 JCT estimates above $250b in total revenue cost and CBO estimates allocating 63% of benefits to the top income quintile. These are historic policy data, not a statutory test or 2026 estimate.

topics.title: H. Qualified Retirement Plans & Distributional Effects
topics.description: Traditional/Roth 401(k), defined-benefit/contribution, ERISA, deferral and plan limits.
topics.assignmentSource: Tax syllabus Week 6, printed pp.219–245 (problem p245) and pp.245–257

entries.title: Debt / loan principal
entries.summary: Debt is an enforceable or otherwise genuine obligation to repay an amount borrowed, often with interest.
entries.laymanExplanation: Borrow $10,000 today, owe $10,000 back later. The money in your bank account is offset by the amount you owe.
entries.legalExplanation: Classic debt generally has fixed principal, stated or determinable interest, maturity, creditor enforcement rights and priority over equity in insolvency. Hybrid instruments may require debt-versus-equity classification.
entries.details: Classic debt generally has fixed principal, stated or determinable interest, maturity, creditor enforcement rights and priority over equity in insolvency. Hybrid instruments may require debt-versus-equity classification.

entries.title: Equity / stock
entries.summary: Equity is a residual ownership claim whose economic return generally depends on enterprise success.
entries.laymanExplanation: Owning company shares means you own a piece of the business and usually get paid after lenders.
entries.legalExplanation: Typical equity lacks fixed maturity, gives residual returns and is subordinate to debt. Voting or control rights may attach. The classification line is fact intensive for preferred, convertible and hybrid instruments.
entries.details: Typical equity lacks fixed maturity, gives residual returns and is subordinate to debt. Voting or control rights may attach. The classification line is fact intensive for preferred, convertible and hybrid instruments.

entries.title: Bond, lender, borrower, principal, interest and maturity
entries.summary: A bond evidences debt; principal is the amount owed, interest is the cost of borrowing, and maturity is the due date.
entries.laymanExplanation: A bond is a formal IOU. You lend principal, collect interest, and expect principal back at maturity.
entries.legalExplanation: The lender/holder is creditor; the issuer/obligor is debtor. Principal is generally distinct from periodic or accrued interest. Bonds can be held by individuals, corporations or tax-exempt institutions.
entries.details: The lender/holder is creditor; the issuer/obligor is debtor. Principal is generally distinct from periodic or accrued interest. Bonds can be held by individuals, corporations or tax-exempt institutions.

entries.title: Hybrid instruments and debt–equity classification
entries.summary: Financial instruments may mix debt and equity traits, affecting return character and tax deductions.
entries.laymanExplanation: A security can act partly like a loan and partly like shares, making tax treatment less obvious.
entries.legalExplanation: Fixed versus contingent return, maturity, creditors' rights, priority, voting/control and actual business risk can matter. Chapter 5 expressly reserves advanced debt/equity characterization and derivative analysis for later courses.
entries.details: Fixed versus contingent return, maturity, creditors' rights, priority, voting/control and actual business risk can matter. Chapter 5 expressly reserves advanced debt/equity characterization and derivative analysis for later courses.

topics.title: A. Financial Instruments — Debt and Equity
topics.description: Definitions of debt, equity, bonds, creditors, and investment instruments.
topics.assignmentSource: Fall 2026 Tax syllabus Week 7: pp259–290 and pp290–321; assigned material from 19th-edition casebook

entries.title: Loan principal received is not gross income
entries.summary: Genuine loan proceeds generally are excluded when received because repayment liability offsets the cash; principal repayment is not deductible.
entries.laymanExplanation: A $10,000 bank loan makes you $10,000 richer in cash, but also $10,000 deeper in debt—no net enrichment.
entries.legalExplanation: The book applies balance-sheet logic and Haig–Simons income Y=C+ΔW: in an arm's-length loan, cash plus a real liability does not increase net worth. Federal income tax generally disregards cashflows of debt principal, while separately taxing interest or discharge.
entries.details: The book applies balance-sheet logic and Haig–Simons income Y=C+ΔW: in an arm's-length loan, cash plus a real liability does not increase net worth. Federal income tax generally disregards cashflows of debt principal, while separately taxing interest or discharge.

entries.sourceRole: Syllabus-assigned textbook; not a separately supplied handout
entries.examTrap: Neither receipt of real loan principal nor repayment of it is ordinarily taxable/deductible; forgiven debt requires a second analysis.

entries.title: Collateralized loan / borrowing against appreciated property
entries.summary: A loan secured by stock or land ordinarily does not realize unrealized appreciation in the collateral.
entries.laymanExplanation: You can borrow $100,000 against shares that rose from $50,000 to $200,000 without selling the shares.
entries.legalExplanation: The chapter contrasts A borrowing $25k against stock still at $50k basis/FMV, B borrowing $100k against stock costing $50k and worth $200k, and C borrowing against expected future salary. In all cases a genuine repayment obligation generally prevents gross income on borrowing.

entries.title: IRC §61(a)(11) — cancellation of indebtedness income
entries.summary: Forgiveness or discharge of a genuine debt generally produces gross income to the debtor unless a statutory exclusion applies.
entries.laymanExplanation: If your bank forgives $10,000 you otherwise had to pay, you typically gained $10,000 of relief.
entries.legalExplanation: The original loan was excluded because repayment was expected. A later discharge removes the liability; §61(a)(11) includes discharge-of-indebtedness income (CODI), analyzed at discharge rather than origination and separately subjected to §108 relief rules.
entries.details: The original loan was excluded because repayment was expected. A later discharge removes the liability; §61(a)(11) includes discharge-of-indebtedness income (CODI), analyzed at discharge rather than origination and separately subjected to §108 relief rules.

entries.sourceRole: Syllabus-assigned textbook; not a separately supplied handout
entries.examApplication: Debt face $100,000, lender accepts $90,000 in full satisfaction: potential $10,000 CODI before §108 exclusions.

entries.title: Discharge / forgiveness / cancellation of debt
entries.summary: A creditor's legally effective relinquishment of some or all repayment rights.
entries.laymanExplanation: If a lender agrees to accept $90,000 instead of the $100,000 you owe, the remaining $10,000 obligation disappears.
entries.legalExplanation: Absent dispute or special rules, CODI generally reflects the face/adjusted debt obligation discharged less qualifying consideration paid. Debt and creditor character, interest included and recourse/nonrecourse arrangements can affect classification.
entries.details: Absent dispute or special rules, CODI generally reflects the face/adjusted debt obligation discharged less qualifying consideration paid. Debt and creditor character, interest included and recourse/nonrecourse arrangements can affect classification.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), assigned Week 7 pp. 262–263

entries.title: 'Freeing of assets' is not a prerequisite to CODI
entries.summary: A debt discharge can be taxable even when a debtor is still insolvent or no particular property becomes free of liens.
entries.laymanExplanation: You can remain broke after debt forgiveness yet still have CODI under §61; a separate exception may help.
entries.legalExplanation: The text distinguishes Kirby Lumber's freeing-of-assets phrasing from the transaction-wide rationale: amounts initially excluded as loans become enriching when no longer repayable. Insolvent debtors seek §108 exclusions, not denial of the §61 CODI definition.

entries.title: IRC §108 — discharge-of-indebtedness exclusions
entries.summary: §108 may exclude specified CODI arising in a title 11 bankruptcy case, insolvency, qualifying farm debt and other statutory categories.
entries.laymanExplanation: Debt forgiveness is normally taxable, but Congress provides exceptions for bankruptcy, insolvency and other specified situations.
entries.legalExplanation: Analyze whether CODI exists first, then whether §§108(a), (d), (e), (f) and related limitations provide exclusion. Coordination and tax attribute reductions may postpone rather than eliminate tax. Some statutory categories have date limits.

entries.sourceRole: Syllabus-assigned textbook; not a separately supplied handout
entries.examTrap: Do not say insolvent taxpayers have no CODI. First compute CODI under §61, then apply §108.

entries.title: Insolvency — liabilities exceeding fair market value of assets
entries.summary: Under §108(d)(3), insolvency is measured immediately before discharge by comparing liabilities and asset FMV.
entries.laymanExplanation: If you own $30,000 of assets but owe $50,000, you are $20,000 insolvent before a discharge.
entries.legalExplanation: The §108(a)(1)(B) exclusion is limited to the extent of insolvency under §108(a)(3); timing and valuation are important. Title 11 exclusions have their own statutory priority. Do not treat mere lack of cash as the whole insolvency test.
entries.details: The §108(a)(1)(B) exclusion is limited to the extent of insolvency under §108(a)(3); timing and valuation are important. Title 11 exclusions have their own statutory priority. Do not treat mere lack of cash as the whole insolvency test.

entries.sourceRole: Syllabus-assigned textbook; not a separately supplied handout
entries.examApplication: Assets FMV $30k, liabilities $50k immediately before discharge: $20k insolvency. Of a $25k CODI amount, generally no more than $20k qualifies for this exclusion (absent other relief).

entries.title: IRC §108(a)(1)(A) — Title 11 case exclusion
entries.summary: CODI from a qualifying discharge in a bankruptcy case may be excluded, subject to attribute reduction and conditions.
entries.laymanExplanation: If a qualifying bankruptcy eliminates debts, the taxpayer may not owe income tax immediately on the forgiven amount.
entries.legalExplanation: §108(d)(2) describes a title 11 case and statutory judicial approval. §108(a)(2)(A) gives bankruptcy priority among some exclusions. §108(b) can require later reduction in NOLs, credits, basis and other tax attributes.

entries.title: IRC §108(b) — reduction of tax attributes
entries.summary: Excluded CODI in certain bankruptcy or insolvency cases generally reduces specified beneficial tax attributes.
entries.laymanExplanation: A company may avoid tax on forgiven debt now but lose tax-loss carryovers it planned to use later.
entries.legalExplanation: Book illustration: company with $3m of NOL and $1m excluded CODI reduces NOL to $2m. When future taxable income is $7m, it can offset only $2m instead of $3m under the simplified illustration. Actual reduction order, §172 limits and other conditions govern final amounts.

entries.title: Qualified farm indebtedness — §108(a)(1)(C), (g)
entries.summary: Eligible farm debt forgiveness can receive a special exclusion subject to farming-income and other statutory requirements.
entries.laymanExplanation: A working farmer may qualify for debt-forgiveness relief even if not bankrupt.
entries.legalExplanation: The book points to debt incurred in operating a farm and gross receipts from farming over prior 3 years; the contemporary statutory test includes aggregate 50% gross receipts as well as eligible lender and limitation rules. This is not a blanket exemption for all farmers.

entries.title: IRC §108(e)(5) — seller-financed purchase-price adjustment
entries.summary: A qualifying solvent buyer's debt reduction owed to the original seller for purchased property may reduce basis rather than cause CODI.
entries.laymanExplanation: You buy a car for $30,000 partly on the dealer's loan; dealer cuts $9,000 from what you owe. It may lower your car's tax cost instead of being taxable debt forgiveness.
entries.legalExplanation: When the qualifying debt arose from purchase of property and is owed to the seller, and statutory criteria are met, §108(e)(5) recharacterizes the reduction as a purchase-price adjustment. Example: cash $6k plus seller note $24k originally yields $30k basis; debt reduced to $15k => $9k price reduction and adjusted basis $21k.

entries.title: Student-loan discharge — §108(f), distinguish tax years
entries.summary: Specific qualifying student-loan forgiveness may be excluded; the broad 2021–2025 temporary exclusion did not continue unchanged into 2026.
entries.laymanExplanation: Some student-loan forgiveness is tax-free, but the reason and year of cancellation matter.
entries.legalExplanation: The 2023 textbook describes §108(f)(2) service conditions and an additional broadly applicable exclusion only for 2021–2025 under the then-current law. CURRENT LAW: Pub. L. 119-21 amended §108(f)(5) for discharges after 2025 to specified death/total permanent disability categories. Other §108(f) exclusions and applicable state tax rules must be examined separately. CURRENT LAW detail: §108(f)(5)(C) imposes an SSN-on-return condition for the specified post-2025 death/total-permanent-disability exclusion. Do not confuse the broader 2021–2025 tax rule with 2026 IDR forgiveness.

entries.title: Qualified principal residence CODI exclusion — expiration conditions
entries.summary: §108(a)(1)(E) has a statutory end-date: generally qualifying discharges before Jan. 1, 2026 or under qualifying pre-2026 written arrangements.
entries.laymanExplanation: A mortgage lender forgiving debt on your main home is not always tax-free, especially if forgiveness happens after 2025.
entries.legalExplanation: The textbook states relief through 2025. Current statutory text preserves it for qualifying discharge before Jan.1,2026 OR discharge subject to an arrangement entered into and evidenced in writing before that date; §108(h) limits qualified acquisition debt and requires relevant basis reduction.

topics.title: B. Loans and Cancellation of Debt — §§61 and 108
topics.description: Principal loans, cancellation of indebtedness, bankruptcy, insolvency and exclusions.
topics.assignmentSource: Fall 2026 Tax syllabus Week 7: pp259–290 and pp290–321; assigned material from 19th-edition casebook

entries.title: Contested liability doctrine — genuine dispute over debt
entries.summary: Some bona fide disputes resolved through settlement fix the amount of the original obligation rather than create CODI from 'forgiveness'.
entries.laymanExplanation: If you genuinely dispute owing $100,000 and settle the disputed claim for $30,000, the tax result may treat $30,000 as what you truly owed.
entries.legalExplanation: Zarin applies a contested-liability rationale to an unenforceable casino-marker obligation, treating $500k settlement as amount of debt for tax purposes. The textbook notes a circuit disagreement with Preslar, which limits the doctrine mainly to disputes over the original amount advanced rather than enforceability alone.

entries.title: Circuit split — Zarin versus Preslar
entries.summary: Courts disagree whether a good-faith contest over legal enforceability, rather than original loan amount, suffices to invoke contested liability.
entries.laymanExplanation: One court thought an illegal casino IOU dispute could avoid cancellation income. Another demanded a dispute about the amount originally received.
entries.legalExplanation: Zarin (3d Cir.) applied doctrine to good-faith contest about enforceability; Preslar v. Commissioner (10th Cir. 1999), cited but not reproduced, disagreed, reasoning a known initial amount treated as a loan should generally produce CODI when forgiven. Jurisdiction matters.

entries.title: Casino markers, gaming chips, and debt enforceability
entries.summary: Gaming markers evidence a casino credit arrangement; state law may affect whether the obligation is enforceable.
entries.laymanExplanation: Zarin signed IOUs for casino chips. The court examined whether those IOUs could legally be collected in New Jersey.
entries.legalExplanation: The Zarin majority applied §108(d)(1)'s debt definition and held the illegal casino markers were not enforceable liabilities; it also characterized chips as accounting mechanisms rather than property subject to the debt. The dissent argued they had real commercial value.

entries.title: Settlement of a disputed debt versus undisputed debt discount
entries.summary: A negotiated payment might either determine original liability (contest) or satisfy an established obligation for less (discharge).

entries.legalExplanation: Classify bona fide initial amount/enforceability dispute before mechanically calculating face less payment. The casebook contrasts Zarin, N. Sobel and Hall with Preslar (supporting authorities, not reproduced opinions).

entries.laymanExplanation: Gambling losses in one year don't automatically erase debt-forgiveness income in the next.

entries.title: Zarin v. Commissioner
entries.summary: No. Third Circuit reversed the Tax Court: the casino's asserted debt was not 'indebtedness' under §108(d)(1) as the majority read it, and the good-faith contested-liability settlement fixed the original debt amount at the $500,000 paid.
entries.laymanExplanation: A casino let a gambler run up $3.435 million of illegal credit. He settled for $500,000; the appeals court said there was no taxable debt forgiveness because the disputed obligation wasn't enforceable under state law.
entries.details: Full excerpt of this court opinion is reproduced in the assigned Week 7 textbook pages; supporting authorities merely cited in it do not receive separate briefs.
entries.facts: Resorts casino illegally continued lending gambling chips to David Zarin after New Jersey gambling regulators prohibited credit extensions. His markers/returned checks totaled $3,435,000, which the casino sued to collect. Zarin contested enforceability because the casino's credit practice violated state regulations. The parties settled for $500,000. IRS asserted $2,935,000 of 1981 CODI; the Tax Court agreed 11–8.
entries.issue: Did Zarin realize CODI equal to the difference between casino marker face amount and settlement after a genuine dispute over illegal credit?
entries.holding: No. Third Circuit reversed the Tax Court: the casino's asserted debt was not 'indebtedness' under §108(d)(1) as the majority read it, and the good-faith contested-liability settlement fixed the original debt amount at the $500,000 paid.
entries.reasoning: Majority reasoned (1) illegal credit unenforceable under New Jersey law did not create legally enforceable liability; (2) casino chips were an accounting mechanism, not property Zarin held subject to a debt; and (3) disputed-liability doctrine treats settlement as fixing amount cognizable, rather than forgiving a valid $3.435m principal. Judge Stapleton dissented: Zarin received gambling value on credit and settled a recognized claim for less, a real taxable benefit. Textbook notes the Tenth Circuit's Preslar rejected extending doctrine to disputes solely about enforceability.
entries.rule: On its unusual facts, a bona fide dispute over an unenforceable casino obligation can cause a settlement to fix the tax-recognized debt instead of producing CODI under the Third Circuit's analysis.
entries.exam: First determine the obligation, actual value/validity, state-law enforceability, and creditor/debtor treatment; then compute disputed settlement versus true forgiveness. Analyze jurisdiction; contrast Preslar.
entries.examApplication: First determine the obligation, actual value/validity, state-law enforceability, and creditor/debtor treatment; then compute disputed settlement versus true forgiveness. Analyze jurisdiction; contrast Preslar.
entries.examTrap: Do not generalize that simply disputing a clear $100k cash bank loan eliminates CODI. Zarin's broad contested-liability theory conflicts with Preslar in another circuit.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), reproduced opinion, syllabus Week 7 pp. 266–274

entries.title: Debt-financed property generally includes debt in cost basis
entries.summary: Acquisition cost for property generally includes purchase-money debt and assumed liabilities, not just cash paid.
entries.laymanExplanation: Buy a $2 million building with a $2 million loan: starting tax basis is usually $2 million, not zero.
entries.legalExplanation: The source treats cash, seller financing, third-party loans and preexisting liabilities as equivalent to fund property purchases, subject to genuine debt and excess nonrecourse debt concerns. §§1012, 1016 and related rules determine adjusted basis.

entries.title: Amount realized generally includes liabilities transferred or discharged
entries.summary: On disposition, amount realized can include nonrecourse mortgage balance assumed by buyer or relieved upon transfer.
entries.laymanExplanation: If someone takes your mortgaged building and takes over the $2 million debt, you're treated as receiving value even without a cash check.
entries.legalExplanation: The textbook illustrates a $2m basis property sold for $3m whether paid wholly in cash, wholly in debt, or $1m cash plus $2m assumed debt; each normally produces $3m amount realized and $1m gain. See §1001 and Reg. §1.1001-2.

entries.title: Adjusted basis after depreciation
entries.summary: Depreciation deductions generally reduce property adjusted basis, increasing later gain or reducing later loss.
entries.laymanExplanation: Claiming depreciation now lowers your tax cost later; you don't get to deduct the same expense twice.
entries.legalExplanation: Chapter 5 repeats §1016 logic: $100 cost minus $60 allowed depreciation gives $40 adjusted basis; selling for $35 creates $5 realized loss even though total economic cash decline is $65 (including prior $60 deductions). Depreciation deductions may have timing value.

entries.title: Recourse versus nonrecourse mortgage
entries.summary: Recourse permits creditor to seek borrower's personal assets; nonrecourse generally limits creditor to collateral.
entries.laymanExplanation: If a nonrecourse loan isn't paid, the lender takes the property and generally cannot pursue you for the shortfall.
entries.legalExplanation: The debt's enforceability affects who bears downside risk; under Crane and Tufts, genuine nonrecourse mortgage debt nonetheless can enter basis and amount realized. Distinguish separate issue of debt discharge on recourse deficiency.

entries.title: Crane v. Commissioner — nonrecourse debt included in basis and sale proceeds
entries.summary: A genuine nonrecourse mortgage equaling property value on acquisition is counted in cost basis and amount realized on transfer.
entries.laymanExplanation: A woman inherited an apartment property with a mortgage and sold it for a little cash plus debt relief. The mortgage counted in her tax math.
entries.legalExplanation: The casebook summarizes (does NOT reproduce) Crane, 331 U.S. 1 (1947): inherited property valued at $262,042.50, matching nonrecourse mortgage; after depreciation, taxpayer sold it subject to mortgage for $2,500 cash. Supreme Court rejected equity-only basis and equity-only sales proceeds, recognizing $23,502.60 gain under IRS computation. Footnote 37 reserved cases where debt exceeded FMV.

entries.summary: Crane left unresolved whether full nonrecourse debt counts in amount realized when it exceeds property value.
entries.laymanExplanation: Even if the property is worth less than the mortgage, do you still count the entire debt as sale proceeds? Tufts answers the key later question.
entries.legalExplanation: Crane reserved issue of worth-less-than-debt; Tufts later held full amount-realized inclusion for genuine nonrecourse loan originally included in basis. Separate initial overvaluation/sham acquisition issues remain.

entries.title: Commissioner v. Tufts — full nonrecourse debt in amount realized
entries.summary: When property subject to genuine nonrecourse debt is disposed of, relief of full debt can enter amount realized even if debt exceeds FMV.
entries.laymanExplanation: If you transfer a $1.4m building along with a $1.85m nonrecourse mortgage, you can be treated as having received $1.85m for tax purposes.
entries.legalExplanation: Tufts held nonrecourse financing included up front in basis is likewise included in amount realized when buyer assumes debt, even where FMV is lower; in the case, $1,851,500 liability against $1,455,740 adjusted basis gives approximately $395,760 realized gain on simplified mortgage-only computation.

entries.title: Justice O'Connor's Tufts bifurcation concurrence
entries.summary: A competing theory would split a transfer with excess nonrecourse debt into property sale at FMV plus CODI for debt excess.
entries.laymanExplanation: You could treat a transfer as selling property for its real value plus forgiving the leftover loan separately—but the Tufts majority didn't do that.
entries.legalExplanation: O'Connor concurred in result but explained a two-part recourse-debt-like analysis: property disposition value and separate discharge. Majority adopted full nonrecourse debt in amount realized given prior basis inclusion. Classify majority as controlling and concurrence as conceptual comparison.

entries.title: Commissioner v. Tufts
entries.summary: Yes. Supreme Court reversed Fifth Circuit and held full nonrecourse liability enters amount realized when debt was included in basis at acquisition, even though it exceeded property FMV at disposition.
entries.laymanExplanation: The partnership gave away an apartment complex worth less than its nonrecourse mortgage. The Supreme Court counted the entire mortgage, not merely the building's market value, as the amount realized.
entries.details: Full excerpt of this court opinion is reproduced in the assigned Week 7 textbook pages; supporting authorities merely cited in it do not receive separate briefs.
entries.facts: A partnership built a 120-unit apartment complex with a $1,851,500 nonrecourse mortgage, contributed only $44,212 in cash and claimed depreciation/operating deductions totaling $439,972. Its adjusted property basis at disposition was $1,455,740; FMV was at most $1,400,000. Partners transferred interests to Fred Bayles, who took the mortgage, reimbursing up to $250 in expenses per partner. They claimed a loss; IRS treated full mortgage relief as part of proceeds.
entries.issue: On disposal of property securing nonrecourse debt, is the full outstanding debt included in §1001 amount realized when its face amount exceeds property FMV?
entries.holding: Yes. Supreme Court reversed Fifth Circuit and held full nonrecourse liability enters amount realized when debt was included in basis at acquisition, even though it exceeded property FMV at disposition.
entries.reasoning: Crane had counted the genuine nonrecourse loan up front in property basis. Transactional consistency requires counting full debt when disposing of the property and escaping repayment. The taxpayer cannot retain tax benefits of debt-financed depreciable basis without reciprocal amount-realized consequences. Justice O'Connor concurred in result but preferred bifurcating property sale at FMV and separate cancellation income for excess debt.
entries.rule: Upon transfer of property subject to genuine nonrecourse debt fully reflected in basis, include the full unpaid debt in §1001 amount realized, even if debt exceeds FMV.
entries.exam: Compute total amount realized including entire nonrecourse debt relief; subtract adjusted basis. In given data, $1,851,500 − $1,455,740 ≈ $395,760 gain before any other adjustments. Distinguish initial sham/overvaluation and cases involving recourse deficiency debt.
entries.examApplication: Compute total amount realized including entire nonrecourse debt relief; subtract adjusted basis. In given data, $1,851,500 − $1,455,740 ≈ $395,760 gain before any other adjustments. Distinguish initial sham/overvaluation and cases involving recourse deficiency debt.
entries.examTrap: Do not use FMV of $1.4m to cap nonrecourse mortgage relief. Crane footnote 37's reserved issue is resolved by Tufts on these bona fide financing facts.

entries.summary: When a buyer takes property worth less than face amount of nonrecourse acquisition debt, basis treatment depends on whether the debt/purchase is genuine.

entries.summary: A stated purchase funded by unrealistic nonrecourse debt may fail to be a bona fide sale.

entries.title: Distressed property acquisition and partial nonrecourse basis
entries.summary: A genuine acquirer can acquire collateral worth less than its mortgage; courts differ over treating full face of debt as cost at that moment.
entries.laymanExplanation: Buying a property worth $400,000 subject to a $1m nonrecourse debt raises a real basis question even if the sale is genuine.
entries.legalExplanation: Pleasant Summit Land Corp. (3d Cir. 1988), cited in textbook, allowed inclusion of indebtedness up to the property's FMV on acquisition on its facts. Basis and later amount-realized treatment should be considered consistently; partial repayments pose additional unresolved timing/amount questions.

entries.title: Midstream acquisition of underwater nonrecourse property
entries.summary: A buyer can take over a property and its nonrecourse debt for reasons other than immediate FMV, such as expected appreciation.

entries.title: Net gift — donee pays donor's gift tax (Diedrich)
entries.summary: When a donor conditions a property gift on the donee paying donor's legal gift-tax obligation, donor realizes taxable gain to extent taxes paid exceed donor's adjusted basis.
entries.laymanExplanation: You give your child valuable stock but make them pay your gift tax. Their paying your bill can be like paying you for part of the stock.
entries.legalExplanation: Diedrich treats the conditional gift as part-sale/part-gift: payment of donor's legally owed gift tax confers an economic benefit (Old Colony principle). Under court's formula, gain realized = gift tax paid by donee less donor adjusted basis, if positive. No loss recognized where that difference is negative under Reg. §1.1001-1(e).

entries.title: Gift tax liability and donee assumption
entries.summary: Federal gift tax generally falls on the donor, even where contract requires the recipient to pay it.
entries.laymanExplanation: If a parent makes a taxable gift, the tax bill is legally the parent's. Letting the child pay it is a valuable benefit to the parent.
entries.legalExplanation: Diedrich relies on donor liability under §2502 and Old Colony's third-party discharge principle; the parties may shift economic burden by contract without erasing the donor's receipt of a benefit.
entries.details: Diedrich relies on donor liability under §2502 and Old Colony's third-party discharge principle; the parties may shift economic burden by contract without erasing the donor's receipt of a benefit.

entries.title: Net gifts do not create deductible donor loss when consideration is below basis
entries.summary: A conditional gift tax payment below the donor's basis does not create ordinary recognized loss.
entries.laymanExplanation: If you give stock with $25k basis and the recipient pays $20k gift tax, you generally can't claim a $5k tax loss.
entries.legalExplanation: Reg. §1.1001-1(e) disallows recognition of loss on part-sale/part-gift; gain recognized to extent received amount exceeds the property’s adjusted basis under Diedrich. The text raises related basis allocation question for charitable bargain sales under §1011(b), a distinct rule.

entries.title: Bargain sale to charity — allocation of adjusted basis
entries.summary: When appreciated property is sold below FMV to charity, basis is allocated between sale and gift components.

entries.title: Why Diedrich is partly a sale despite donative intention
entries.summary: The donor's generosity does not negate the objective benefit of having someone else pay a debt.
entries.laymanExplanation: You can make a real gift and still receive a taxable financial advantage if the recipient pays your own tax bill.
entries.legalExplanation: The source contrasts the donor's motive to give with the recognized economic benefit of the donee's payment. Whether gift-law exemptions should change this result is for Congress. This is background, not a separate exclusion.
