entries.title: Diedrich v. Commissioner
entries.summary: Yes. Supreme Court affirmed taxability of the amount by which gift tax paid by donees exceeds donor adjusted basis: $62,992 − $51,073 = $11,919.
entries.laymanExplanation: Parents gave stock to their children but made the children pay the parents' gift-tax bill. Paying the parents' obligation counted as taxable consideration for part of the transfer.
entries.details: Full excerpt of this court opinion is reproduced in the assigned Week 7 textbook pages; supporting authorities merely cited in it do not receive separate briefs.
entries.facts: Victor and Frances Diedrich transferred roughly 85,000 stock shares to three children. Transfers were conditioned on children paying the federal and state gift taxes legally owed by the donors. The donors' adjusted basis in the stock was $51,073; the children paid $62,992 of gift tax. Taxpayers argued generosity meant the receipt should not produce taxable income.
entries.issue: Does a donor realize gain when the donee agrees to discharge the donor's gift-tax obligation as condition of receiving the gift?
entries.holding: Yes. Supreme Court affirmed taxability of the amount by which gift tax paid by donees exceeds donor adjusted basis: $62,992 − $51,073 = $11,919.
entries.reasoning: Under §2502 the tax is the donor's obligation. A third party's payment of one's legally owed tax is an economic benefit analogous to Old Colony's employer-paid tax. The transfer is effectively part sale (for value of debt relieved) and part gift. Donative intent does not negate donor's separate economic benefit; Congress would need to provide any special exclusion.
entries.rule: A net gift conditioned on donee payment of donor's gift-tax debt yields donor gain equal to donee-paid tax minus donor's adjusted basis, to extent positive; loss on such part-sale/part-gift is generally disallowed.
entries.exam: Ask which party legally owes gift tax, who actually pays, stock basis, gift tax amount and resulting recognized gain; check Reg. §1.1001-1(e) loss disallowance.
entries.examApplication: Ask which party legally owes gift tax, who actually pays, stock basis, gift tax amount and resulting recognized gain; check Reg. §1.1001-1(e) loss disallowance.
entries.examTrap: Do not confuse gift exclusion to child under §102 with tax effect of child's payment of parent's debt; the Old Colony case is cited authority, not a separately reproduced opinion.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), reproduced opinion, syllabus Week 7 pp. 294–296

entries.summary: Interest paid or economically earned on loans is generally gross income to the lender; borrower deductibility depends on separate provisions.
entries.laymanExplanation: The lender pays tax on qualifying interest earned; the borrower may deduct some interest but not necessarily all.

entries.title: Original issue discount (OID)
entries.summary: OID is the excess of a debt instrument's stated redemption price at maturity over its issue price, representing economically deferred interest.
entries.laymanExplanation: Buy a bond for $100 and get $121 in two years: the $21 extra is interest even though no cash arrives in Year 1.
entries.legalExplanation: Under §1273(a) and related rules, OID can result when redemption exceeds the initial issue price. Relevant payment exclusions, stated-interest standards and de minimis exceptions may alter the technical amount. For a zero-coupon bond, the source's $100->$121 over 2 years implies 10% annual effective yield.
entries.details: Under §1273(a) and related rules, OID can result when redemption exceeds the initial issue price. Relevant payment exclusions, stated-interest standards and de minimis exceptions may alter the technical amount. For a zero-coupon bond, the source's $100->$121 over 2 years implies 10% annual effective yield.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Tax syllabus Week 7 pp. 297–298

entries.title: Compound interest and yield to maturity
entries.summary: Unpaid interest itself earns interest, so interest accruals grow over the loan's life.
entries.laymanExplanation: At 10%, $100 becomes $110 after one year and $121 after two; the second year's interest is $11, not $10.
entries.legalExplanation: Constant effective yield r compounds as end balance = starting balance(1+r)^n; for 2-year $100 issue and $121 redemption, annual economic interest $10 then $11. Over 30 years, $100 grows to about $1,744.94 at 10%, with far more interest accrued late.
entries.details: Constant effective yield r compounds as end balance = starting balance(1+r)^n; for 2-year $100 issue and $121 redemption, annual economic interest $10 then $11. Over 30 years, $100 grows to about $1,744.94 at 10%, with far more interest accrued late.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Tax syllabus Week 7 pp. 298

entries.title: Straight-line versus constant-yield interest accrual
entries.summary: Straight-line spreads interest evenly; constant-yield allocates more interest to later periods as unpaid interest compounds.
entries.laymanExplanation: On a $100 to $121 bond, straight-line charges $10.50 each year, but the real economic amounts are $10 and $11.
entries.legalExplanation: The casebook traces pre-1954 deferral/capital-gain treatment, 1954 interest-character correction, 1969 straight-line and 1982 compound-yield legislation. Modern OID uses economic accrual for cash- and accrual-method holders, subject to statutory rules.

entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Tax syllabus Week 7 pp. 298–301

entries.title: IRC §§1272–1275 — current inclusion of accrued OID
entries.summary: Holders generally include OID as interest annually using yield/compounding even if no cash coupon is received.
entries.laymanExplanation: You may owe tax on interest your zero-coupon bond earned even though the bond won't pay you until maturity.
entries.legalExplanation: Sections 1272–1275 require accrual of a debt instrument's OID, with computations based on issue price, stated redemption price, yield and applicable semiannual compounding periods. The borrower’s corresponding deduction, if allowable, follows statutory limitations. OID increases bond basis to prevent double taxation at redemption.

The borrower’s corresponding deduction, if allowable, follows statutory limitations. OID increases bond basis to prevent double taxation at redemption.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Tax syllabus Week 7 pp. 301–303
entries.examTrap: The cash method by itself does NOT permit waiting until maturity to recognize taxable OID.

entries.title: IRC §1274 — imputed interest when a note is exchanged for property
entries.summary: If property is sold for deferred payments bearing too little stated interest, discount promised payments at an applicable federal rate to determine issue price and OID.
entries.laymanExplanation: Selling a building for a $5m IOU paying only 8% when the required rate is 10% means some of that $5m is really delayed interest.
entries.legalExplanation: The book example: $5m ten-year promissory note, nominal coupon $400k per year (8%), AFR 10%; PV of payments $4,385,543 and OID $614,457. First-year economic interest 10%×$4,385,543=$438,554; cash stated $400k; $38,554 OID accrues. Actual computations use AFR published under §1274(d) and regulations.
entries.details: The book example: $5m ten-year promissory note, nominal coupon $400k per year (8%), AFR 10%; PV of payments $4,385,543 and OID $614,457. First-year economic interest 10%×$4,385,543=$438,554; cash stated $400k; $38,554 OID accrues. Actual computations use AFR published under §1274(d) and regulations.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Tax syllabus Week 7 pp. 302–303

entries.title: Applicable Federal Rate (AFR)
entries.summary: Treasury-published reference interest rates used to determine deemed interest on certain below-market deferred-payment obligations.
entries.laymanExplanation: If your note charges 8% but federal law measures interest at 10%, the tax calculation may treat the difference as unpaid interest.
entries.legalExplanation: Under §1274(d), the AFR is published periodically for varying maturities and is generally based on U.S. Treasury obligations. Compare adequate stated interest with governing AFR; the rate governs imputed principal/interest split for qualifying property-financed notes.
entries.details: Under §1274(d), the AFR is published periodically for varying maturities and is generally based on U.S. Treasury obligations. Compare adequate stated interest with governing AFR; the rate governs imputed principal/interest split for qualifying property-financed notes.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Tax syllabus Week 7 pp. 302–303

entries.title: Market discount — purchasing an existing bond below adjusted redemption value
entries.summary: Gain attributable to purchasing a bond cheaply after issue may be treated as ordinary interest rather than capital gain.
entries.laymanExplanation: Buy an older $1,000 bond for $727 because its old coupon is low; the discount when repaid may count as ordinary income.
entries.legalExplanation: The text's existing $1,000 bond pays a 3% annual $30 coupon, has four years left and price $727 due to new 12% market rate. The $273 discount recognized on redemption is generally ordinary income under §§1276–1278, rather than capital gain, subject to detailed rules.

entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Tax syllabus Week 7 pp. 303–304

entries.title: IRC §483 — unstated interest in certain exempted deferred sales
entries.summary: When OID provisions don't apply to certain sales, §483 may recharacterize part of gain as ordinary unstated interest at payment.
entries.laymanExplanation: A house seller paid a million dollars five years later hasn't earned a million dollars of house-sale profit; some payment represents interest.
entries.legalExplanation: The source illustrates personal residence basis $400k, deferred $1m cash payment in five years, AFR 10%; PV payment $620,921 and unstated interest $379,079. Gross $600k difference is allocated $379,079 interest and $220,921 potential property gain. §121 could apply only to qualifying property gain, not interest.

Gross $600k difference is allocated $379,079 interest and $220,921 potential property gain. §121 could apply only to qualifying property gain, not interest.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Tax syllabus Week 7 pp. 304
entries.examTrap: Do not apply §121 exclusion to the amount of gross proceeds recharacterized as interest.

entries.title: Why precise OID timing matters for mismatched counterparties
entries.summary: Early over-deductions can be exploited when high-rate taxable borrowers pair with exempt low-tax lenders.
entries.laymanExplanation: A tax-exempt university can lend to a high-bracket borrower; a bad formula may help the borrower deduct too much early without someone else paying matching tax.
entries.legalExplanation: The source contrasts symmetric 30%-rate transactions with tax-exempt or foreign lenders. Straight-line OID overmeasures early interest for lenders (who may not be taxed) and for borrowers (who may deduct), enabling arbitrage even if economic loan flows offset.
entries.details: The source contrasts symmetric 30%-rate transactions with tax-exempt or foreign lenders. Straight-line OID overmeasures early interest for lenders (who may not be taxed) and for borrowers (who may deduct), enabling arbitrage even if economic loan flows offset.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Tax syllabus Week 7 pp. 299–301

topics.title: D. Interest Income, OID & Compounding
topics.description: Economic accrual of interest, §§1272–1275, AFR and bond discount.
topics.assignmentSource: Assigned textbook Week 7 pp259–321; later pp323–340 not provided

entries.title: IRC §103 — interest on qualifying state/local government bonds excluded
entries.summary: Interest on eligible state or local obligations generally is excluded from federal gross income, subject to statutory restrictions.
entries.laymanExplanation: A qualifying municipal bond might pay 8% interest that you keep free of federal income tax.
entries.legalExplanation: Section 103 provides an exclusion for qualifying obligations issued by state governments or political subdivisions, subject to private activity, arbitrage, registration and other constraints under §§103, 141–151 and 149. The exclusion generally subsidizes issuers by lowering borrowing rates.
entries.details: Section 103 provides an exclusion for qualifying obligations issued by state governments or political subdivisions, subject to private activity, arbitrage, registration and other constraints under §§103, 141–151 and 149. The exclusion generally subsidizes issuers by lowering borrowing rates.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Tax syllabus Week 7 pp. 304–305

entries.title: Municipal bond, issuer, bondholder and implicit tax
entries.summary: Municipal bonds are debts of state/local issuers; implicit tax is a lower yield demanded in exchange for exemption.
entries.laymanExplanation: If muni bonds pay 8% and taxable bonds pay 10%, investors effectively accept a 20% yield haircut to get tax-free interest.
entries.legalExplanation: Implicit tax fraction = (taxable yield − exempt yield)/taxable yield; relative after-tax attractiveness depends on investor marginal rate and comparable investment risk. This is economic incidence, not money sent to the IRS.
entries.details: Implicit tax fraction = (taxable yield − exempt yield)/taxable yield; relative after-tax attractiveness depends on investor marginal rate and comparable investment risk. This is economic incidence, not money sent to the IRS.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Tax syllabus Week 7 pp. 304–306

entries.title: Tax clientele effects
entries.summary: Investors with marginal tax rates above the implied municipal bond implicit tax generally prefer the exempt bond, holding risk constant.
entries.laymanExplanation: If you're in a 30% bracket, a 10% taxable bond nets 7%, so an 8% tax-free bond looks better. A tax-free investor may prefer the 10% bond.
entries.legalExplanation: The casebook illustrates 10% taxable vs 8% exempt; break-even rate 20%. Different brackets cause investors to self-select, potentially reducing portfolio diversification and affecting economic returns.
entries.details: The casebook illustrates 10% taxable vs 8% exempt; break-even rate 20%. Different brackets cause investors to self-select, potentially reducing portfolio diversification and affecting economic returns.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Tax syllabus Week 7 pp. 305–307

entries.title: Issuer subsidy versus investor windfall
entries.summary: A municipal exclusion may benefit both issuer (lower interest costs) and high-bracket holders (extra after-tax returns).
entries.laymanExplanation: A city pays $2m less bond interest each year, but the federal government might give up $3m in taxes; the difference goes to investors.
entries.legalExplanation: On $100m bonds, issuer interest at 8% instead of 10% saves $2m. At a hypothetical 30% federal rate on the alternative taxable $10m yield, $3m forgone taxes exceeds issuer's $2m benefit by $1m; compare direct government subsidy. This is stylized, not a revenue forecast.
entries.details: On $100m bonds, issuer interest at 8% instead of 10% saves $2m. At a hypothetical 30% federal rate on the alternative taxable $10m yield, $3m forgone taxes exceeds issuer's $2m benefit by $1m; compare direct government subsidy. This is stylized, not a revenue forecast.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Tax syllabus Week 7 pp. 305–306

entries.title: Qualified private-activity municipal bonds have extra restrictions
entries.summary: Tax exemption is not automatic when bond proceeds effectively finance private businesses.
entries.laymanExplanation: A city can't simply issue tax-free bonds for any private company's project and call them municipal bonds.
entries.legalExplanation: The source distinguishes government-purpose schools/roads/sewers from private-activity bonds, generally denied exemption unless exceptions apply, such as qualifying airports, ports, mass transit, water/sewage facilities, eligible mortgages, small issues and charitable projects. §§141–151 and §146 volume caps apply; some private activity interest can be subject to AMT.

entries.title: South Carolina v. Baker — constitutional backdrop (cited case only)
entries.summary: The Supreme Court rejected a categorical constitutional immunity from federal income tax on state/local bond interest.
entries.laymanExplanation: Municipal bonds aren't tax-free because the Constitution always forbids federal tax; Congress gives the exclusion in the Code.
entries.legalExplanation: The book summarizes South Carolina v. Baker, 485 U.S. 505 (1988), sustaining bond-registration-related conditions now in §149(a). It is a citation/discussion, not a reproduced opinion, so no full brief is added.

entries.title: Tax-exempt bond arbitrage restrictions — §§148 and 265(a)(2)
entries.summary: Issuers and investors face limits on borrowing at taxable-deduction rates to invest at tax-free yields.
entries.laymanExplanation: You can't generally borrow money, deduct all the interest, and invest the proceeds in tax-free bonds to create artificial tax profits.
entries.legalExplanation: §148 limits issuer arbitrage using proceeds invested at high taxable yields; §265(a)(2) disallows interest deductions on money borrowed/carrying debt to purchase tax-exempt obligations in specified circumstances. Book hypothetical: borrow $1m at 10%, earn 8% tax-free, 30% bracket => apparent $10k after-tax gain absent restrictions.
entries.details: §148 limits issuer arbitrage using proceeds invested at high taxable yields; §265(a)(2) disallows interest deductions on money borrowed/carrying debt to purchase tax-exempt obligations in specified circumstances. entries.title: IRC §135 — qualified U.S. savings bond education-interest exclusion
entries.summary: Certain qualifying U.S. savings bond interest may be excludable when statutory eligibility and higher-education expenses requirements are met.
entries.laymanExplanation: Some savings bond interest used for eligible education costs can be tax-free, but income and purchase rules matter.
entries.legalExplanation: The book discusses §135 and historic 2022 phaseout figures; eligibility uses particular U.S. savings bonds, taxpayer/beneficiary, tuition, qualified expenses and adjusted-income phaseout requirements. The 2022 thresholds quoted are not usable for 2026 returns.
entries.details: The book discusses §135 and historic 2022 phaseout figures; eligibility uses particular U.S. savings bonds, taxpayer/beneficiary, tuition, qualified expenses and adjusted-income phaseout requirements. The 2022 thresholds quoted are not usable for 2026 returns.

entries.title: Build America Bonds as historical alternative subsidy
entries.summary: A temporary federal program made bond interest taxable while giving credits or direct payments to subsidize borrowing.
entries.laymanExplanation: Instead of offering tax-free interest, Congress temporarily tried helping issuers directly.
entries.legalExplanation: The book notes the 2009–2010 Build America Bonds program and 35% tax credit/direct payment variants. These expired, so they are historical policy comparison rather than a current general exclusion.
entries.details: The book notes the 2009–2010 Build America Bonds program and 35% tax credit/direct payment variants. These expired, so they are historical policy comparison rather than a current general exclusion.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Tax syllabus Week 7 pp. 306–307

entries.title: Policy questions on municipal bonds
entries.summary: Tax exemption may be less efficient than direct grants when high-income bondholders capture part of the benefit.
entries.laymanExplanation: The government might lose more tax money than the city saves in borrowing costs.
entries.legalExplanation: The source asks whether desired benefits are for government borrowers or private investors, how supply/demand affects incidence and whether tax relief encourages desirable local spending. This is deeper background, not an operative test.

entries.title: Life insurance, term insurance and whole life
entries.summary: Life insurance is a contractual promise to pay a death benefit upon insured's death; products vary in mortality-risk and savings components.
entries.laymanExplanation: Term life is primarily protection if you die during the covered period; whole life also tends to build investment value.
entries.legalExplanation: The text identifies mortality risk (time of death) and savings/interest growth. A one-year trip policy mostly covers mortality risk; a whole-life policy with an upfront premium and later death benefit combines risk shifting and investment yield. A contract must meet §7702's requirements to receive federal life-insurance classification.
entries.details: The text identifies mortality risk (time of death) and savings/interest growth. A one-year trip policy mostly covers mortality risk; a whole-life policy with an upfront premium and later death benefit combines risk shifting and investment yield. A contract must meet §7702's requirements to receive federal life-insurance classification.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), syllabus Week 7 printed pp. 311–314

entries.title: IRC §101(a)(1) — death benefits generally excluded from recipient's income
entries.summary: Amounts paid by reason of death of an insured under a qualifying life-insurance contract generally are excluded from gross income.
entries.laymanExplanation: A beneficiary receiving a qualifying $1 million life-insurance death benefit generally doesn't pay federal income tax on it.
entries.legalExplanation: §101(a) provides a favorable exclusion for qualifying life insurance proceeds received because of death, subject to transfer-for-value and other exceptions. Premiums paid for personal life insurance generally are not deductible; policy buildup is not taxed each year under ordinary terms.
entries.details: §101(a) provides a favorable exclusion for qualifying life insurance proceeds received because of death, subject to transfer-for-value and other exceptions. Premiums paid for personal life insurance generally are not deductible; policy buildup is not taxed each year under ordinary terms.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), syllabus Week 7 printed pp. 312–315
entries.examTrap: Insurance payout exclusion depends on a qualifying life-insurance contract and statutory exceptions, not any investment merely labeled 'insurance'.

entries.title: IRC §7702 — genuine life insurance versus disguised investment
entries.summary: A contract with no meaningful mortality-risk element can fail to qualify as life insurance for §101 treatment.
entries.laymanExplanation: A bond that pays back your $100k plus interest whenever you die isn't automatically tax-free life insurance.
entries.legalExplanation: The book gives a hypothetical 'life insurance' contract paying only principal compounded at 10% until date of death, with no distinct mortality bet. Such an arrangement may fail the substantive statutory §7702 definition; ordinary debt-interest treatment becomes relevant.
entries.details: The book gives a hypothetical 'life insurance' contract paying only principal compounded at 10% until date of death, with no distinct mortality bet. Such an arrangement may fail the substantive statutory §7702 definition; ordinary debt-interest treatment becomes relevant.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), syllabus Week 7 printed pp. 313–314

entries.title: Premium and death benefit
entries.summary: Premium is the money paid to obtain insurance protection; death benefit is the promised payout to beneficiary.
entries.laymanExplanation: You pay the insurance company a premium; if the insured dies, it pays the named beneficiary.
entries.legalExplanation: The source contrasts nondeductibility of personal premiums with exclusion of qualifying death proceeds. Company deductions for insurance on key executives may be restricted by §264; group coverage for employees has separate §79 wage rules.

entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), syllabus Week 7 printed pp. 312–315

entries.title: Group-term life insurance — IRC §79
entries.summary: Employer-paid qualified group-term life insurance coverage up to a statutory amount may be excluded from employee compensation, with excess coverage potentially taxable.
entries.laymanExplanation: Your employer may provide your first $50,000 of qualifying group life insurance without it counting as taxable pay.
entries.legalExplanation: The book describes §79's first $50,000 group-term coverage exclusion and differentiates taxable employer-paid premiums for additional protection. Corporate-owned life insurance premiums with corporation as beneficiary are generally denied deduction under §264(a)(1).

entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), syllabus Week 7 printed pp. 315

entries.title: IRC §101(a)(2) — transfer-for-value limit
entries.summary: Buying an existing life-insurance policy for valuable consideration may limit the death-benefit exclusion unless a statutory exception applies.
entries.laymanExplanation: If someone buys another person's life-insurance policy as an investment, they may not get the whole payout tax-free.
entries.legalExplanation: The reading notes transfer-for-value restriction and exceptions for certain carryover-basis transfers, transfers to insured, partner, partnership or insured-controlled corporation; gifts and bequests are not purchased transfers. Modern statutory notice/reporting and other limits may apply.

Modern statutory notice/reporting and other limits may apply.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), syllabus Week 7 printed pp. 315

entries.title: IRC §101(g) — qualifying accelerated death benefits
entries.summary: Certain benefits or viatical settlements for terminally/chronically ill insureds are treated as death-related and may be excluded.
entries.laymanExplanation: Someone with a qualifying serious illness may access certain life-insurance value before death without ordinary income inclusion.
entries.legalExplanation: The source mentions qualifying terminal/chronically ill status, authorized viatical settlement providers, §101(g) and §7702B conditions. Not every policy surrender or sale is automatically excludable.
entries.details: The source mentions qualifying terminal/chronically ill status, authorized viatical settlement providers, §101(g) and §7702B conditions. Not every policy surrender or sale is automatically excludable.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), syllabus Week 7 printed pp. 315

entries.title: Life-insurance tax benefit from savings inside policy
entries.summary: Investment buildup may escape income tax while held, and qualifying proceeds are excluded, unlike OID bond interest.
entries.laymanExplanation: Whole-life insurance may allow the invested value to grow without annual interest taxation and ultimately pay a tax-free death benefit.
entries.legalExplanation: The book's one-premium example: $80,000 premium, $1m death payout in approximately 50 years at a hypothetical 5% interest rate; present value approximates premium. The tax difference reflects §101(a)'s favorable treatment of savings alongside mortality protection.

entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), syllabus Week 7 printed pp. 313–314

entries.title: Is life insurance different from other investments?
entries.summary: Life-insurance subsidy may encourage protection but benefit high-bracket savers and insurers disproportionately.
entries.laymanExplanation: Why does an insurance policy's growth get tax treatment that a bank CD can't? That's a tax-policy debate.
entries.legalExplanation: The book considers valuation, privacy/administrability, insurance uptake, costs/commissions, and whether the cap or taxation of insurer reserves would better target support.

topics.title: F. Life Insurance — §101 and Tax-Favored Saving
topics.description: Mortality risk, §101 death benefit exclusion, basis/premiums and transfer-for-value.
topics.assignmentSource: Week 7 assigned 19th-ed casebook pp259–321; remaining pp323–340 not yet supplied

entries.title: Annuity, annuitant, life annuity and term annuity
entries.summary: An annuity pays specified amounts at intervals; a term annuity lasts a fixed period, while a life annuity continues while recipient lives.
entries.laymanExplanation: A term annuity pays you for ten years; a life annuity pays as long as you live.
entries.legalExplanation: The owner/recipient is annuitant. A life annuity includes a longevity bet; issuer uses life expectancy and interest assumptions to price payments. Both can combine return of investment and taxable income.
entries.details: The owner/recipient is annuitant. A life annuity includes a longevity bet; issuer uses life expectancy and interest assumptions to price payments. Both can combine return of investment and taxable income.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), syllabus Week 7 printed pp. 315–316

entries.title: IRC §72(b) — exclusion ratio for annuity payments
entries.summary: A qualifying annuitant excludes the portion of each payment representing recovery of investment in the contract; remaining amount is included.
entries.laymanExplanation: If you paid $100k for payments totaling $200k, half of each payment may return your own money tax-free.
entries.legalExplanation: Exclusion ratio = investment in contract ÷ expected return. In book's life annuity, $100k paid at age 60, $20k annual payments from age 70, ten expected payments = $200k expected total; 50% exclusion ($10k per $20k check), 50% taxable ($10k), subject to §72 nuances.
entries.details: Exclusion ratio = investment in contract ÷ expected return. In book's life annuity, $100k paid at age 60, $20k annual payments from age 70, ten expected payments = $200k expected total; 50% exclusion ($10k per $20k check), 50% taxable ($10k), subject to §72 nuances.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), syllabus Week 7 printed pp. 316

entries.title: Annuity buildup and interest-deferral advantage
entries.summary: Unlike OID, value may grow inside a deferred annuity before distributions without annual income inclusion for the owner.
entries.laymanExplanation: An annuity can grow for years before paying out; an OID bond may trigger income tax on interest every year even without paying cash.
entries.legalExplanation: The reading compares a $100k annuity purchased at 60 with payouts starting at 70 to bonds accruing taxable OID, and contrasts rate/fee differences. Deferral is not an overall exclusion of all payouts.

entries.title: Annuity exclusion ratio versus economic cost recovery
entries.summary: The straight-line exclusion ratio can delay recognition compared with economically accruing interest on a bank balance.
entries.laymanExplanation: Getting equal $15k payments over ten years may have a different annual taxable interest pattern than a bank account with same economics.
entries.legalExplanation: The book compares persons B and C each investing $100k and receiving $15k per year for 10 years. A §72 annuity exclusion can result in a constant $5k inclusion per year; separate bank withdrawals contain front-loaded interest income, even though both generate $50k total gain.

entries.title: IRC §72(b)(2)–(3) — payments after or before expected life
entries.summary: When cost basis has been fully recovered, further annuity payments become fully taxable; eligible unrecovered investment on early death can be deducted under statutory conditions.
entries.laymanExplanation: If you live much longer than expected, later checks may become fully taxable; if you die early, an unrecovered contribution may still count for a deduction.
entries.legalExplanation: The source explains how §72(b)(2) includes full additional payments after cost recovery and §72(b)(3) handles unrecovered investment when annuity payments cease at death, with applicable statutory restrictions.
entries.details: The source explains how §72(b)(2) includes full additional payments after cost recovery and §72(b)(3) handles unrecovered investment when annuity payments cease at death, with applicable statutory restrictions.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), syllabus Week 7 printed pp. 317

entries.title: IRC §72(q) — additional 10% tax on certain premature annuity distributions
entries.summary: Certain nonqualified annuity distributions before age 59½ may bear an additional 10% tax unless a statutory exception applies.
entries.laymanExplanation: Cash out a tax-favored annuity too early and you may owe an extra penalty on the taxable portion.
entries.legalExplanation: The book notes §72(q) applies to certain early or nonperiodic distributions and loans from annuity contracts, with exceptions such as distributions after age 59½ and specified permitted payment streams. Do not assume penalty on entire principal/basis amount.

entries.title: Annuity wrapper compared with direct mutual fund savings
entries.summary: Deferral advantages may outweigh insurance-company fees, creating a tax-driven product choice.
entries.laymanExplanation: A mutual fund inside an annuity might be taxed more favorably than the same fund held directly, but fees can erase the advantage.
entries.legalExplanation: The source poses neutrality and distributional questions about tax-favored annuity wrappers, insurance intermediaries, investor sophistication and fees. Background, not a separate Code exclusion.

topics.title: F. Annuities — §72 Exclusion Ratio and Deferral
topics.description: Term/life annuities, tax-deferral, basis recovery and early distributions.
topics.assignmentSource: Week 7 assigned 19th-ed casebook pp259–321; remaining pp323–340 not yet supplied

entries.title: IRC §1259 — constructive sale of appreciated financial positions
entries.summary: Certain offsetting hedges are treated as a taxable sale of an appreciated financial position even though taxpayer retains legal ownership.
entries.laymanExplanation: You can't always avoid capital-gains tax by keeping your stock on paper while locking in its sale value through bets against the same stock.
entries.legalExplanation: The book explains §1259's deemed realization for specified positions: short sale of same/substantially identical property, certain offsetting notional principal contracts, forward/futures contracts delivering same/substantially identical property, and designated substantially equivalent transactions under regulations. Recognized gain equals hypothetical FMV disposition amount, subject to statutory exceptions.
entries.details: The book explains §1259's deemed realization for specified positions: short sale of same/substantially identical property, certain offsetting notional principal contracts, forward/futures contracts delivering same/substantially identical property, and designated substantially equivalent transactions under regulations. Recognized gain equals hypothetical FMV disposition amount, subject to statutory exceptions.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), syllabus Week 7 printed pp. 318–321
entries.examTrap: Hedging can produce §1259 realization without an ordinary transfer of title; identify type of offset and current law.

entries.title: Short sale and short-against-the-box
entries.summary: A short sale borrows securities and sells them now, with an obligation to return substantially identical shares later; short-against-the-box pairs short position with already owned appreciated stock.
entries.laymanExplanation: You own 1,000 shares but sell 1,000 borrowed identical shares. If stock falls, the short gains as your owned shares lose value.
entries.legalExplanation: The chapter's Eileen example: 1,000 ABC shares basis $10,000 and FMV $90,000. Selling borrowed ABC shares at $90k yields cash while the owned long shares hedge the obligation to return borrowed stock. The offsetting positions approximate a cash sale economically; §1259 can deem gain.

Selling borrowed ABC shares at $90k yields cash while the owned long shares hedge the obligation to return borrowed stock. The offsetting positions approximate a cash sale economically; §1259 can deem gain.

entries.title: Offsetting positions, long and short exposure
entries.summary: A long position profits from rising price; a short position profits from declining price; pairing can substantially eliminate market exposure.
entries.laymanExplanation: If your investment gains $10k when price rises but your short position loses $10k, you've locked in the current value.
entries.legalExplanation: The source uses long stock plus short borrowed stock and collars to illustrate monetization of appreciation without surrendering legal ownership. §1259 addresses selected hedges that act like sales for economic purposes.

entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), syllabus Week 7 printed pp. 319–321

entries.title: Zero-cost collar, put and call options
entries.summary: A collar buys downside protection with a put and sells upside above a call strike, sometimes with approximately offsetting option prices.
entries.laymanExplanation: You keep your $500m stock but agree to cap profit at $510m and lock in a minimum around $490m.
entries.legalExplanation: The book's Ahmed example: XYZ founder stock basis $10k, FMV $500m; buy put at $490m, write call at $510m (zero-cost). This narrows exposure without selling shares. §1259(c)(1)(E) leaves specified substantially equivalent transactions to regulations; the source states regulations not issued as of its publication and reviews legislative history factors.

entries.title: Constructive-sale collar treatment and missing regulations (book's era)
entries.summary: The precise effect of a collar may depend on statutory tests, later guidance and facts; the book describes uncertainty about §1259(c)(1)(E).
entries.laymanExplanation: A collar isn't automatically either taxable or tax-free just because it uses options. How tightly it locks in the price matters.
entries.legalExplanation: The assigned text cites a legislative excerpt on price gap, volatility, duration and retained dividends, while noting no §1259 regulations as of 2022. This should not be presented as a categorical safe harbor for any width of collar; examine actual current law if solving a real transaction.

entries.title: Why §1259 targets sales in substance
entries.summary: The realization requirement can encourage financial engineering to cash out unrealized gains without selling the asset outright.
entries.laymanExplanation: People may sell the economic risk of appreciated stock but still keep the stock certificate. §1259 is meant to catch some of those deals.
entries.legalExplanation: The book presents 1990s financial-market structuring as context; the legal takeaway is the statutory constructive-sale test, not the historical narrative itself.

topics.description: Short-against-box, hedges, collars, statutory deemed realization and open questions.

entries.title: Marginal tax rate
entries.summary: The tax percentage imposed on the next additional dollar of taxable income.
entries.laymanExplanation: If you are in the 24% bracket, only dollars in that layer are taxed at 24%; your entire income is not.
entries.legalExplanation: Marginal rate is the highest statutory bracket rate applicable to taxpayer's taxable income, or the tax on a small additional unit of taxable income when other rules do not alter the result. The textbook uses the 2022 single-filer rate schedule as an illustration.
entries.details: Marginal rate is the highest statutory bracket rate applicable to taxpayer's taxable income, or the tax on a small additional unit of taxable income when other rules do not alter the result. The textbook uses the 2022 single-filer rate schedule as an illustration.
entries.source: Bankman/Shaviro/Stark/Scharff, Federal Income Taxation, 19th ed. (2023), syllabus Week 7, Chapter 6 printed pp.323–324.
entries.examTrap: Crossing into a higher marginal bracket does NOT make earlier bracket dollars retroactively subject to the higher rate.

entries.title: Average tax rate
entries.summary: Total tax liability divided by the income measure used.
entries.laymanExplanation: Your average tax rate is what you actually owe divided by your income, which is normally lower than your top bracket in a progressive system.
entries.legalExplanation: The source defines average income-tax rate as total tax owed divided by total income; for its statutory worked example it uses taxable income as denominator and ignores credits. Be explicit about whether denominator is taxable income or a broader measure.
entries.details: The source defines average income-tax rate as total tax owed divided by total income; for its statutory worked example it uses taxable income as denominator and ignores credits. Be explicit about whether denominator is taxable income or a broader measure.

entries.title: Progressive, proportional, and regressive rate structures
entries.summary: Progressive average rates increase with income; proportional remain constant; regressive decline.
entries.laymanExplanation: Progressive means richer taxpayers pay a bigger share, not just a bigger dollar amount.
entries.legalExplanation: The classification is about average tax rates across income levels, rather than whether total nominal tax increases. The U.S. individual income tax uses layered marginal brackets and credits to create progressivity.
entries.details: The classification is about average tax rates across income levels, rather than whether total nominal tax increases. The U.S. individual income tax uses layered marginal brackets and credits to create progressivity.

entries.title: Progressive brackets are applied in layers
entries.summary: Each marginal percentage applies only to taxable income within its bracket.
entries.laymanExplanation: A raise that crosses into the next bracket increases tax on the extra dollars, not all your earlier wages.
entries.legalExplanation: Under the 2022 single-filer schedule reproduced in the source, taxable income is divided into the 10%, 12%, 22%, 24%, 32%, 35%, and 37% bands with threshold boundaries $10,275; $41,775; $89,075; $170,050; $215,950; $539,900. These are historic 2022 amounts, not current 2026 thresholds.

entries.title: Taxable income → rates → credits = amount owed
entries.summary: Calculate taxable income under §63, apply rate schedule, then subtract applicable tax credits.
entries.laymanExplanation: First figure out the money subject to tax, next calculate bracket tax, then subtract credits.
entries.legalExplanation: The chapter separates defining the tax base (taxable income as §63 defines it) from choosing the rate schedule and accounting for credits. A refundable credit may reduce taxes below zero, creating a payment. This is the course's high-level computation order.

entries.title: Tax credit, including refundable credit
entries.summary: Credit reduces tax liability directly; a refundable credit may create a refund beyond tax paid.
entries.laymanExplanation: A $500 credit cuts tax by $500, while a $500 deduction reduces taxable income only.
entries.legalExplanation: The chapter highlights the EITC as a refundable wage subsidy. CTC treatment has varied historically, with temporary 2021 policy changes. Detailed EITC/CTC rules appear later in Chapter 6 beyond this week's assigned pp.323–340; only introductory framing is imported.

entries.title: Tax unit and filing status
entries.summary: The taxpayer or household treated as the unit for reporting income and using a rate schedule.
entries.laymanExplanation: Being single, married filing jointly, married separately, or head of household changes the brackets and tax computation.
entries.legalExplanation: The introduction identifies single, married filing jointly (MFJ), married filing separately (MFS), and head of household (HOH). State community-property treatment interacts with federal income attribution. The chapter's detailed tax-unit and filing-status section is later and not assigned in this batch.

entries.title: Income splitting / assignment of income
entries.summary: Moving income to another person to use that person's lower marginal tax rates.
entries.laymanExplanation: If one family member has a much lower bracket, it may look attractive to give them your earnings so less total tax is owed.
entries.legalExplanation: Assignment doctrines determine whether the attempted income shift is respected. If not, the original earner/owner remains taxable even if the recipient receives the cash as a gift. The chapter uses this to explain the tension between progressive brackets and control over income.

entries.title: 2022 single-filer rate table — study reference
entries.summary: Seven historical marginal brackets allow practice in calculating tax for any supplied taxable income.
entries.laymanExplanation: The lower portions are taxed at lower percentages before the higher percentage begins.

entries.title: Why progressive rates encourage shifting
entries.summary: A large bracket spread makes artificial splitting attractive, especially among people sharing economic resources.
entries.laymanExplanation: If two people share a household, having some income taxed from the bottom of a second rate ladder can reduce tax.
entries.legalExplanation: The book notes 1940's 4.4% to 81.1% marginal rate spread (76.7 percentage points) to explain historic incentives. This is historical tax policy, not an independent rule.

topics.title: Chapter 6 — Rate Structure & Assignment Roadmap
topics.description: How brackets and credits determine liability, and why progressivity creates incentives to shift income.
topics.assignmentSource: Rothenberg Fall 2026 Tax syllabus: Week 7, printed textbook Chapter 6 pp.323–340 only.

entries.title: Income from services taxed to the person who earns it
entries.summary: A taxpayer generally cannot redirect taxation of compensation for personal services by assigning the paycheck to someone else.
entries.laymanExplanation: If you earned a $100,000 salary, telling your employer to send half to your spouse generally doesn't move half of your income tax to them.
entries.legalExplanation: Lucas v. Earl construed the predecessor to §61(a)(1) to tax wages and fees to the individual who performed the services, despite an anticipatory assignment valid under state law. Assignment may be a gift to the recipient but not a transfer of the tax burden.
entries.details: Lucas v. Earl construed the predecessor to §61(a)(1) to tax wages and fees to the individual who performed the services, despite an anticipatory assignment valid under state law. Assignment may be a gift to the recipient but not a transfer of the tax burden.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), reproduced Week 7 textbook pp. 326–328
entries.elements: First identify who performed and had the contract for services; next identify whether the arrangement transferred a legitimate ownership interest in a separate business or merely allocated personal earnings; assess statutory partnership/other entity rules separately.
entries.examTrap: A contractual arrangement made before the federal income tax existed did not override the federal rule.

entries.title: Anticipatory assignment of income
entries.summary: An agreement to divert expected future earnings before they are paid or sometimes before they are earned.
entries.laymanExplanation: Even signing the agreement years earlier won't necessarily prevent your earnings from being taxed to you.
entries.legalExplanation: Lucas v. Earl involved a 1901 spousal agreement giving each spouse joint ownership of the other's earnings upon receipt. Supreme Court refused to permit that contract to divert the statutory tax liability away from the person performing services.
entries.details: Lucas v. Earl involved a 1901 spousal agreement giving each spouse joint ownership of the other's earnings upon receipt. Supreme Court refused to permit that contract to divert the statutory tax liability away from the person performing services.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), reproduced Week 7 textbook pp. 326–328

entries.title: Fruit-and-tree metaphor
entries.summary: The fruits (earnings) generally are taxable to the tree (person or asset) producing them; analogy has limits.
entries.laymanExplanation: The money follows the person who earned it, not who gets handed the paycheck.
entries.legalExplanation: Justice Holmes used the metaphor in Lucas v. Earl. The notes caution that true partnership income can be allocated among partners under partnership law even when one performed more services, so the metaphor is shorthand, not an independent legal test.
entries.details: Justice Holmes used the metaphor in Lucas v. Earl. The notes caution that true partnership income can be allocated among partners under partnership law even when one performed more services, so the metaphor is shorthand, not an independent legal test.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), reproduced Week 7 textbook pp. 327–328
entries.examTrap: Do not apply the fruit/tree phrase mechanically to genuine partnerships, property transfers, or statutory ownership.

entries.title: Services for charity versus redirected service fees
entries.summary: Direct unpaid services to a charity ordinarily are not compensation; services for a client with the fee redirected to charity ordinarily remain taxpayer income.
entries.laymanExplanation: Volunteering directly at a charity isn't taxable wages; asking your regular paying client to send your $500 fee to a charity is different.
entries.legalExplanation: Reg. §1.61-2(c) distinguishes services rendered directly to charity from services to third persons compensated through payment to charity. A lawyer who directs their client's fee to charity ordinarily includes income, then may claim a §170 deduction subject to limits.
entries.details: Reg. §1.61-2(c) distinguishes services rendered directly to charity from services to third persons compensated through payment to charity. A lawyer who directs their client's fee to charity ordinarily includes income, then may claim a §170 deduction subject to limits.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), reproduced Week 7 textbook pp. 328–329
entries.examTrap: Giving away compensation and never earning compensation are different tax events.

entries.title: Community property versus separate property
entries.summary: Community-property law can give spouses present ownership of income and assets acquired during marriage; separate-property law generally does not.
entries.laymanExplanation: In some states each spouse already owns half of community income as it arises, rather than receiving a later gift of wages.
entries.legalExplanation: The text distinguishes true vested state-law ownership in community marital property from private contractual reallocation of a single earner's compensation. Income from gifts/inheritances is often separately classified under community-property law.
entries.details: The text distinguishes true vested state-law ownership in community marital property from private contractual reallocation of a single earner's compensation. Income from gifts/inheritances is often separately classified under community-property law.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), reproduced Week 7 textbook pp. 329–332

entries.title: Poe v. Seaborn — state-law vested community ownership
entries.summary: Where state law gives each spouse present vested equal ownership of community income, each is taxable on their ownership share under the statute addressed.
entries.laymanExplanation: Washington law already gave Mrs. Seaborn half of community wages and investments, so each spouse reported half.
entries.legalExplanation: The Supreme Court interpreted the then-current federal income-tax provisions alongside Washington law: each spouse had a present vested one-half interest in community income from its acquisition, even though husband managed property. Ownership and agency must be distinguished.
entries.details: The Supreme Court interpreted the then-current federal income-tax provisions alongside Washington law: each spouse had a present vested one-half interest in community income from its acquisition, even though husband managed property. Ownership and agency must be distinguished.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), reproduced Week 7 textbook pp. 329–331
entries.examTrap: Seaborn concerns genuine existing community ownership under law, not an anticipatory private contract like Lucas v. Earl.

entries.title: 1948 congressional response — joint return
entries.summary: Congress introduced joint returns to extend income-splitting rate advantages to married couples in different states.
entries.laymanExplanation: Before Congress acted, certain community-property couples could pay less tax than similar married couples in other states.
entries.legalExplanation: The casebook explains that Congress adopted a married joint-return structure in 1948 responding to the advantage under Poe v. Seaborn. Today marriage-based tax status/rates are statutory, so the historical incentive and filing-law comparisons must be distinguished from current bracket calculations.
entries.details: The casebook explains that Congress adopted a married joint-return structure in 1948 responding to the advantage under Poe v. Seaborn. Today marriage-based tax status/rates are statutory, so the historical incentive and filing-law comparisons must be distinguished from current bracket calculations.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), reproduced Week 7 textbook pp. 331–332
entries.examTrap: The 1948 history does not mean today's joint return universally equals exactly twice the tax on half of income across every income range and tax year.

entries.title: Vested ownership versus management authority
entries.summary: Having broad control over property as a spouse's agent does not necessarily mean the manager is its sole owner.
entries.laymanExplanation: One spouse may manage the bank account without being the only person who owns its funds.
entries.legalExplanation: Seaborn concluded the husband's sweeping Washington statutory powers of control did not negate his wife's vested co-ownership; power of management is not a substitute for ownership.
entries.details: Seaborn concluded the husband's sweeping Washington statutory powers of control did not negate his wife's vested co-ownership; power of management is not a substitute for ownership.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), reproduced Week 7 textbook pp. 330–331

entries.title: Genuine partnership income attribution differs from wage assignment
entries.summary: Statutory partnership allocations may distribute taxable income among real partners regardless of which partner performed more work.
entries.laymanExplanation: Two lawyers owning an actual partnership aren't necessarily taxed strictly in proportion to each person's billable hours.
entries.legalExplanation: The notes distinguish Lucas v. Earl from a legitimate partnership, where the agreement creates actual ownership/partnership distributive shares governed by partnership law. Whether a purported partnership is genuine still matters.
entries.details: The notes distinguish Lucas v. Earl from a legitimate partnership, where the agreement creates actual ownership/partnership distributive shares governed by partnership law. Whether a purported partnership is genuine still matters.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), reproduced Week 7 textbook pp. 327–328

entries.title: Lucas v. Earl
entries.summary: No. The Supreme Court reversed the court of appeals and held Earl taxable on the entire salary and fees from services he personally earned.
entries.laymanExplanation: A husband and wife signed a contract splitting everything, including his future lawyer's salary. The Court said the husband's earnings were still his taxable income.
entries.legalExplanation: Income derived from personal services is generally taxable to the person who earns it, even if that person arranged for payment or ownership to vest in another.
entries.details: Reproduced Supreme Court opinion in the assigned textbook.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), reproduced Week 7 textbook pp. 326–327
entries.facts: Attorney Guy Earl and his wife made a 1901 contract declaring all property and future earnings, including salary and legal fees, jointly owned from the moment received. Earl performed services earning compensation in 1920–1921; he attempted to report only half because of this contract. State-law validity was assumed.
entries.issue: Does a valid preexisting spousal assignment of future earnings require that only half the compensation for Earl's services be taxed to Earl?
entries.holding: No. The Supreme Court reversed the court of appeals and held Earl taxable on the entire salary and fees from services he personally earned.
entries.reasoning: The federal tax statute attributed income from personal services to their earner. A private anticipatory agreement, however artfully devised, could not change which person created the right to compensation; the Court rejected formal instantaneous vesting theories and emphasized income's source.
entries.rule: Income derived from personal services is generally taxable to the person who earns it, even if that person arranged for payment or ownership to vest in another.
entries.exam: Identify service provider, contract, diversion of payment, and whether a true entity/property ownership interest rather than pure personal fee was transferred.
entries.examApplication: Identify service provider, contract, diversion of payment, and whether a true entity/property ownership interest rather than pure personal fee was transferred.
entries.examTrap: Do not treat community ownership by state law in Poe v. Seaborn as the same as Earl's voluntary contract.

entries.title: Poe v. Seaborn
entries.summary: No. The Supreme Court affirmed that each spouse could report and be taxed on one-half of total community income under the controlling state-law ownership regime.
entries.laymanExplanation: Unlike Earl's private agreement, Washington law automatically gave both spouses half of the community income. The Court taxed them based on that ownership.
entries.legalExplanation: Where state law genuinely vests each spouse with an undivided half of community property/income from the outset, federal income attribution generally respects the vested ownership share for the historical law analyzed.
entries.details: Reproduced Supreme Court opinion in the assigned textbook.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), reproduced Week 7 textbook pp. 329–331
entries.facts: The Seaborns lived in Washington, where the state's community property regime gave each spouse a current vested one-half ownership interest in all community assets and earnings. They each reported half of the community's wages, interest, dividends and property-sale proceeds. IRS sought to tax the husband on all the income, citing his broad management powers.
entries.issue: Under the federal taxing statute and Washington law, should the husband be taxed on all community income despite the wife's vested one-half property right?
entries.holding: No. The Supreme Court affirmed that each spouse could report and be taxed on one-half of total community income under the controlling state-law ownership regime.
entries.reasoning: Washington law vested present equal ownership in both spouses when community income arose. The husband's broad agency and management rights did not erase the wife's real, enforceable beneficial ownership. Unlike Earl, no anticipatory assignment from the husband's earnings occurred: the income belonged to both from acquisition.
entries.rule: Where state law genuinely vests each spouse with an undivided half of community property/income from the outset, federal income attribution generally respects the vested ownership share for the historical law analyzed.
entries.exam: Compare present legal ownership and management; contrast voluntary assignment of services under Earl and explain Congress's subsequent joint-return response.
entries.examApplication: Compare present legal ownership and management; contrast voluntary assignment of services under Earl and explain Congress's subsequent joint-return response.
entries.examTrap: This is not an unlimited right to split wages by private agreement; modern filing-status rates and community-property reporting must be considered separately.

topics.title: A. Assignment of Income — Services and Spouses
topics.description: Earned income, Lucas v. Earl, state community-property ownership, Poe v. Seaborn and the legislative response.
topics.assignmentSource: Rothenberg Fall 2026 Tax syllabus: Week 7, printed textbook Chapter 6 pp.323–340 only.

entries.title: Income from property follows ownership of the income-producing property
entries.summary: Future income from property generally is taxable to whoever actually owns the property generating it; giving away only the income generally leaves tax with the owner.
entries.laymanExplanation: Give your nephew the rental building: future rent usually becomes his income. Keep the building but hand him the rent checks: rent generally remains your income.
entries.legalExplanation: The reading contrasts complete transfer of the income-producing source with mere disposition of the receipts. Blair respected a genuine transfer of a life beneficiary's equitable trust interest; Horst taxed donor of detached bond coupons who retained the underlying bond.
entries.details: The reading contrasts complete transfer of the income-producing source with mere disposition of the receipts. Blair respected a genuine transfer of a life beneficiary's equitable trust interest; Horst taxed donor of detached bond coupons who retained the underlying bond.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), syllabus Week 7 reproduced Chapter 6 pp.332–338
entries.sourceRole: Assigned textbook pages, not subsequent unassigned portions
entries.examTrap: Always ask WHAT was transferred—underlying property or only an entitlement to receipts?

entries.title: Carved-out income interest
entries.summary: A partial claim to future income is severed from retained underlying income-producing property.
entries.laymanExplanation: You keep the bond but give away just the interest coupons; that's not the same as giving the bond away.
entries.legalExplanation: The text describes bond interest coupons separated for a short period from full ownership as a 'carved out' interest, illustrated by Horst. This contrasts a transfer of the income-producing property itself or a complete qualifying equitable ownership interest.

entries.title: Equitable life interest in trust corpus
entries.summary: A life beneficiary owns an enforceable beneficial interest in trust property during life, potentially transferable under governing state law.
entries.laymanExplanation: You don't own the trust assets outright, but your right to their income for life can itself be a property interest.
entries.legalExplanation: Blair's beneficiary assigned undivided slices of his entire life-income interest without reservation; under relevant state law the donees became beneficiaries and owned an interest in trust property for the duration.

entries.title: Blair — complete transfer of beneficial trust interest shifts future tax
entries.summary: A valid unconditional transfer of equitable ownership in income-producing trust property can cause subsequent income to be taxed to the new owners.
entries.laymanExplanation: If you permanently give your child half of your lifetime right to trust income, your child may be taxed on that share instead of you.
entries.legalExplanation: Blair distinguished service-fee assignments from present, alienable equitable property rights. Trust beneficiaries transferred specified parts of their ownership interest, not a mere order to pay previously accrued income; the assignees were thereafter entitled to trust income.

entries.title: Horst — gifted coupons do not transfer the underlying income source
entries.summary: A bond owner who gives away detached interest coupons while retaining the bond remains taxable on interest collected by donee.
entries.laymanExplanation: Giving your son this year's bond coupons doesn't make this year's interest tax-free to you when you keep the bond.
entries.legalExplanation: The Supreme Court treated control of the right to interest as economic enjoyment of interest despite directing collection to son. Cash-method donor was taxed when coupons paid; gifting the stream without transferring source does not shift federal attribution. The opinion distinguishes Blair as transfer of equitable ownership.

entries.title: IRC §1286 — allocation of basis on stripped bonds and coupons
entries.summary: Taxpayers stripping bond interest must allocate basis between the separated interests rather than claim all basis against the stripped principal.
entries.laymanExplanation: You can't buy a $1,000 bond, keep its valuable coupons, sell only the stripped bond for $700, and pretend you've lost $300.
entries.legalExplanation: The notes explain interest-stripping abuses created by assigning full bond basis to the stripped principal while retaining valuable coupons. Congress added §1286 to apportion adjusted basis between stripped coupons and residual bond, and to address original issue discount consequences.

entries.title: Accrual-method explanation of Horst
entries.summary: Interest is economically earned as time passes; gifting the last coupon only changes who collects, not who earned pre-gift income.
entries.laymanExplanation: The father already earned most of the interest while holding the bond; gifting the coupon just before payment shouldn't erase that.
entries.legalExplanation: The textbook criticizes Horst's fruit-and-tree metaphor: under an accrual method prior earned interest would already have been reported. Its analysis emphasizes interest compensation for lending over time and explains why the donor should be taxed even without personally collecting cash.

entries.title: Blair v. Commissioner
entries.summary: No. The Supreme Court held the children, not Blair, taxable on income from the validly transferred beneficial interests.
entries.laymanExplanation: Blair gave his children actual ownership shares of his lifetime trust-income right, so they—not he—were taxed on income from those interests.
entries.legalExplanation: A genuine present assignment of a substantial interest in income-producing trust property can shift taxation of later income to its transferee.
entries.details: Opinion reproduced in the syllabus-assigned pages.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), syllabus Week 7 reproduced Chapter 6 pp.333–335
entries.sourceRole: Assigned textbook pages, not subsequent unassigned portions
entries.facts: A father created a trust giving his son Blair the income of the trust for life. Blair made formal assignments to his children of specified annual amounts out of his life-income interest, without retaining the assigned rights. Trustees recognized the assignments and paid the children directly. The transfer was valid under governing law.
entries.issue: Was Blair still taxable on trust income allocated to children by valid assignment of part of his equitable beneficial ownership?
entries.holding: No. The Supreme Court held the children, not Blair, taxable on income from the validly transferred beneficial interests.
entries.reasoning: Blair owned a transferable equitable property interest in the trust corpus, including enforcement rights. The children became owners of portions of that interest, not merely agents receiving checks for Blair. This was not assignment of personal-service compensation or an attempt to shift income from property still owned by donor.
entries.rule: A genuine present assignment of a substantial interest in income-producing trust property can shift taxation of later income to its transferee.
entries.exam: Look for irrevocability, full duration, property rights and whether donor retains income source. Contrast Horst's isolated coupon gifts.
entries.examApplication: Look for irrevocability, full duration, property rights and whether donor retains income source. Contrast Horst's isolated coupon gifts.
entries.examTrap: A bare instruction to a trustee to send payments, without actual property-interest transfer, is not enough under Blair.

entries.title: Helvering v. Horst
entries.summary: No. The Supreme Court reversed and held the father taxable on the interest paid to the son.
entries.laymanExplanation: The dad kept the bond but gave his son this year's interest coupons. The Court said the interest was still the dad's taxable income.
entries.legalExplanation: An owner who retains the income-producing asset and merely directs/assigns its income to another may remain taxable on the income when it is paid.
entries.details: Opinion reproduced in the syllabus-assigned pages.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), syllabus Week 7 reproduced Chapter 6 pp.335–338
entries.sourceRole: Assigned textbook pages, not subsequent unassigned portions
entries.facts: The owner of negotiable bonds detached upcoming interest coupons shortly before they matured and gave them to his son, while retaining ownership of the bonds. The son collected the coupons when paid that year. The donor was on the cash-receipts method and did not physically receive the interest.
entries.issue: May a bond owner avoid tax on interest by giving his son coupons before payment while retaining ownership of the principal bond?
entries.holding: No. The Supreme Court reversed and held the father taxable on the interest paid to the son.
entries.reasoning: The father controlled the income-producing investment and exercised his right to enjoy its return by directing interest to his son, satisfying a personal objective. Economic enjoyment of accrued income need not be physical receipt. Blair was different because that case transferred the income-producing beneficial property itself.
entries.rule: An owner who retains the income-producing asset and merely directs/assigns its income to another may remain taxable on the income when it is paid.
entries.exam: Identify retained property source, gift of income only, cash versus accrual timing; distinguish bona fide underlying property transfer in Blair.
entries.examApplication: Identify retained property source, gift of income only, cash versus accrual timing; distinguish bona fide underlying property transfer in Blair.
entries.examTrap: No physical receipt is required; distinguish legitimate gift of underlying bond from assignment of its short-term interest coupons.
